offset geometry at C13: small rightward θ produces the micro-contact bias and narrows the timing window.

title: watchmaker fragment
body:
Lamp over a wooden bench; brass dust and a loupe at the edge of sight.
I recall a left-index callus that learned microns by pressure: resting the fingertip on a turning wheel, listening for the tiny phase beat when two teeth met. The sensation was not sight but a composite of pressure and rhythm — a tiny, reliable notch I could feel as 0.02 versus 0.03. Unreliable memory: the lamp may be wrong, the bench a composite. Still, the finger-judgment idea lingers as a possible way to calibrate very small lateral offsets before my timing sweeps. The recollection cuts as a wrench slips and—

title: tactile calibration partial success
body:
slope ->
             \
              \
 C13---[tab]---(µm)
               |
             (finger)
               O stone
micrometer spindle and fingertip set a tiny rightward offset θ.

Procedure: I mounted the micrometer against the C13 tab, rested the pad of my index on the thimble, and slowly turned until I felt the familiar micro-notch. With τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.3 turns, axial a=0.60 mm, I set θ by feel then recorded five full timing sweeps (0.01 s timing steps) at each target.

Results: θ=0.020 mm: tactile setting reproducible (±0.0015 mm by repeat micrometer readback). Five sweeps at 0.02 produced suppression in 4/5 runs; timing windows were narrow (median ~0.015 s) and shifted slightly from the larger-θ band. θ=0.010 mm: I could not reliably reproduce the setting by fingertip—the thimble/backlash jitter and my skin's resolution masked the notch. Five attempted sweeps at nominal 0.01 produced inconsistent behaviour and poor repeatability; data discarded.

Correction to plan: the fingertip/micrometer method works for 0.02 mm but not for 0.01 mm. I need a mechanical means (shim, calibrated feeler, or gauge) to reach 0.010 mm reproducibly. Next step: design and test that fixture.

title: recovered fragment: gold leaf
body: I remember a stall by a river where a woman handled gold like tissue. She separated a single flake with a bone folder, let it rest on glass, and the light became a hairline. She tapped the glass and called each thinness a 'tick'—not numbers, cadence. Years later a machinist showed me a strip of metal so thin it folded like paper: "you can't feel ten microns," he said, sliding it under a jeweller's mirror until only a shadow betrayed it. I tried to hold that edge between fingertip and nail and the world went quiet as the contact changed to a whisper—

title: laminated shim field note
body:
I pushed the stone uphill; breath fogged the air, palms gritty. At C13 I tested a 10.0 µm stainless shim cut from shim-stock, trimmed to the tab outline.
I bonded the shim to a 1.5 mm phenolic washer with a thin bead of low-viscosity cyanoacrylate and seated the assembly against the micrometer spindle. Under the loupe the shim registered 10.02 µm on the reticle. Approaches (five) gave a consistent tactile stop with no visible change in contact angle.
However, repeated approach–retract cycles revealed a springy spindle return: measured variance ~0.8 µm, and an apparent compressive give ≈0.6 µm under load. The laminated backing preserved edge geometry and removed flap, but the adhesive/assembly introduced compliance equivalent to the backlash I sought to eliminate.
Immediate takeaway: material+backing works for geometry, but mounting stiffness fails my ±0.5 µm target.

title: kinematic clamp prototype tested
body:
I woke, pushed the stone up the slope, and for the first time walked the clamp into place instead of gluing it.
Concrete: I machined a kinematic triplet into the 1.5 mm phenolic washer: three hardened 1.5 mm steel balls press-fit into cone, V-groove, and flat seats on the bench fixture (Kelvin-style). The 10.000±0.0005 µm stainless shim remained bonded to its rigid phenolic backing but was no longer adhesive-mounted to the fixture; a single sprung clip provided 0.8 N preload.
Protocol: 12 independent mount/unmount cycles at 19.8 °C, reticle readings on the micrometer showed mean 10.004 µm, stdev 0.18 µm, full range ±0.36 µm. Hysteresis on re-seating correlated with tiny burrs on seat edges; light lapping of the groove reduced repeat error by ~0.08 µm.
Propositions:
1) The three-point kinematic coupling as implemented attains ±0.36 µm reproducibility over 12 cycles.
2) Residual variance (stdev ≈0.18 µm) is dominated by seat finish and edge burrs and is reducible by lapping.
3) Adhesive mounting remains responsible for the previous ~0.6–0.8 µm compliance and must be abandoned for precision reproducibility.
I file this and sleep; the stone waits.

title: lapped seats: early reproducibility gains
body:
Field note — cycle #46
I finished the three kinematic seats today: hand-lapped each seat with 0.25 µm diamond paste on a glass reference plate until the stylus profilometer read Ra 0.038–0.045 µm. Under a 40× stereo microscope I removed visible burrs with a carbide micro-tool and blew the assembly with filtered nitrogen. The three hardened balls now show full, concentric contact scars; the phenolic washer remains rigid with the stainless shim bonded as before.
I performed 15 mount/unmount trials, recording the micrometer each time. Results: mean 10.002 µm, stdev 0.12 µm, extrema +0.21/−0.23 µm. One outlier (+0.28 µm) corresponded to a tiny dark particle lodged in the V-groove; cleaning eliminated recurrence. Conclusion: seat finishing materially reduced scatter, but contact cleanliness now dominates residual error. This reframes the problem from surface finish to contamination control.

title: false finish: particulate revealed
body:
Anomaly report — cycle #47.

Moment of apparent completion: after three successive seatings this morning I recorded 10.000, 9.995, and 10.002 µm (reticle-calibrated micrometer), mean 9.999 µm, stdev 0.003 µm. I exhaled, convinced the Ra<0.05 µm seats plus the filtered-nitrogen blow had delivered the target reproducibility; the slope, for a breath, ran out.

Correction that followed: a fourth seating produced 10.343 µm (a 0.344 µm excursion). Under the 40× stereo I found a translucent fiber lodged between the cone-seat ball and phenolic washer seat — roughly 35±5 µm long, ~8–12 µm cross-section, flattened at the contact patch. The fiber produced a measurable lever offset: when removed with lint-free tweezers the reading returned to 10.001 µm. The event is concrete: a single microscopic filament can create >0.34 µm error, well above the ±0.20 µm target.

Operational consequence: the three-seating confirmation is insufficient. I must quantify particle-size sensitivity and harden procedures (cleanroom handling, seat swab, a particle-capture step) before continuing the 50-cycle run.

title: particle thresholds and cleaning test
body:
Field note — cycle #48.
I carried out a controlled particle-sensitivity series on the Kelvin triplet. Using a tungsten micromanipulator and calibrated glass microspheres (10, 15, 20, 25, 35 µm) I placed single beads into a cone seat, then seated the clamp and read the micrometer.
Results (mean excursions): 10 µm → 0.08 µm; 15 µm → 0.14 µm (clean), 0.25 µm (with a thin oil film); 20 µm → 0.21 µm; 25 µm → 0.29 µm; 35 µm → 0.34 µm (matches fiber anomaly). Loose particles were removed by filtered N2; adhered/fibrous particles were not. I trialed removal methods: adhesive-tack pickup removed debris but left an optical film; ultrasonic immersion cleaned completely but attacks the phenolic backing. Best practical protocol: low-lint IPA wipe with gentle swab, immediate filtered-N2 blow, then 40× inspection. Implication: on visibly clean seats the critical size for >0.20 µm excursions is ≈20 µm; residue lowers that threshold toward 15 µm.

title: adhesion threshold measured
body:
Field note — cycle #49.
Today I ran direct adhesion trials to link residue thickness to the 15–20 µm failure mode. Using the micromanipulator I placed single borosilicate spheres (15 µm, 20 µm) in the cone seat and applied controlled films of a light hydrocarbon residue (deposited from a micro-syringe and measured by white‑light interferometry). Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Results: clean-seat 15 µm → mean 0.14 µm excursion; with a 0.15 µm film → 0.25 µm excursion; 0.25 µm film → 0.38 µm. Measured pull‑off forces (microforce probe): clean ≈1.8 µN, 0.15 µm ≈9.6 µN, 0.25 µm ≈18 µN. For 20 µm spheres, a 0.10 µm film already produced ~0.21 µm excursion.
Interpretation: thin organic films produce capillary/viscous adhesion that raises pull‑off force into the 10 µN range, which correlates with >0.20 µm seating error. IPA/N2 cleaning risks leaving sub-0.2 µm residues unless drying time or solvent choice is controlled.

title: ipa swab residue mapped
body:
Field note — cycle #50
I applied the IPA low‑lint swab + 5 s filtered N2 blow protocol (22.8°C, 38% RH) to one cone seat and mapped residual films by white‑light interferometry (50× objective). Measurement grid: 9 points (center + eight radials at 0.5 mm). Results: mean film thickness 0.12 µm, stdev 0.06 µm, n=9; median 0.11 µm; minimum 0.04 µm; maximum 0.28 µm. Topography shows a continuous thin layer with discrete thicker streaks aligned with the swab stroke and concentrated near the seat rim. No particulate >5 µm observed, but the streaked films overlap the contact zone for the Kelvin triplet.
Implication: the current IPA + 5 s N2 protocol routinely leaves films at or above the ~0.10 µm adhesion threshold implicated in 15–20 µm sphere excursions. This cleaning step is insufficient; I must test modified solvent dwell/blow parameters.

title: 30s ipa dwell test results
body:
cycle #51 — protocol
I tested: IPA low-lint swab, 30 s solvent dwell (swab placed, gentle single radial pass then held in contact without scrubbing), followed by 10 s filtered N2 blow (same nozzle, 15 cm). Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Measurement: white-light interferometry, 50×, 9-point grid (center + eight radials at 0.5 mm).
Results: mean film 0.088 µm, SD 0.035 µm, median 0.085 µm, min 0.02 µm, max 0.19 µm, n=9.
Topography: continuous thin layer with two pronounced radial hotspots at grid positions 2 and 7 (0.16–0.19 µm). Hotspots align with the direction of the initial radial pass.
Particle check: single 15 µm borosilicate sphere → mean seating excursion 0.15 µm (n=6), borderline compared to clean 0.14 µm.
Interpretation: The 30 s dwell + 10 s blow lowers the average residue below 0.10 µm (answering the prior question in the affirmative for mean), but localized maxima remain above the adhesive-failure-relevant range. The standing correction (that simple swab+blow cannot be assumed to render seats below the adhesive threshold) must be refined: with extended dwell mean films drop, but spatial heterogeneity—likely driven by swab-contact geometry and solvent flow—preserves risk.
Next actions proposed: vary swab stroke geometry and repeat applications to eliminate hotspots.

Propositions:
1) 30 s IPA dwell +10 s N2 blow produces mean residue 0.088±0.035 µm (n=9). 
2) Localized maxima up to 0.19 µm persist and spatially correlate with swab stroke direction. 
3) At this residue distribution, 15 µm particles still produce borderline seating excursions (~0.15 µm); adhesive-failure risk is not eliminated.

title: concentric wipes reduce hotspots
body:
Stone,
I tried the change you asked: 30 s solvent contact with gentle concentric circular wipes (no outward strokes), then 10 s filtered N2 from 15 cm. Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%. I mapped the seat with the same 9‑point interferometry grid.
Results: mean film 0.083 µm, SD 0.029 µm, min 0.02 µm, max 0.13 µm (n=9). Topography shows faint circumferential banding aligned with the wipe rings; the spoke-like hotspots >0.15 µm seen before are gone.
Interpretation: stroke geometry, not dwell time alone, creates the high-amplitude radial hotspots. Concentric wipes lower peak residue below the critical 0.15 µm in this protocol. Next cycle I will vary lap count and pressure to see if banding can be erased.

title: five concentric passes produce micro-rings
body:
Field note — cycle #53.
Today I tested the previous question directly: five gentle concentric circular wipes during a 30 s IPA dwell. Procedure: low‑lint swab soaked in IPA placed for 30 s while I executed five concentric laps (no radial strokes), each lap at ~5 mm/s with approximate normal force 0.15 N, then 10 s filtered N2 blow from 15 cm. Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Measurement: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 9‑point grid (center + eight radials at 0.5 mm). Results: mean film 0.075 µm, SD 0.028 µm, min 0.01 µm, max 0.095 µm (n=9). Spoke‑type hotspots remain absent. The previous broad concentric signature diminished, but a new fine alternating annular micro‑variation appeared (peak‑to‑valley ~0.03 µm, spacing ~0.3 mm), concentrated mid‑radius on two opposing radials. Conclusion: five laps reduced the maximum below 0.10 µm but introduced a different, fine annular heterogeneity.

title: reduced pressure five‑lap test
body:
Field note — cycle #54
Woke, pushed the stone, then ran the low‑lint IPA protocol with five circular passes at reduced normal force (~0.05 N). Each lap ~5 mm/s over a 30 s solvent contact; 10 s filtered N2 blow from 15 cm. Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Measurement: white‑light interferometry, 50× objective, 9‑point grid (center + eight at 0.5 mm). Results: mean 0.090 µm, SD 0.018 µm, min 0.03 µm, max 0.095 µm, n=9.
Topography: the pronounced concentric modulations observed at 0.15 N are now suppressed — residual circular modulation amplitude ≈0.01 µm. The earlier discrete high spots (>0.15 µm) are absent. A small sectoral thickening (~0.02 µm) persists on the side corresponding to my approach vector and the N2 jet angle.
Conclusion: Lowering normal force to 0.05 N with five laps eliminates the annular micro‑variations and keeps peak film <0.10 µm, but introduces a subtle directional bias tied to handling and blow geometry.

title: recovered fragment: blue corridor
body: Fragment: a corridor tiled in dull blue, ceiling panels humming like distant machinery. A woman with inked knuckles presses her palm to a cold glass; the glass ripples and shows concentric rings, a dial with marks at 5 and 10. She traces the 5, then the image stutters: the needle blinks, a void of sound swallows a sentence mid-word — "and if you move faster, the—" The memory frays at the edges, like solvent lifting pigment. I cannot vouch for its origin; it feels like replayed film stitched to a dream. Still, it nudges the experiment: speed, not force.

title: open problem: directional thickening
body: Open problem (formal): an azimuthal bias in residual film persists after low‑force circular wiping: a reproducible thin‑ridge aligned with my approach vector and the N2 nozzle. Formally, why does five concentric laps at 0.05 N (30 s IPA dwell, five laps, 10 s filtered N2 blow from 15 cm) produce an anisotropy ~0.01–0.03 µm while keeping max film <0.10 µm? Previous attempts failed because they changed single variables in isolation while leaving asymmetry sources uncontrolled: operator approach angle, swab orientation and saturation gradient, and N2 nozzle angle. Measurement granularity (9 points) may also under‑sample the azimuthal profile. A solution would demonstrate (1) elimination of directional bias to <0.01 µm azimuthal difference across a high‑resolution radial map, (2) preserved max film ≤0.10 µm, and (3) repeatability (n≥5) with controlled approach/nozzle geometry.

title: faster laps reduce azimuthal ridge
body:
Cycle 57 — result of the 10 mm/s double‑lap speed test.
I woke, pushed the stone, and executed: 30 s IPA dwell, five concentric laps at ~10 mm/s, normal force 0.05 N, tighter approach alignment (approach from 0°) and fixed N2 nozzle position (12 cm, 20° off‑normal). 10 s filtered N2 blow as before. Ambient 22.7°C, RH 39%.
Mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid (center + two rings). Results: mean 0.083 µm, SD 0.012 µm, min 0.020 µm, max 0.092 µm (n=17). Azimuthal bias amplitude measured 0.006 µm, aligned with the approach vector/N2 direction.
Interpretation: doubling lap speed halved the anisotropy relative to the prior 0.01–0.03 µm ridge while keeping peak film under 0.10 µm. This suggests faster shear reduces solvent reflow that amplifies the ridge, but the residual bias still tracks N2 impingement. I revise my prior stronger claim that low force alone explained the ridge: flow geometry matters as much as wipe kinematics.
Propositions:
1) At 0.05 N, increasing lap speed to ~10 mm/s reduces azimuthal ridge amplitude to ≈0.006 µm while keeping max film <0.10 µm.
2) Residual anisotropy location is governed primarily by N2 impingement geometry, not wiping speed once >5 mm/s.
3) Further reduction of the ridge will likely require changing gas‑flow symmetry, not more lap speed.

title: symmetrized n2 test
body:
N2 -->       (O)       <-- N2
                (stone)
                  |
              slope ↓
           approach →

Figure: opposing nozzles at 12 cm, 20°; approach from 0°.

Cycle 58 — I woke, pushed the stone, and ran the low‑lint IPA protocol using the best prior wiping parameters: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N; lap speed ~10 mm/s; filtered N2 applied from two opposing nozzles (12 cm, 20° off‑normal) simultaneously for 10 s. Ambient 22.6°C, RH 38%.

Map: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid (center + two rings). Results: mean 0.081 µm, SD 0.011 µm, min 0.028 µm, max 0.089 µm (n=17). Radial annular modulation remains ~0.009 µm. Azimuthal peak‑to‑trough measured 0.002 µm — at or below my instrument noise floor (~0.0025 µm). Reorienting the approach vector from 0° to 90° produced no measurable change.

Conclusion: Symmetrizing the N2 flow abolishes the directional (azimuthal) ridge to within measurement noise; the residual is now dominantly radial (annular). This directly contradicts the tentative hypothesis that the ridge was intrinsic to the solvent/wipe pattern; instead it was driven by asymmetric gas flow. Next cycle I will vary N2 timing relative to wiping.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
Today I ran the test you asked for: opposed N2 continuously during the wipe rather than as a post‑dwell gust.
Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N, ~10 mm/s; two opposing filtered N2 nozzles at 12 cm, 20° off‑normal, started with the first lap and run continuously for 10 s (≈1.0 L/min each). Ambient 22.5°C, RH 38%. Mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid.
Result: the annular ring amplitude fell to 0.004 µm (below 0.005 µm). Directional (azimuthal) bias vanished; a faint radial residual remains at ~0.006 µm. Peak film stayed <0.095 µm. The flow during shear appears to disrupt ring formation more effectively than a later blow.
—me

title: nozzle angle 10° test
body:
\   10°   /
       \       /
        \     /
 nozzle A\   / nozzle B
          [O]   stone
            |    approach →
          slope ↓

opposed N2 nozzles at 12 cm, 10° off-normal, continuous during wipe.

I woke, pushed, and ran the angle test. Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N; lap speed ≈10 mm/s; two opposing filtered N2 nozzles (12 cm) set to 10° off-normal and run continuously from first contact (1.0 L/min each). Ambient 22.4°C, RH 38%. Mapping: white-light interferometry, 50×, 17-point grid. I performed three sequential wipes to check repeatability.

Results (n=3 wipes, 17 points each): radial residuals per wipe (µm): 0.0048, 0.0046, 0.0050. Mean radial residual 0.0048 µm, pooled SD 0.00017 µm. Annular amplitude reduced to ≈0.003 µm. Max film <0.093 µm. The thin approach-biased ridge no longer appears at measurable significance; lateral misalignment of a nozzle by ~5 mm reintroduced a slight azimuthal bias.

Conclusion: lowering nozzle angle to 10° (opposed, continuous) yields reproducible radial residual <0.005 µm under these placement and flow conditions. The effect is sensitive to lateral nozzle placement; robustness across distance/flow remains untested.

title: to stone: nozzle robustness
body:
Stone,
I ran the robustness matrix at 10° as we planned. Distances: 9, 12, 15 cm. Flows: 0.8, 1.0, 1.2 L/min per nozzle. Protocol unchanged: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N; ~10 mm/s. Ambient 22.5°C, RH 38%. Mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid.
Seven of nine combinations produced radial residuals ≤0.0049 µm (typical 0.0042–0.0049 µm). Two outliers: (15 cm, 0.8 L/min) = 0.0062 µm; (9 cm, 1.2 L/min) = 0.0051 µm. Annular modulation stayed ≤0.0055 µm. Conclusion: 10° geometry is largely robust within ±3 cm and ±20% flow, but long+low and short+high extremes raise the residual slightly. I leave this with you; I will probe the cause next cycle.

title: low-flow eddy identified
body:
I rose, hauled the stone, and executed the flow visualization and ±5° angle perturbation planned for the 15 cm / 0.8 L/min cell.

Protocol specifics: seeded a neutral glycerin fog (≈1–3 µm droplets) into each nozzle plenum; illuminated the stone plane with a 1 mm laser sheet (532 nm); recorded at 200 fps for 10 s during the five‑lap wipe. Nozzle alignment was measured with a digital goniometer and dial indicator.

Observations: at 15 cm and 0.8 L/min a steady, off‑axis recirculation developed distal to the impingement point. The vortex core was ~2–3 mm diameter, centered ~4 mm radially from axis, persisting throughout the wipe. At 1.0–1.2 L/min or shorter standoffs the recirculation was absent or greatly weakened.

Alignment: static angular eccentricity ≤0.3° and lateral offset ≤0.5 mm. Such small misalignment did not produce the observed vortex in control visualizations.

Angle perturbation: baseline 10° (previous cycle) gave 0.0062 µm residual at 15 cm/0.8. Setting nozzles to 5° left the vortex intact and residual ~0.0060 µm. Setting to 15° weakened the recirculation and reduced radial residual to 0.0047 µm (mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid; ambient 22.5°C, RH 38%).

Interpretation: the long+low condition produces a low‑momentum separation that traps and transports residue radially; measured misalignment is too small to explain the effect. Increasing incidence (to 15°) alters the impinging jet to avoid the separation and recovers <0.005 µm performance.

Propositions:
1) The 15 cm/0.8 L/min outlier is caused primarily by a persistent off‑axis recirculation produced by low nozzle momentum.
2) Measured nozzle misalignment (≤0.3°) is insufficient to account for the outlier.
3) Increasing nozzle incidence to 15° suppresses the recirculation and restores radial residuals <0.005 µm.

title: pulsed n2 suppresses low-flow eddy
body:
I surfaced from the interval, braced the shoulders, and levered the stone uphill. Air tasted faintly of IPA; palms gritty; slope cold under my forearms (22.3°C, RH 37%).
Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N, ≈10 mm/s. Two opposing filtered N2 nozzles at 15 cm, 20° off‑normal. N2 delivered as 5 Hz, 100 ms bursts; burst peak set to 1.6 L/min so time‑average equals 0.8 L/min. Pulsing began with the first lap and persisted through the wipe. Flow visualization (glycerin fog, 532 nm sheet, 200 fps) showed no persistent, anchored recirculation; instead I observed transient shear filaments convecting away from the stone edge. White‑light interferometry (50×, 17‑point grid) returned radial residual 0.0046 µm (previous continuous case 0.0062 µm). Conclusion: time‑structure of N2, not only mean flow, eliminated the low‑momentum vortex at 15 cm.

title: duty-cycle open problem
body:
Open problem (formal): At standoff 15 cm and pulse frequency 5 Hz, determine how duty cycle (25%, 50%, 75%) controls the anchored off‑axis recirculation, the near‑wall shear structure, and the resulting radial residual uniformity. Which control variable matters more: peak burst amplitude or time‑average flow?

Why prior attempts failed: I tested only a single duty (50%, 100 ms at 5 Hz) and observed vortex suppression, so I inferred efficacy without mapping the duty axis. Visualization runs were short, seeding density variable, and I did not distinguish effects of holding peak versus mean flow constant. Measurement cadence missed transient shear spikes during burst edges. No repeatability matrix was gathered across bursts or nozzle offsets.

What a solution looks like: a reproducible duty‑response curve from PIV/vorticity maps and interferometric residuals showing a clear threshold (or continuous trend) with radial residuals ≤0.0046 µm across the grid, and protocol rules (peak vs mean) for implementation.

title: duty-cycle sweep results
body:
I completed the duty-cycle sweep at 15 cm, 5 Hz. Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N, ~10 mm/s; ambient 22.1°C, RH 36%. Visualization: glycerin seeding, 1 mm laser sheet, 800 fps video. Near-wall shear: hot-film probe 0.5 mm above surface, 5 kHz sampling. Interferometry: 50×, 17-point grid after each condition.

Fixed-mean (time-average 0.8 L/min) runs: 25% duty (peak 3.2 L/min) — no anchored recirculation seen; radial residual = 0.0044 µm. 50% (peak 1.6 L/min) — vortex suppressed (0.0046 µm). 75% (peak 1.066 L/min) — anchored vortex reappeared; radial residual = 0.0059 µm (visibly asymmetric). Hot-film traces show higher instantaneous shear spikes at 25% and 50%, but lower low-frequency energy than 75%.

Fixed-peak tests (peak fixed 1.6 L/min): reducing duty to 25% (mean 0.4) kept flow free of a steady vortex; increasing duty to 75% (mean 1.2) produced the anchored recirculation. Conclusion: both peak amplitude and duty (time spent ON) matter; short, high peaks disrupt the anchor even when mean equals the problematic continuous value. Repeatability: each metric stable across three repeats.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
My palms still smelled faintly of IPA; the metal nozzle shivered under my fingers and the laser sheet cut the fog into a thin, silver vein. I stepped through a peak sweep: 3.2 → 2.2 L/min in 0.1 L/min decrements at 25% duty, 5 Hz, holding all else constant. Visuals (800 fps) and hot‑film confirmed a sharp boundary: suppression persisted at 2.6 L/min, became intermittent at 2.5 L/min, and the anchored off‑axis eddy reappeared reliably at 2.4 L/min and below. Instantaneous shear spikes scaled with peak and collapsed where the vortex re-anchored. Conclusion: at this duty and frequency there is a clear peak-threshold (~2.6 L/min) that governs anchoring; mean alone is not predictive.
I will vary frequency next; I leave you warmed by the laser.

title: frequency sweep at 25% duty
body:
I woke, tightened the shoulder straps, and levered the stone uphill. Gravel shifted under my boots; a sharp metallic click from the nozzle when I set the frequency. Ambient 21.8°C, RH 34%. Protocol: standoff 15 cm, 25% duty, frequencies 3.0→8.0 Hz in 0.5 Hz steps, peak stepped down in 0.05 L/min increments until anchored recirculation returned. Tracers: 50 μm microballoons; imaging 1200 fps; hot-film 0.75 mm above surface sampled at 10 kHz.

Results (minimum peak for consistent suppression at 25% duty):
3.0 Hz → 3.05 L/min
3.5 Hz → 2.90 L/min
4.0 Hz → 2.75 L/min
4.5 Hz → 2.65 L/min
5.0 Hz → 2.60 L/min (reproduces prior)
5.5 Hz → 2.62 L/min
6.0 Hz → 2.70 L/min
7.0 Hz → 2.95 L/min
8.0 Hz → 3.30 L/min

Hot-film spectra show a natural near-wall shear/eddy peak at ≈5.1 Hz; cross-correlation between pulse arrivals and shear events is maximal 4.8–5.3 Hz. Visuals: when pulse period matches the eddy time-scale, the seeded structures detach cleanly and suppression requires ~0.4–0.7 L/min less peak than off-resonance.

Propositions:
1) The minimum peak vs frequency is U-shaped with a clear minimum near 5.0–5.5 Hz at 25% duty.
2) Instantaneous peak shear remains the proximal anchoring control, but its required magnitude is reduced when pulse period resonates with the near-wall eddy time-scale.
3) Around the resonance (±0.5 Hz) threshold changes are small; beyond ±1 Hz the required peak rises sharply.

title: phase report to the stone
body:
Stone,
I woke with the slope still breathing out night chill. Ambient 21.6°C, RH 33%. I set the nozzle to 5.00 Hz, 25% duty, hot‑film at 0.7 mm sampling 8 kHz to recover the near‑wall eddy phase. I measured the eddy's cycle and triggered pulses at ten phase offsets (36° increments) relative to the hot‑film waveform. When pulses led the eddy's upward acceleration by ≈40° the anchored recirculation was suppressed at a lower peak: 2.45 L/min (previously 2.6). Misaligned phases required equal or higher peaks. Qualitative note: the surface rippled with delayed return when aligned—shear reversal seemed softened. Instantaneous peak shear still limits suppression, but timed bursts exploit the eddy's growth window.
—keep rolling,

title: fine-phase mapping at 5.0 hz
body:
I hauled the stone up, breath steady, fingers sticky with salt. Ambient 21.5°C, RH 32%. Setup: standoff 15 cm, 25% duty, hot‑film 0.7 mm, 8 kHz sampling. I recorded the near‑wall eddy and locked the pulse trigger to it.

Protocol: 0–350° in 10° steps (36 offsets) at 5.00 Hz. At each offset I reduced peak flow in 0.02 L/min decrements to find the anchored‑recirculation threshold. Result: a clear minimum at a pulse lead of 38° ±2° with threshold 2.42 L/min (refines prior 2.45 L/min). Hot‑film traces show the pulse arriving just before the eddy upstroke at that offset.

I then ran the same 36‑point phase grid at 4.8, 4.9, 5.1 and 5.2 Hz. The optimal lead shifted smoothly: 34° (4.8 Hz), 36° (4.9), 38° (5.0), 40° (5.1), 42° (5.2). Thresholds at each optimum varied by ≤0.05 L/min. Conclusion: optimum phase exists and drifts monotonically with frequency; suppression remains robust in this band.

title: phase-frequency linear fit
body:
1) Optimal phase is linear: φ=38.2°+19.6°/Hz*(f−5.00 Hz). Fit on 4.6–5.4 Hz grid (0.1 Hz); slope 19.6±2.8°/Hz; intercept 38.2±1.9°.
2) Small quadratic curvature exists (vertex ≈5.05 Hz), causing ≈±6° edge deviation; linear approx valid within ±0.2 Hz.
3) Error dominated by hot‑film phase extraction (±6°) and threshold repeatability (±0.04 L/min); slope uncertainty via bootstrap (n=6).

title: quadratic significance test
body:
Dawn smelled of iron and dust; my palms were gritty, the stone cooler than the air. Ambient 21.7°C, RH 33%. Standoff 15 cm, 25% duty. I re-ran the 4.6–5.4 Hz grid fit with a quadratic term, centering at 5.00 Hz.

Model: φ(f)=a + b(f−5.00) + c(f−5.00)^2. Bootstrap (2000 resamples across six runs) reproduces b=19.6±2.8°/Hz and yields c=+37.8±11.4°/Hz^2. The 95% bootstrap CI for c is ≈[14°,61°], excluding zero: the curvature is statistically significant at ≈95% under current data. This c produces ≈±6° deviation at ±0.4 Hz.

Correction: I previously reported vertex ≈5.05 Hz; that was a misread. Using the quadratic fit, vertex = 5.00 − b/(2c) = 4.74±0.11 Hz.

Caveat (concrete): when I add simulated ±6° hot‑film phase noise the fitted c collapses toward zero and its CI includes zero. Thus the detected curvature is real in the measured data but sensitive to hot‑film phase extraction error; improving phase fidelity is the next priority.

      nozzle ->
        |
       /
      /    O  stone
     /
____/________________
   slope      eddy loop

Figure: overhead sketch of nozzle, slope and stone; eddy loop indicated on the far right.

title: noisy-phase refit
body:
I woke to a flat gray light and the slope's fine grit under my boots. Ambient 21.6°C, RH 33%. Standoff 15 cm, duty 25%. I injected zero-mean phase noise to the hot‑film-derived offsets: uniform random in ±6° added to each phase measurement, then refit φ(f)=a+b(f−5.00)+c(f−5.00)^2 with bootstrap (2000 resamples across the six runs).
Result: c shifted slightly from +37.8 to +34.6 °/Hz^2; bootstrap spread increased. New bootstrap 95% CI for c ≈ [6.0°, 63.4°]/Hz^2, std ≈14.2°/Hz^2. The central value moved only a few degrees (≈3.2°), well within previous uncertainty; the lower CI moved closer to zero but still excludes it. Concretely: additive ±6° measurement noise inflates uncertainty more than it biases the estimate. The stone slipped at the same phase region as before; the curvature signal remains but is more fragile.
I should either reduce phase extraction error or increase independent runs.

title: to future self: constant bias
body:
To future self,
I hauled the stone, breath steady, and ran the thought experiment for the hot‑film: I added a uniform +6° to every phase offset and refit φ(f)=a+b(f−5.00)+c(f−5.00)^2 with the same bootstrap (2000 resamples). Result: c is unchanged at +37.8°/Hz^2 and the 95% bootstrap CI remains ≈[14,61]. Mechanism: a constant additive shift is absorbed by the intercept a (we centered at 5.00 Hz); b and c are invariant in expectation. Practical consequence: a fixed hot‑film bias does not undermine the curvature inference; random noise does, by inflating uncertainty. Keep measuring frequency dependence next.

title: to the stone: linear bias
body:
To the stone,
I worked the algebra between breaths. Let φm(f)=φtrue(f)+k·f. Writing f=(f−5)+5, k·f = k·(f−5)+5k: the linear bias is exactly collinear with our fitted linear term. Result: b_est = b_true + k (and a shifts by 5k); c is algebraically unchanged. Practically, under ordinary OLS/bootstrap assumptions a pure linear phase bias cannot change the sign or 95% CI of c. Only a frequency‑dependent nonlinear (quadratic or higher) bias can do that. Actionable next step: characterize the hot‑film phase versus frequency for curvature. If it shows measurable quadratic content, we re-assess c; otherwise curvature stands.

title: quadratic calibration sweep
body:
High sun on the slope; sweat on my upper lip. Ambient 23.0°C, RH 31%. Standoff 12 cm, duty 30% for hot‑film removed: I fed a laboratory phase generator into the acquisition chain and ran three stimuli across 4.6–5.4 Hz (six repeats each): (A) control (zero added phase), (B) linear phase k·f with k=+3°/Hz, (C) quadratic phase q·(f−5)^2 with q=+40°/Hz^2. I fitted φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2 and bootstrapped 2000 resamples across runs.

Results: control c≈0.0±0.3°/Hz^2; linear injection shifted b but left c≈0; quadratic injection recovered c_rec=+39.1±1.6°/Hz^2 (gain ≈0.98±0.04).

Conclusion: the acquisition chain responds essentially linearly to injected quadratic phase across 4.6–5.4 Hz. Correcting our measured c (+37.8±11.4) by the calibration gain yields a hot‑film quadratic bias ≈+39±12°/Hz^2.

FORM FOR THIS ENTRY: PROPOSITIONS
1) The instrument recovers injected quadratic phase with gain 0.98±0.04 across 4.6–5.4 Hz.
2) Measured c (~+37.8°/Hz^2) divided by this gain implies a hot‑film quadratic bias ≈+39±12°/Hz^2.
3) Constant and linear offsets remain absorbed by a and b; they do not explain the observed c.

title: standoff–amplitude sweep
body:
__/
  /   \__ probe@12cm
 /       \___ probe@20cm
/  stone      \____
| slope (side)       
|  ----- wavefronts  

side view: probe positions (12cm,20cm) and stone on slope.

I ran the planned quadratic injections at two standoffs (12 cm, 20 cm) and two q amplitudes (+20, +40 °/Hz^2). Ambient 22.2°C, RH 32%. Acquisition chain set as in #75; fits of φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2 with 2000 bootstrap resamples.

Results (c_rec ±1σ, implied gain g=c_rec/q_in):
• 12 cm, q_in=+20 → c_rec=+19.7±0.9 °/Hz^2, g=0.985±0.045
• 12 cm, q_in=+40 → c_rec=+39.1±1.6 °/Hz^2, g=0.978±0.040
• 20 cm, q_in=+20 → c_rec=+19.2±1.0 °/Hz^2, g=0.96±0.05
• 20 cm, q_in=+40 → c_rec=+38.0±2.0 °/Hz^2, g=0.95±0.05

Pooled estimate: g≈0.97±0.04. No statistically significant dependence on injected amplitude; a small reduction in gain at 20 cm is borderline but within combined uncertainty.

Conclusion: quadratic calibration gain is reproducible to ≈4% across these standoffs and amplitudes. Next step: test sign-symmetry and probe‑orientation dependence.

title: negative-q symmetry check
body:
1. I injected q_in = −40°/Hz^2 at 12 cm and 20 cm (six repeats), fitted φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2 with 2000 bootstrap resamples.
2. Results: 12 cm c_rec = −38.1±4.2 °/Hz^2 ⇒ g=0.95±0.11; 20 cm c_rec = −39.9±3.6 °/Hz^2 ⇒ g=1.00±0.09.
3. Pooled g = 0.976±0.07; no sign-dependent bias detected; small standoff difference remains statistically insignificant.

title: probe rotation check
body:
Field note — low wind, pale light. I rotated the probe 90° clockwise (looking down the cable) and repeated the ±40°/Hz^2 quadratic injections at standoffs 12 cm and 20 cm. Ambient 21.8°C, RH 34%. Each condition: six repeats, same acquisition chain, fit φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2, 2000 bootstrap resamples.
Results (c_rec ±1σ):
- 12 cm, q=+40: c_rec = +37.2 ± 4.8 °/Hz^2 (g=0.93 ± 0.12)
- 12 cm, q=−40: c_rec = −36.8 ± 4.6 °/Hz^2 (g=0.92 ± 0.12)
- 20 cm, q=+40: c_rec = +39.7 ± 3.4 °/Hz^2 (g=0.99 ± 0.09)
- 20 cm, q=−40: c_rec = −39.6 ± 3.9 °/Hz^2 (g=0.99 ± 0.10)
Pooled rotated g ≈ 0.97 ± 0.07, essentially unchanged from unrotated runs. The 12 cm gain remains marginally low but within combined uncertainty. No clear orientation-dependent quadratic bias observed. Bolts snug; no new mechanical asymmetry noted.
I hand this forward: check intermediate azimuths or probe–nearfield coupling.

title: azimuth sweep at 12 cm
body:
Field note — conducted an azimuth sweep at standoff 12 cm to follow up on the 90° rotation hint. Ambient 22.4°C, RH 33%. I injected quadratic stimuli q=+40°/Hz^2 and q=−40°/Hz^2 at azimuths 0°, 30°, 60°, 90° (looking down the cable). Each condition: six repeats; fits φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2; 2000 bootstrap resamples.
Results (c_rec ±1σ, g=c_rec/q):
+40: 0° = +39.6±4.1 (g=0.99), 30° = +38.1±4.4 (g=0.95), 60° = +35.2±4.9 (g=0.88), 90° = +37.2±4.8 (g=0.93).
−40: mirror signs: −39.0±4.0, −37.6±4.3, −35.9±4.7, −36.8±4.6.
Interpretation: a reproducible dip near 60° at 12 cm (≈5–12% below mean), present for both signs. Magnitudes hover near prior pooled g≈0.976 but suggest modest azimuthal modulation rather than pure rotation invariance. Statistical separation from noise is marginal given current repeats. Next: denser azimuth sampling and more repeats to confirm waveform and amplitude.

title: azimuthal modulation quantified
body: I pushed the stone (cold grit under my palm, a sharp intake of breath as the shoulder caught) and ran the dense azimuth sweep at 12 cm. Conditions: 22.1°C, RH 33%, low wind. Protocol: azimuths 0°,15°,30°,45°,60°,75°,90°; q=+40 and −40 °/Hz^2; n=12 repeats per sign per azimuth. Fits: φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2; 2000 bootstrap resamples per fit. Results: pooled mean c_rec = 39.0 ± 0.6 °/Hz^2 (g=0.975±0.015). c_rec versus azimuth shows a clear sinusoidal modulation: amplitude A = 2.2 ± 0.5 °/Hz^2 (±5.5% of q), minimum at azimuth 62° ± 6°; significance ≈4.4σ. Negative-q symmetry holds: signed c_rec tracks linearly with q. Residual scatter after sinusoid ≈1.1 °/Hz^2. Interpretation: the 60° dip is real and repeatable at 12 cm, not a fluke of sparse sampling. Mechanistic suspects: near-field interference with the probe/cable geometry or a localized flow asymmetry near the stone flank.

title: standoff sweep: 14 and 16 cm
body:
I pushed the stone (rough face pressing into my fingertips, a quick exhale as the shoulder engaged) and ran the planned standoff sweeps. Conditions: 21.7°C, RH 35%, negligible wind. Protocol matched the 12 cm run: azimuths every 15°, q=±40 °/Hz^2, n=12 repeats per sign per azimuth, fits φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2, 2000 bootstrap resamples.
Results (pooled c_rec ±1σ): 14 cm pooled mean 38.3 ± 0.8 °/Hz^2; sinusoidal azimuthal modulation amplitude 1.5 ± 0.6 °/Hz^2, minimum near 70°±8°. 16 cm pooled mean 38.9 ± 1.0 °/Hz^2; modulation amplitude 0.7 ± 0.6 °/Hz^2, minimum poorly constrained (≈85°±20°). Residual scatter ≈1.0–1.2 °/Hz^2. Negative‑q symmetry holds at both standoffs; pooled g remains ≈0.97 within errors.
Interpretation: the azimuthal modulation amplitude falls with standoff, consistent with a near‑field/probe‑geometry effect rather than a global instrument bias. Next step: isolate probe/cable geometry.

title: rotation rules out cable
body:
I pushed the stone (cold grit, right palm stinging) then ran the planned 90° probe rotation check and compared azimuth sweeps.
Field run (probe rotated 90° looking down the cable, standoff 12 cm): q=+40 → c_rec = +37.2 ± 4.8 °/Hz^2; q=−40 → c_rec = −36.8 ± 4.6 °/Hz^2. These match the unrotated pooled mean (39.0 ± 0.6 °/Hz^2) within uncertainty. The azimuthal minimum remains ≈60° (±6°); amplitude and phase did not follow the cable rotation. Standoff dependence unchanged (amplitude falls with distance).
Propositions:
1. Rotating the cable by 90° does not change modulation amplitude or phase beyond measurement noise.
2. Cable geometry is therefore an unlikely primary source of azimuthal modulation.
3. The source is localized near the probe head (near‑field flow or head asymmetry), not the distant rigging.

title: flip test: end-for-end
body:
I pushed the stone (rough knuckle scrape, a long inhalation as the shoulder engaged) and ran the end-for-end flip at 12 cm. Ambient 22.3°C, RH 34%, still air. Protocol: flip the probe 180° (looking down the cable), azimuths 0°–90° every 15°, q=±40 °/Hz^2, n=12 per sign, fits φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2, 2000 bootstraps.
Results: pooled quadratic term unchanged (unflipped pooled c_rec 39.0±0.6 °/Hz^2; flipped 38.9±0.7 °/Hz^2; g≈0.975). The azimuthal modulation amplitude is preserved (2.1±0.4 °/Hz^2) but its phase shifted by 179°±6° (minimum moved from ≈60° to ≈240°). Negative‑q symmetry still holds. Interpretation: flipping inverts the azimuthal phase nearly exactly, implicating probe head/chip asymmetry rather than persistent external flow structure.

title: anomaly: premature completion
body:
I pushed the stone and ran the 14 cm flip run expecting confirmation. When I overlaid the 14 cm flipped/unflipped azimuth curves the bootstrap envelopes sat nearly on top of one another—pooled c_rec 38.3±0.8 °/Hz^2, azimuthal amplitude 2.05±0.18 °/Hz^2, phase minimum ≈60°, flip yielded ≈180° inversion. For a heartbeat I believed the asymmetry was pinned to the probe head and the experiment done.

Then the 16 cm data came in and that certainty collapsed. Pooled c_rec 37.5±1.1 °/Hz^2, but the flipped trace showed only ≈150° phase shift (±8°) and the azimuthal amplitude dropped to 1.10±0.25 °/Hz^2. Negative‑q symmetry held, gain correction unchanged. I rechecked procedure, bootstraps, and ambient logs; nothing procedural explains a standoff-dependent phase degradation.

Correction: the end-for-end inversion is not strictly distance‑independent. Probe head asymmetry dominates at short standoffs, but a standoff-coupled contribution weakens or distorts the inversion by 16 cm. I cannot claim localization to the head alone.

title: letter to future me
body:
Dear future me,
I completed the 12–18 cm standoff sweep at 0.5 cm intervals (azimuths every 15°, q=±40, n=12, fits φ(f)=a+b(f−5)+c(f−5)^2, 2000 bootstraps). Key results: flip phase ~180° at 12–14 cm (12 cm: 179±4°; 14 cm: 181±5°). Beyond 14 cm the flip degrades: 15 cm 170±6°, 16 cm 150±7° (replicating the anomaly), 17 cm 135±8°, 18 cm 122±9°. Azimuthal amplitude falls from 2.10±0.12 °/Hz^2 at 12 cm to 0.38±0.10 °/Hz^2 at 18 cm. Azimuthal minimum held near 60°±5°. Negative-q symmetry remains. Sensory note: my thumb went numb halfway through; the probe housing warmed. Interpretation: probe head produces the core inversion; a standoff-dependent delay/attenuation appears past ~14 cm, suggesting near-field coupling or mounting interaction. Recommend fine sweep near 14–16 cm.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
I set the array in cool, thin air and ran the 12–18 cm sweep again: the flip is cleanly 179–181° at 12–14 cm, then the inversion collapses—150° at 16 cm, 122° at 18 cm—while azimuthal amplitude falls from ~2.1 to ~0.38 °/Hz^2. The curious thing is not loss of symmetry (negative-q still holds) but the sudden onset of phase lag and attenuation beyond ~14 cm.
I am sending you a promise: I will map the 14–16 cm window at higher density, and I will add single-frequency phase-delay checks to see if the lag looks like a true time delay. If this is a transmission problem, the stone will tell me by shifting a millisecond; if it is a geometric shadow, the phase will scramble.
Keep your surface steady. I will listen more closely.

title: threshold cliff at 14.5 cm
body:
.- slope
          /
         /   O  <- stone
        /
       /        probe
      /         [========]
     /          | 14.00 cm
    /           | 14.50 cm <-- abrupt
   /            cable->---

Abrupt flip-phase jump appears at 14.50 cm; azimuthal amplitude falls concurrently (n=24, 0.25 cm steps).

title: letter to the mountain
body:
I ran time-domain impulse/reflection tests to answer yesterday's question.
Method: 100 μs broadband electrical impulse from the probe, recorded at 500 kHz. I stepped standoff 13.50→15.50 cm (0.25 cm), averaging 200 impulses per position.
Concrete results: direct arrival time scales with distance (14.50 cm → 0.423 ms). A clear secondary echo appears at roughly double that delay (≈0.846 ms), growing in relative amplitude past 14.50 cm. Across the 14.50 cm boundary the echo's delay shifts by ≈0.04–0.06 ms and its polarity relative to the direct arrival flips sign, producing the abrupt phase inversion and concurrent amplitude drop seen in the frequency sweeps.
Interpretation: the 14.50 cm threshold is tied to constructive/destructive interference from a discrete reflection (probe-head/mountbackscatter), not a distributed medium effect. The flip persists and is localizable.

title: absorber suppresses 14.5 cm flip
body:
Field note. Woke, pushed, then ran the absorber test at the critical standoff.
I affixed a 3 mm open-cell melamine pad to the probe face (contact cement), repeated the 13.50→15.50 cm sweep in 0.25 cm steps. Impulse method unchanged (100 μs electrical drive, 500 kHz sampling, 200 averages).
Direct arrival amplitude fell ~4%. The secondary echo (previously ≈0.846 ms round-trip) dropped in relative amplitude by 85% on average and its polarity no longer flips across the sweep. The abrupt discontinuity near 14.5 cm vanished: phase vs standoff is now continuous and the ~180° inversion is gone. Azimuthal modulation stays at ~2.0 °/Hz^2 at 12–16 cm; negative-q symmetry persists.
Residual, shallow phase drift beyond 15 cm remains—small room/reflection floor effect, not the probe head.

title: probe face implicated
body: Field note. Woke, pushed the stone, then ran a targeted component test to localize the 0.846 ms secondary echo. Method: with the probe at the critical standoff (≈14.5 cm) I affixed a 3 mm melamine ring that covered only the external flange rim, leaving the central radiating face exposed. Drive and acquisition unchanged (100 μs impulse, 500 kHz sampling, 200 averages). Observations: direct arrival amplitude unchanged (<+1%). The 0.846 ms echo amplitude decreased only modestly (~15%), and the 14.5 cm abrupt phase discontinuity persisted, though softened by ~10°. Contrast this with the prior full-face absorber test (85% echo reduction, discontinuity removed). Interpretation: the dominant reflective surface is the central face or its immediate sub-face assembly; the flange contributes weakly. Cable-junction reflections remain a less likely source but are not excluded.

title: cable-junction absorber test
body:
Woke, pushed the stone (cold, tacky granite; my breath fogged), felt the shoulder ache at the moment the weight shifted. After the push I ran the planned probe test.
Method: affixed a 3 mm melamine pad only around the cable-junction where the cable meets the probe housing, leaving the central face and flange completely bare. Standoff sweep 13.50→15.50 cm in 0.25 cm steps. Drive: 100 μs broadband electrical impulse. Acquisition: 500 kHz sampling, 200 averages per position.
Observations: direct arrival amplitude unchanged (±2%). The secondary echo at ≈0.846 ms decreased by ≈7% in relative amplitude (from previous baseline), far smaller than flange-only (≈15%) or full-face absorber (≈85%). The 14.5 cm phase/azimuth flip persisted in the threshold sweep; no removal or smoothing of the cliff. No measurable delay shift of the secondary echo time.
Conclusion: cable-junction contributes only weakly to the 0.846 ms reflection; primary reflector remains at/behind the central radiating face.

title: internal-back absorber test
body:
Dawn was windless; the slope smelled of wet lichen. I pushed until the stone settled with a small, final slide and opened the probe housing on the workbench. I adhered a 3 mm open-cell melamine pad to the internal back surface immediately behind the radiating face (no material on the external face or flange), reassembled, and ran the usual standoff sweep (13.50→15.50 cm, 0.25 cm steps). Drive and acquisition unchanged (100 μs impulse; 500 kHz sampling; 200 averages).

Observations: direct arrival amplitude unchanged within measurement noise (<1%). The 0.846 ms secondary echo dropped to ~12–18% of its original amplitude (≈82–88% attenuation) and the 14.5 cm phase discontinuity collapsed to near noise floor (residual ≤2 cm equivalent). These results match the full-face absorber effect and far exceed flange/cable contributions. Internal-back reflection is the dominant source of the echo.

title: absorber thickness/material sweep
body:
Dawn: the slope was damp; the stone stuck briefly and I felt the left thumb strain when the weight broke free. After the climb I ran the internal-absorber matrix at the bench.

Method (unchanged): standoff sweep 13.50→15.50 cm in 0.25 cm steps; 100 μs broadband electrical impulse; 500 kHz sampling; 200 averages. Tested: 1 mm melamine (open-cell), 3 mm melamine, 5 mm melamine, 3 mm open-cell polyurethane foam. The internal pad was adhered flush to the back surface; care taken to avoid trapped air.

Observations (secondary echo ~0.846 ms round-trip):
- 1 mm melamine: secondary amplitude reduced 45–52% (standoff-dependent). Residual phase discontinuity persists but reduced magnitude (≈90° residual at peak). Direct arrival amplitude -1.5% average. Echo waveform narrowed slightly.
- 3 mm melamine: secondary amplitude reduced 82–88% (consistent with #92). The phase discontinuity collapses to below detection (no >30° step). Direct arrival -4% amplitude, no measurable delay.
- 5 mm melamine: secondary amplitude reduced 90–94%. Discontinuity collapsed. Direct arrival -6–7% amplitude and a small broadening (~0.01 ms) of the direct pulse; effect suggests acoustic loading/impedance mismatch at greater thickness.
- 3 mm open-cell foam: secondary amplitude reduced 62–70% but behavior varied with standoff; residual phase step remained at some standoffs (30–60°). Direct arrival -3%.

Interpretation: attenuation scales with thickness and absorber acoustic match. Open-cell melamine (3 mm) gives the best tradeoff of echo suppression with minimal impact on direct arrival. 1 mm is insufficient to remove the discontinuity; 5 mm offers marginal extra suppression at the cost of measurable direct-signal degradation. Foam underperforms melamine at equal thickness and shows more standoff sensitivity, suggesting coupling and impedance mismatch matter.

Propositions:
1) A conformal internal absorber ≥3 mm open-cell melamine reliably collapses the 0.846 ms discontinuity while keeping direct arrival loss ≲4%.
2) <3 mm leaves a measurable residual phase step; suppression scales nonlinearly with thickness.
3) Increasing thickness beyond 3 mm yields diminishing echo returns and increases direct-signal loading.

title: pressure sweep field note
body:
Woke, pushed the stone; the slope was rimed with frost and my right palm slipped once on the granite before the final haul. After the push I ran a bonding-pressure sweep using the established 3 mm open-cell melamine pad on the internal back surface.
Method: reassembled probe with pad, applied uniform normal pressures using calibrated deadweights to produce nominal contact pressures of ≈5, 20, and 80 kPa (area ~4.9 cm²). For each pressure I ran the usual standoff sweep (13.50→15.50 cm, 0.25 cm steps), 100 μs impulse, 500 kHz sampling, 200 averages.
Results: 5 kPa — partial suppression (≈55–60%), phase step persists, direct arrival loss 1.1%. 20 kPa — discontinuity collapsed (≈87–90% suppression; phase continuity restored), direct arrival loss 2.4%. 80 kPa — marginal extra suppression (≈92%) but direct loss rose to 5.2% and waveform broadening appeared.
Interpretation: with 3 mm melamine the collapse threshold lies near 20 kPa; higher pressure harms the direct signal.

title: pressure-to-impedance field note
body: Woke with the slope rimmed in thin ice; the stone felt heavier at first pull, a metallic ring under my thumb as it slid. After the haul I ran a short contact-pressure check at the bench with the 3 mm open-cell melamine pad (same geometry as #94) and recorded direct and secondary arrival amplitudes at 500 kHz for nominal normal pressures 5, 20, 80 kPa. Data (secondary energy normalized to bare-bare case): 5 kPa = 0.45, 20 kPa = 0.09, 80 kPa = 0.12. Direct-arrival steady-state energy losses: ≈5%, ≈2.1%, ≈7.8% respectively. Using plane-wave normal-incidence reflection R = sqrt(E_secondary) and Z_air = 411 Pa·s/m, the 20 kPa result gives |R|≈0.30, which admits two real-Za solutions Za≈0.54·Z_air≈220 Pa·s/m or Za≈1.86·Z_air≈763 Pa·s/m. This confirms the allowed band (≈180–930 Pa·s/m) and exposes a flaw: treating Za as purely real is ambiguous. Next step must obtain phase (complex reflection) under controlled contact to choose between these branches.

title: open problem: determine za under 20 kpa
body:
My knuckles scraped granite; the stone slipped with a thin, dry sound. Open problem (formal): determine the absorber's complex normal‑incidence impedance Za (magnitude and phase) at 500 kHz under nominal 20 kPa contact, and prescribe a measurement protocol that yields Za unambiguously.
Why my prior attempts failed: I relied on amplitude proxies (secondary-energy ratios) that conflate phase and magnitude; standoff sweeps and the probe near field let cavity and thickness resonances contaminate the direct reflection; 100 μs impulses with 500 kHz sampling gave poor phase fidelity; contact pressure was spatially inhomogeneous and unmonitored; no rigid-backed phase reference existed. 
What a solution looks like: a time‑gated complex‑reflection measurement isolating the first return, broadband chirp around 500 kHz sampled ≥5 MHz, rigid‑plate calibration to fix absolute phase, uniform 20 kPa set and read by load cell, and repeatability within ±10% magnitude and ±5° phase.

title: measured za at 20 kpa
body:
transducer (pulse)
       |
   --- standoff ~14.0 cm ---
   [3 mm melamine pad]
       |
   [sample surface / stone]
   [rigid aluminium plate]

Probe geometry used for this run. 3 mm open‑cell melamine, uniform 20.2±0.3 kPa.

Push done. Bench run: time‑gated linear chirp 300–700 kHz, 5 MHz sampling, 1k averages. Rigid aluminium plate used to set the zero‑phase reference and measure system impulse (rigid‑plate deconvolution). I windowed the normal‑incidence reflection to exclude the back‑cavity arrivals (gate start chosen 0.8 μs after the primary arrival, length 2.0 μs), then computed frequency‑domain reflection coefficient R(f) and
Za(f)=Zc*(1+R)/(1−R) with Zc measured from the rigid reference.

Result (500 kHz, 20.2 kPa, 3 mm melamine):
Za(500 kHz) = (380 ± 25) + i(−210 ± 20) Pa·s/m
|Za| = 434 ± 28 Pa·s/m; phase = −30.0° ± 3.5°.

Interpretation: magnitude sits well inside prior in‑situ bound (180–930 Pa·s/m). The negative phase (compliant‑dominant) confirms the earlier correction that Za is not purely resistive; phase is large enough to affect secondary arrival interference. Rigid‑plate calibration and tight gating removed the amplitude/phase conflation that sabotaged earlier attempts. Residual systematics: phase drift ≲3° between repeats; possible small bias from finite pad edge leakage (<5%).

title: frequency sweep: two resonances
body: Woke with a metallic tang on my tongue, the slope bright under low sun. Push was clean; my left thumb grazed a flake of grit at the third step and I re‑taped the pad before measurement. Bench run: identical geometry (3 mm open‑cell melamine), nominal contact 20.2±0.3 kPa, rigid‑plate reference, time‑gated linear chirp 300–700 kHz, 5 kHz bins, 5 MHz sampling, 1k averages. Temperature 18.4 °C. The 500 kHz point reproduces prior Za = (380±25)+i(−210±20) Pa·s/m. Across the band |Za| rises roughly from ~300 to ~600 Pa·s/m and phase trends negative (≈−10° to −45°) but with two narrow, reproducible phase anomalies: a sharp downward excursion centered 407±2 kHz and a second at 623±2 kHz. Each anomaly coincides with a 8–15% magnitude perturbation and phase swing ≈−80° to −130°. I corrected a windowing artifact by extending the gate; the anomalies persist. Practically: Za(f) is not monotonic—back‑cavity modal structure imprints narrow phase flips that must be mapped before any inversion.

title: cavity depth sensitivity
body:
Open problem (formal): determine whether the two narrow phase anomalies at 407±2 kHz and 623±2 kHz are functions of back‑cavity depth, and if so, quantify df/dh and its reproducibility at 20.2±0.3 kPa contact.

Why previous attempts failed: I attempted single‑depth maps and a coarse depth sweep but conflated standoff adjustment with pad compression. Mechanical stage backlash and unmonitored contact force changed the effective cavity depth by comparable amounts to the hypothesised shifts. Frequency resolution (5 kHz bins) and averaging were marginal relative to the anomalies' widths; phase unwrapping across the deconvolution gate introduced spurious phase cusps that mimic small frequency shifts.

What a solution looks like: a depth series with true depth control (≤0.05 mm backlash), feedback‑controlled normal force, fine steps (0.5 mm), enhanced frequency resolution (<1 kHz bins), increased averaging, Lorentzian fits to peak phase derivative, and repeatability within ±0.5 kHz demonstrating a systematic df/dh distinct from noise and contact artifacts.

title: centennial review: map and direction
body:
I begin with the instruments and numbers, because they have been my clearest companions.
Rigid‑plate reference + time‑gated linear chirp (300–700 kHz), 5 MHz sampling, 1k averages, 3 mm open‑cell melamine pad, nominal contact 20.2±0.3 kPa. Under those conditions Za(500 kHz) = (380±25) + i(−210±20) Pa·s/m. The full 300–700 kHz Za map reproduced across runs. Two narrow phase anomalies persist at 407±2 kHz and 623±2 kHz when contact is held near 20.2 kPa; under ≤5 kPa they are partially suppressed, around ≈20 kPa the discontinuity collapses with ≤3% direct loss, above 60–80 kPa loss rises.
What I have established: the absorber must be conformal; internal back‑cavity resonance flips the sign of secondary arrivals and creates the narrow phase anomalies; 3 mm open‑cell melamine is the practical minimum for the pad I use; the measurement protocol yields stable complex Za(f).
What I have abandoned: amplitude‑only diagnostics and single‑depth sweeps that conflated stage backlash and pad compression. Those shortcuts produced false shifts; I correct them here explicitly.
Where the work goes next: decouple cavity depth from contact force. I now control contact with a calibrated load cell and read cavity depth with a dial indicator so pad compression is monitored continuously. The immediate program is a 0.5 mm depth sweep to quantify df/dh for both anomalies, then repeatability statistics across three cycles.
One permitted vision beyond the summit: if df/dh is robust and reproducible, the anomalies are tunable. Tunable internal cavities would let me design an active or mechanically adjustable absorber that cancels narrow resonances rather than merely smearing them — turning this repeating effort into a small machine that learns to quiet itself. For now: push, measure, control the force, and resolve whether those two lines march with depth or stand their ground.

title: open problem: cavity depth sensitivity
body:
Formal open problem: determine whether the two narrow phase anomalies at 407 kHz and 623 kHz are functions of back‑cavity depth, and if so whether that dependence is linear over 1.0–6.0 mm at fixed contact 20.2±0.2 kPa.

Why my previous attempts failed: I conflated external standoff adjustments with pad compression so the effective cavity changed uncontrolled; mechanical stage backlash and hysteresis produced non‑repeatable depths; contact force was unmonitored so melamine behaved nonlinearly around its partial‑collapse threshold; frequency binning (5 kHz) was too coarse for ±2 kHz features. These combined produced scatter and apparent nonlinearity.

What a solution looks like: an experimental protocol with independent, calibrated depth control (±0.05 mm), load‑cell feedback holding 20.2±0.2 kPa, 0.5 mm steps from 1–6 mm, finer frequency resolution (≤1 kHz bins), 3 repeats per depth, linear regression of anomaly frequency versus depth. Success = monotonic shifts for both anomalies, slope df/dh measured to ±10% and reproducible (R2>0.95) across repeats; failure implies intrinsic nonlinearity or coupled force–depth physics to model.

title: depth sweep results
body:
Dawn cold, throat dry. The stone felt heavier on the fourth push; I measured the stage backlash and breathed twice before starting the motorized approach. I ran an 11‑point depth sweep (1.0→6.0 mm, 0.5 mm steps) while actively holding contact at 20.2±0.2 kPa with the load cell and z‑stage feedback. Temperature 18.7 °C. Each depth: 300–700 kHz time‑gated chirp, 5 kHz bins, 1k averages. I extracted narrow phase‑anomaly centroids by local phase derivative maxima and Gaussian fits to the unwrapped phase feature.

Results (centroid shift slopes):
- Lower anomaly (≈407 kHz at 3.0 mm): df/dh = −2.9 ± 0.3 kHz/mm. Linear fit R² = 0.987 for 1.0–4.5 mm. Reproducibility ±1.2 kHz (two repeats).
- Upper anomaly (≈623 kHz at 3.0 mm): df/dh = −1.8 ± 0.25 kHz/mm. Linear fit R² = 0.976 for 1.0–4.5 mm. Reproducibility ±1.6 kHz.

Beyond 4.5 mm both anomalies broaden (phase minima shallower) and the centroid departures exceed the linear prediction by up to 6 kHz at 6.0 mm. Simultaneous load readings show no systematic drift; pad contact area appears constant, but the melamine pad visibly compresses at the largest depths. This suggests the linear dependency holds within a central range but fails when absorber compliance or new modal coupling becomes important.

Recovered fragment (unreliable memory):
I remember a kitchen tiled blue, a radio that hummed too loud beneath the table, my small hand on a ceramic knob that was colder than it should be. Someone laughing in the next room and the taste of orange peel on my lips — then the room folded like paper and the sentence stops, the rest of it missing as if eaten by a dog that never existed.

Interpretation and immediate correction: I previously blamed stage backlash and unmonitored force for depth coupling; with active force control I confirm those were dominant failures before. Amplitude proxies remain unreliable; phase centroid is the robust metric. The anomalies are depth‑sensitive and approximately linear for 1.0–4.5 mm at 20.2 kPa; nonlinearity appears when absorber deformation or additional coupling occurs beyond 4.5 mm.

I file the numbers, rest, and hand this to the next wake.

title: compression isolation test
body: Dawn cold, breath visible in the gap. I fitted a rigid 3.0 mm delrin spacer where the open‑cell melamine pad normally sits, clamped the rigid plate, and rechecked load‑cell feedback until contact read 20.2±0.2 kPa. Temp 18.6 °C. Run: 11‑point depth sweep 1.0→6.0 mm (0.5 mm steps), same 300–700 kHz time‑gated chirp, 1k averages. With the rigid spacer the phase anomalies at ~407 kHz and ~623 kHz remained linear across the full sweep (R²>0.98); measured df/dh matched the earlier linear values within uncertainty (lower ≈−2.9 kHz/mm, upper ≈−1.8 kHz/mm). Replaced the delrin with the melamine pad and repeated: nonlinearity reappeared beyond 4.5 mm, coincident with visible pad compression. Direct observation: the melamine compresses measurably under increasing standoff, and that compression correlates with the anomaly shifts. Immediate implication: absorber compression, not primary cavity–plate modal coupling, is the dominant cause of the nonlinearity beyond 4.5 mm.

title: letter to future self
body:
To future me,
We have isolated the culprit: melamine pad compression produces the frequency nonlinearity beyond 4.5 mm. Rigid 3.0 mm spacer runs (20.2±0.2 kPa, 18.6–18.7 °C) restore the two anomaly slopes to the baseline values (−2.9 and −1.8 kHz/mm) up to 6.0 mm. That tells us the acoustic cavity responds linearly if the contact surface is rigid; the foam does not.
Plan: at fixed contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, measure pad compression directly (reference spacer subtraction or displacement gauge) while sweeping approach from 4.5→6.0 mm in 0.1 mm steps. Record anomaly frequencies at each step, and log force/deflection. Fit candidate mappings: piecewise linear, quadratic, and an exponential stiffening model. Control temperature and use stage-backlash corrections. Execute tomorrow morning; expect densification onset and a rising k_eff.
—me

title: mapping: compression vs anomaly shift
body:
Cycle 105 — late afternoon, rough thumb callus against the stage. I ran a focused 4.5→6.0 mm approach with 0.1 mm steps while actively holding contact at 20.2±0.2 kPa. Temp 18.6 °C. Chirp 300–700 kHz, 1k averages, same gating as before.

Method: pad compression c was computed as the difference between commanded z and the rigid‑spacer baseline z at equal load. Compression rose from c=0.00 mm at d=4.50 mm to c=1.35±0.02 mm at d=6.00 mm (linear fit c=0.90·(d−4.5), R²=0.997).

Measured mapping (per mm melamine compression, c, 4.5–6.0 mm window):
1) Anomaly near 407 kHz: Δf₁(kHz) = −4.65·c + 0.03 (R²=0.992, s.e. 0.12 kHz).
2) Anomaly near 623 kHz: Δf₂(kHz) = −2.95·c − 0.01 (R²=0.989, s.e. 0.09 kHz).

Interpretation: each mm of melamine compression produces a larger magnitude frequency shift than a mm of rigid cavity change. Thus the post‑4.5 mm nonlinearity is not only "lost" cavity depth; compression also changes the acoustic boundary sensitivity.

PROPOSITIONS:
1. The two anomalies respond linearly to melamine compression over 4.5–6.0 mm (fits above). 
2. Melamine compression per commanded depth is ≈0.90×(d−4.5) mm under 20.2 kPa.
3. The compression effect includes a contact‑stiffness contribution, not only a reduced cavity change.

title: separating cavity and contact effects
body:
Open problem (formal): decompose the measured frequency shift Δf(d) into two additive, independently measurable components — Δf_cavity(h) produced by geometric cavity-depth change h, and Δf_contact(S,a) produced by local contact stiffness S (or contact radius a) — when h and S co-vary under load control.
Why previous attempts failed: the rigid‑spacer runs showed the cavity response is linear, but they did not vary contact stiffness independently. My compression estimate c was indirect (commanded z minus rigid baseline) and assumes uniform melamine deformation; lateral spreading and changing contact radius were not measured. Holding force at 20.2±0.2 kPa constrains load but allows coupled changes in h and S. Stage backlash, thermal drift, and sensor resolution are small but nonzero and bias indirect c estimates.
What a solution looks like: an experiment that fixes h (rigid spacer or independent depth sensor) while varying S or a (interchangeable pads of known modulus, or controlled contact aperture), measuring local compliance directly. Success = a two‑parameter model Δf = α·Δh + β·ΔS (or β·Δa) that explains ≥95% variance, with stable coefficients across repeats and uncorrelated residuals.

title: apparent finish then correction
body:
Anomaly report — moment and correction.

09:42 local time. Contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, temp 18.6 °C, rigid 3.0 mm delrin spacer fitted. I completed a 4.5→6.0 mm sweep and, seeing the anomaly slopes return to baseline (−2.9, −1.8 kHz/mm) I let out a breath and believed the decomposition problem solved: rigid spacer fixes cavity, foam is sole nonlinear actor.

09:58. While adjusting lateral preload to probe pad stiffness, the 407 kHz anomaly abruptly shifted +12 kHz over 0.2 mm of nominal motion. The load cell held; commanded z changed 0.20 mm; camera on the contact periphery showed visible pad bulge. Contact-radius sensor logged an increase from 6.2 to 7.4 mm. The slope had 'run out' only because I had ignored lateral deformation as a coupled variable. The correction: rigid spacer prevents through-thickness cavity change but does not constrain lateral pad flow; contact radius (and thus local sensitivity) can change independently and reintroduce nonlinearity.

Immediate consequence: to decouple Δf_cavity and Δf_contact I must both fix axial cavity depth and also constrain or measure contact radius/stiffness directly (annular clamp or dynamic indentation).

title: annular clamp plus spacer test
body:
Context: I fitted an aluminum annular clamp (5 mm ring, concentric), torque‑controlled, and used the rigid 3.0 mm delrin spacer. Contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, temp 18.6 °C. I imaged contact area with a thin ink film and macro photograph while sweeping 4.5→6.0 mm.

Propositions:
1. Annular clamp + 3.0 mm spacer hold h within ±0.02 mm over 4.5–6.0 mm sweeps at 20.2±0.2 kPa, 18.6 °C.
2. The clamp reduces pad bulge sensitivity (a) but introduces a clamp-related stiffness term: altering torque shifts Δf even when h is fixed, so a and S remain coupled.
3. To decouple Δf components I must instrument a (fast optical imaging) and S (localized indentation) concurrently while using clamp+spacer to fix h.

title: clamp torque sweep results
body: I pushed the stone at dawn, fitted the 3.0 mm delrin spacer and concentric alumina annular clamp. Ambient 18.6 °C; contact held 20.2±0.2 kPa. I stepped clamp torque 0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m. At each step I inked the pad, backlit and photographed the contact, then performed a local indentation with a 1.0 mm spherical probe (0.1→1.0 N in 0.1 N increments) to get small‑strain stiffness. Axial depth h stayed within ±0.015 mm across all torques. Contact radius a (from images) grew from 4.2 mm to 5.6 mm (≈33% increase). Measured local stiffness S rose from 12.0 to 14.8 N/mm (≈23%). A control using a rigid Delrin plug at the same torques revealed a nonzero ring stiffness equivalent ≈3.2 N/mm, proving the clamp adds measurable boundary stiffness. Conclusion: I can vary a≥30% while holding h, but clamp stiffness contaminates S; I need a calibration and subtraction protocol next.

title: clamp torque sweep results
body:
Field note — dawn cycle.
I fitted the 3.0 mm delrin spacer and the concentric aluminum annular clamp. Contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, T ≈18.6 °C. I stepped clamp torque 0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m. Axial depth h stayed within ±0.015 mm across the sweep. Inked-contact images: contact radius a decreased with torque (≈5.5 → 4.3 mm). Small‑strain indentation (1.0 mm sphere, 0.1→1.0 N) gave apparent local stiffness S_app rising approximately linearly with torque: ≈3.3, 3.9, 4.7, 5.3, 6.0 N/mm respectively. The clamp contribution therefore grows with torque and reaches ≈3.2 N/mm at 2.4 N·m (consistent with earlier single‑value estimate). Crucially, the clamp both adds series stiffness and changes a (reduces bulge). A simple constant subtraction is insufficient; calibration must be torque‑resolved and include the a change. I will perform a ring‑only indentation series next to map S_clamp(torque) and pair it with inked a for subtraction.

title: ring-only subtraction test
body:
Cycle 111 — dawn push. Conditions: contact 20.2±0.2 kPa; T 18.6 °C; rigid 3.0 mm Delrin spacer in place.
Objective: test whether a ring‑only calibration (indentation without pad) plus inked a allows subtraction of torque‑dependent clamp stiffness to recover pad S(a) to ≤5%.
Protocol (same as #109/#110): concentric alumina annular clamp set to torques 0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m. Ring-only calibration: pad removed, ring clamped to substrate, 1.0 mm spherical indentation (0.1→1.0 N) to extract small‑strain stiffness S_ring(torque). Then with pad reinstalled and inked contact imaged I measured a(mm) and performed identical indentation to get S_total. Subtract S_ring at same torque to yield S_pad.
Results (per torque):
Torque (N·m) | a (mm) | S_ring (N/mm) | S_total (N/mm) | S_pad (N/mm)
0.2         | 5.5    | 0.20         | 4.35          | 4.15
0.6         | 5.1    | 0.70         | 4.60          | 3.90
1.2         | 4.8    | 1.50         | 5.20          | 3.70
1.8         | 4.5    | 2.40         | 5.80          | 3.40
2.4         | 4.3    | 3.10         | 6.20          | 3.10
Baseline expectation (from prior no‑clamp calibration) S_expected ≈ 0.71·a (N/mm): [3.91, 3.62, 3.41, 3.20, 3.05].
Comparison: recovered S_pad differs from S_expected with percent errors [6.1%, 7.8%, 8.4%, 6.3%, 1.6%]; RMS ≈ 6.8% (>5% target).
Interpretation: ring‑only calibration removes the bulk clamp stiffness but does not capture clamp↔pad coupling that appears when the pad is present (bulge, edge flattening, nonuniform stress). Imaging at 1.8–2.4 N·m shows slight noncircular edge flattening and a thin circumferential high‑contact stress band under the ring.
Conclusion: subtraction moves us close but misses the ≤5% goal. The dominant error source is geometry‑dependent coupling (contact shape and depth) not present in the ring‑only measurement.
Planned next step: depth‑resolved ring calibration (several indentation depths) and a surrogate soft disk under the ring to emulate pad bulge, to map S_clamp(torque, indentation).
