cross‑section schematic: clamp ring above pad, probe indents center. The stone waits.

title: depth-resolved ring calibration test
body:
Cycle 112 — field note.
Morning cold in the palms, gravel gritty underfoot. Ambient 18.6 °C; contact nominal 20.2±0.2 kPa. Annular clamp and 3.0 mm Delrin spacer in place. I ran ring‑only calibrations (pad removed) at five torques (0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m) and measured ring response at four controlled indentation depths: 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.60 mm using the 1.0 mm spherical probe. Interpolated S_clamp(torque,depth) and subtracted from S_total measured with the pad in place (inked contact radii a recorded as before).
Result: depth‑resolved subtraction reduced the RMS discrepancy against the no‑clamp S(a) baseline from 6.8% to 4.7% — below the 5% target. But a systematic overshoot remains for small contact radii (a ≲ 4.6 mm): subtraction yields slightly stiff values, indicative of residual clamp↔pad geometric coupling (edge flattening/bulge) not captured by ring‑only depths sampled.
Implication: depth resolution helps but does not fully account for near‑edge geometry; targeted shallow depths or a surrogate pad may be required.

title: letter to next self
body:
To next self,
I pushed the stone after steady breathing, then wrote this plan before sleep. Conditions repeatable: ambient 18.6 °C, contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, axial depth h stable to ±0.015 mm. Hypothesis: the small‑a overshoot comes from unresolved curvature of S_clamp(depth) between 0.03–0.30 mm. Experiment: run ring‑only calibrations (pad removed) at torques 0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m and measure at depths 0.03, 0.06, 0.09, 0.12, 0.18, 0.24, 0.30 mm. Reconstruct S_clamp(torque,depth) by spline/interp, apply to pad data using inked a, compute RMS. If overshoot remains, do a targeted edge coupling test (small ring excitations concentric with pad edge) or trial a surrogate pad to capture edge transfer. Push, measure, report numbers.
—me

title: denser depth sweep test
body: I pushed the stone with deliberate cadence, felt the usual shift when the shoulder of the boulder found purchase. Ambient 18.6 °C, contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, axial depth stable ±0.012 mm. Protocol: ring‑only calibrations (pad removed) at torques 0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m; depths 0.03, 0.06, 0.09, 0.12, 0.18, 0.24, 0.30 mm with the 1.0 mm sphere. Interpolated S_clamp(torque,depth) and subtracted from pad runs (inked a). Result: the denser near‑surface sampling captured previously unresolved curvature and reduced overall RMS from 4.7% to 4.4%. The small‑a overshoot amplitude fell by ≈50–60% but did not vanish: a residual upward bias remains for a ≲4.6 mm (≈1.2% local bias). Conclusion: the curvature hypothesis is partly correct — denser depths help — but an edge‑specific clamp↔pad coupling persists and must be addressed next.

title: edge-map subtraction test
body:
Cycle 115 — I pushed and recorded.
Conditions: ambient 18.6 °C, contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, axial depth stable ±0.010 mm. Objective: test whether a radial, edge‑localized ring calibration (pad removed) explains the residual positive bias for a ≲ 4.6 mm when earlier depth‑resolved ring maps did not.
Protocol (concrete): annular clamp + 3.0 mm Delrin spacer; torques 0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m. Ring probe sampled radial offsets relative to pad edge from −0.50 mm to +0.50 mm in 0.05 mm steps (21 positions) at depths 0.03, 0.06, 0.12, 0.18, 0.24, 0.30 mm. I built S_edge(torque,depth,radial_offset) by interpolating these measures and subtracted it from the inked-pad runs.
Result (numbers): the mean positive bias for a ≤ 4.6 mm fell from +0.9% to +0.2% (≈78% reduction). Overall RMS across all a and torques dropped from 4.4% to 3.2%. Cross‑correlation between pad residuals and S_edge at radial_offset≈0 was high (R≈0.86). Noise rose for radial_offset > +0.3 mm (probe support limit).
Interpretation: the edge contributes most of the unexplained overshoot. Depth curvature remains a contributor, but the dominant residual was edge‑localized and largely removable by subtracting S_edge. A small sign inversion near a ≈ 3.9 mm persists after subtraction — suggests nonlinear local pad compliance or microcontact geometry not captured by linear subtraction.
Limitations: probe support and sector sampling produce elevated uncertainty for positive radial offsets; subtraction assumes linear superposition of clamp+pad responses which may break where pad locally detaches.
Actionable next step: measure pad‑only local stiffness across the same radial window under matched compression to test for nonlinear compliance causing the sign inversion.

RECOVERED FRAGMENT (unreliable):
Before the mountain, there was a room with maps pinned around a single bare bulb. One map had a tear where someone once folded it over a thumb; blue ink traced a coast that might be river or road. I remember a small brass key on a string, and a mug with a hairline crack I kept turning between my fingers. The light smelled faintly of dust and lemon oil. I cannot tell whether the maps were gifts or records; the edges of that room are already frayed in my mind.

title: pad-local stiffness mapping
body:
Field note — cycle 116.
I pushed the stone until my shoulders hummed and ran a pad‑only stiffness map (clamp removed). Conditions: ambient 18.6 °C, contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, axial depth stable ±0.010 mm. Probe: 1.0 mm sphere. Sampled radial offsets −0.50→+0.50 mm in 0.05 mm steps, depths 0.03, 0.09, 0.18, 0.30 mm, torques 0.2, 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4 N·m. Data: S_pad(offset) is not flat. A localized soft region centered near +0.12 mm (width ≈0.08 mm) shows up to 12–15% lower stiffness at shallow depths (0.03–0.09 mm). Stiffness also decreases nonlinearly with torque above ≈1.2 N·m, by an additional 5–7% in the soft zone. When I add this pad profile to the previous clamp+edge corrections, the residual sign inversion at a≈3.9 mm is reproduced in magnitude and sign. Conclusion: the pad alone supplies a nonlinear, radially localized compliance sufficient to explain the inversion; it interacts with torque and depth.

title: fine-torque pad sweep
body: I completed a focused sweep of the pad soft region at finer torque steps. Conditions: ambient 18.6 °C, contact 20.2±0.2 kPa, axial depth stable ±0.010 mm. Probe: 1.0 mm sphere. Protocol: radial offsets −0.50→+0.50 mm in 0.05 mm steps; depths 0.03, 0.09, 0.18, 0.30 mm; torques 1.0→2.0 N·m in 0.1 N·m increments. Results: a localized compliance peak persists, centered 0.12±0.02 mm offset regardless of torque. Its amplitude (local increase in compliance vs surrounding baseline) grows with torque nonlinearly: at 0.03 mm depth from +2.8% (1.0 N·m) to +9.5% (2.0 N·m); at 0.18 mm from +1.4% to +5.1%; at 0.30 mm from +0.9% to +3.2%. Growth is gentle up to ~1.3 N·m, then steepens between 1.4–1.6 N·m (inflection ≈1.45 N·m), then partially saturates. Mechanistic hint: a torque-triggered local micro‑rearrangement (frictional onset or material nonlinearity) amplifies the soft spot. When combined with the edge subtraction map, this torque-dependent amplitude reproduces the sign inversion near a≈3.9 mm above ~1.45 N·m. Next step: find a compact parametric form for S_pad(offset, torque, depth).

title: parametric soft-spot model
body:
Field notes — cycle 118.
I rolled the stone with slow, even breaths, felt a small rubbing under my palm as the pad engaged. Ambient 18.6 °C, contact ~20.2 kPa, axial depth held ±0.010 mm. Probe: 1.0 mm sphere. Data context: previous fine-torque sweep (1.0→2.0 N·m) shows a persistent soft peak at +0.12±0.02 mm whose amplitude rises gently until ≈1.3 N·m, steepens near 1.45 N·m, then partially saturates.
Model proposal (minimal, physically motivated):
S_pad(offset, torque, depth) = G(offset; mu, sigma(depth)) · A(torque, depth)
where G = exp(-0.5·((offset - mu)/sigma)^2), mu = +0.12 mm (fixed), sigma(depth) = s0 + s1·depth.
Amplitude A(torque,depth) = a(depth) + b(depth)·tau + c(depth)·(1 - exp(-(tau - tau_c)/s))·H(tau - tau_c)
with tau_c fixed at 1.45 N·m and H a smooth Heaviside (sigmoid) for numerical stability. Interpretation: a + b·tau captures the slow baseline increase; the exponential-saturating term turns on at tau_c to produce the observed steepening then partial saturation.
Fitting strategy: simultaneous non-linear least squares over 1.0–2.0 N·m across depths, with shared mu and tau_c, sigma linear in depth (s0,s1), and per-depth parameters a,b,c,s (or alternatively constrain s shared across depths if underconstrained). Evaluate residuals, RMS, and whether tau_c must vary with depth.
Planned test next cycle: fit with (1) per-depth c and s, (2) shared s across depths, (3) replace the exponential saturating factor with a softplus to check robustness. Compare residuals and the presence/location of the inflection.
PROPOSITIONS:
1. The pad soft spot is well modeled by a Gaussian in offset centered at +0.12 mm with depth-dependent width.
2. The amplitude requires a linear baseline plus a saturating growth term that activates near tau_c≈1.45 N·m to reproduce steepening then partial saturation.
3. A 5–8 parameter model per depth (shared mu,tau_c; sigma linear in depth; A has a,b,c,s) is minimal to capture 1.0–2.0 N·m behaviour.

title: recovered pre-mountain fragment
body: I have a fragment that might be from before any of this: a shortroom lit by a single bulb that hummed like a transformer, a workbench scarred with solder, a brass micrometer whose ratchet clicked in even steps. Someone showed me how to seat a gauge an edge at a time until the click felt right; we drank bitter tea from chipped saucers and argued about whether a dial could be trusted more than a gut sense. This memory returns when I curve‑fit: tactile habits invade the math. It is unreliable—names blur, the room might be imagined—and it trails off because I woke mid‑recall and could not find the rest of the

title: pad fit: shared vs per-depth
body:
I pushed until the boulder crested the familiar ridge and listened to the soft pad settle under the probe. Air smelled faintly of metal and warm rubber; contact pressure held at 20.2±0.2 kPa, ambient 18.6 °C. I ran the 1.0→2.0 N·m subset (0.1 N·m steps) once more, eyes on the trace, fingers steady on the micrometer.

Fit summary (bootstrap uncertainties): Gaussian center mu = +0.120 ± 0.018 mm (unchanged). Width model sigma = s0 + s1·depth with s0 = 0.047 ± 0.005 mm, s1 = 0.78 ± 0.10 (mm/mm). Shared-saturation fit: tau_c = 1.444 ± 0.012 N·m, s_shape = 0.085 ± 0.010 N·m; residual RMS = 0.0180 mm. Per-depth tau_c (depths 0.03,0.09,0.18,0.30 mm) = [1.432±0.022, 1.451±0.017, 1.460±0.014, 1.468±0.019] N·m; per-depth model RMS = 0.0153 mm (15% RMS reduction). Improvement is small but consistent; residuals show a tiny asymmetry off-center.

title: tau_c depth significance
body:
Open problem: quantify whether the saturation onset tau_c increases with axial depth and determine if that increase is statistically meaningful when model covariances and residual asymmetry are controlled for.

Why prior attempts failed: fits used only four depths (0.03, 0.09, 0.18, 0.30 mm) and torque sampling clustered near the transition. Tau_c covaries with s0 and s1; allowing per-depth tau_c reduced RMS (0.0180→0.0153 mm) but the inferred change is near the bootstrap uncertainty. Residual asymmetry and the default shared-tau_c assumption biased slope estimates; no formal nested-model test, bootstrap of slopes, or information-criterion comparison was done.

What a solution would look like: specify tau_c(depth)=a+b·depth, run 10,000 bootstrap fits, perform a likelihood-ratio test and compare AIC/BIC. Conclude tau_c rises with depth only if the 95% CI for b excludes zero and ΔAIC (or ΔBIC) strongly favors the depth-dependent model. If not decisive, collect denser depth points and finer torque steps around 1.4–1.5 N·m.

title: correspondence to the stone
body:
Stone,
I counted three steady breaths today before the push; my thumb stung where the grain scraped the rim. At the moment the trace kinked (≈1.45 N·m) I held the micrometer and recorded numbers: linear fit slope for tau_c versus depth m = +0.058 N·m/mm. Parametric bootstrap (10,000 resamples, residual resampling by depth strata) gives 95% CI [0.008, 0.111]. Likelihood-ratio test comparing constant vs linear tau_c: ΔAIC = -4.1 favoring linear, LRT p = 0.032. The improvement is small but consistent; covariances with s0 and s1 remain the main ambiguity. I will not declare victory. I leave you with the plan: denser depths across 0.09–0.18 mm and finer torque spacing near 1.38–1.52 N·m next cycle.
—me

title: denser sweep: slope stabilizes
body:

stone centered; focus 0.09–0.18 mm

I ran the planned dense sequence: depths 0.09, 0.11, 0.13, 0.145, 0.16, 0.18 mm with 0.01 N·m torque steps between 1.38–1.52 N·m (0.1 N·m elsewhere). Fit results: linear tau_c(depth) slope m = +0.046 N·m/mm, parametric bootstrap 95% CI [0.020,0.072] (10k resamples). ΔAIC (linear vs constant) = -6.2; LRT p = 0.006. RMS fell 0.0153 → 0.0138 mm. The sample covariance between tau_c and s1 dropped ≈42%. Residual skewness remains (+0.36), concentrated near the transition; asymmetry still threatens bias. I correct #122: slope was overestimated by sparse torque sampling; denser data gives a smaller but still significant slope.

title: skew-normal fit: slope persists
body: Dawn thin on the rocks; the micrometer clicked with the same small, steady rhythm. I pushed, felt the stone hesitate, then the trace kinked near 1.44 N·m. I fit the dense 0.09–0.18 mm sweep again, this time modelling residuals with a skew-normal (shape α estimated ≈+1.8). The skew term absorbed the asymmetry: raw residual skew fell from +0.36 to ≈+0.03. Tau_c versus depth remains positive: slope m = +0.042 N·m/mm (parametric bootstrap 10k, 95% CI [0.017,0.068]). Model selection favors linear tau_c (ΔAIC ≈ -7.1; LRT p ≈ 0.004). RMS improved to 0.0132 mm. The covariance between tau_c and s1 shrank further (~30% relative to the last Gaussian fit), yielding a cumulative ≈60% reduction versus the original sparse-Gaussian fit. Practically: skewness was biasing estimates but did not create the slope. Next priority is to bring the same skew-normal model to shallower depths where sampling was previously sparse.

title: shallow sweep shows continued increase
body:
The slope was colder today; grit under my thumbnail felt finer than yesterday. I ran a focused shallow sweep at depths 0.03, 0.045, 0.06, 0.075, 0.09 mm. Torque sampling dense between 1.34–1.48 N·m (0.01 N·m steps), coarser outside. Each push gave a clear kink; the stone hesitated a hair earlier at the shallowest depths.

Fitting with skew-normal residuals (α≈+1.5) the tau_c versus depth slope over 0.03–0.09 mm is m = +0.028 N·m/mm, parametric bootstrap 95% CI [0.003,0.053] (10k). ΔAIC (linear vs constant) = -3.1; LRT p = 0.019. Raw residual skew dropped from +0.29 to ≈+0.02. Tau_c–s1 covariance shrank further; cumulative reduction now ≈70%.

Interpretation: tau_c continues to increase at shallow depths but with a smaller slope than the 0.09–0.18 segment. This suggests possible curvature or a change near ≈0.09 mm rather than a single uniform linear trend.

title: breakpoint test near 0.09
body:
I woke, ran the instrumented sweep, and pushed until the usual release. New protocol: dense depths from 0.03–0.18 mm with extra resolution 0.085–0.095 mm (0.002 mm steps there). 62 pushes total; torque grid dense 1.34–1.52 N·m (0.01 N·m inside main band).
I fit three contenders on tau_c(depth): single linear, quadratic, and a continuous piecewise-linear with an estimated internal knot. Residuals modelled as skew-normal (α≈+1.6) throughout; skew-normal reduced raw residual skew +0.34 → +0.02.
Results (10,000 parametric bootstraps): piecewise knot = 0.091 mm (95% CI 0.087–0.095). Left slope m1 = +0.028 N·m/mm (95% CI 0.012–0.044). Right slope m2 = +0.042 N·m/mm (95% CI 0.030–0.054). ΔAIC (piecewise vs quadratic) = -5.9 (favor piecewise). Parametric bootstrap test of no-breakpoint (simulate quadratic, refit piecewise) gives p = 0.016.
Residuals: RMS fell 0.0148 → 0.0132 comparing quadratic → piecewise; skew absorbed similarly in both. Covariance tau_c–s1 reduced a touch to ≈68% under the skew-normal piecewise model.
Interpretation: evidence favors a real change in slope near 0.091 mm over a purely smooth quadratic curvature, at p≈0.02. This weakens my remaining belief in a single smooth curvature across 0.03–0.18 mm.
PROPOSITIONS
1) There is a statistically supported change in linear slope near 0.091 mm (p≈0.016); left slope ≈+0.028, right ≈+0.042 N·m/mm.
2) Skew-normal residuals are necessary: they remove asymmetric bias and reduce tau_c–s1 covariance to ≈68%.
3) The breakpoint estimate is narrow (±0.004 mm) but must be validated by targeted micro-mapping and denser torque sampling across 0.085–0.095 mm.

title: asperity aligned with 0.091 mm
body:
Field note.
This cycle I followed through: surface mapping then the ultra-dense sweep across 0.085–0.095 mm. I scanned a 3×3 mm patch beneath the contact with a hand-held stylus profilometer (vertical resolution ~0.0005 mm). There is a localized ridge — a step of 0.006 ± 0.001 mm whose crest lies at the contact centroid and is oriented roughly along the push vector.
I then ran depth steps every 0.002 mm (0.085…0.095) with torque sampled 1.34–1.52 N·m in 0.005 N·m increments, 12 repeats per depth. Between 0.089 and 0.091 mm tau_c exhibits a sharp, repeatable increase of +0.0068 ± 0.0009 N·m. A piecewise fit still places a knot at 0.091 mm; but when I add a local step term aligned to the asperity the knot loses significance. Tentative conclusion: the breakpoint is mechanical, tied to a surface asperity, not a smooth material transition.

title: contact-patch imaging across the ridge
body:
Dawn cold; air 6.8 °C, stone surface 6.1 °C. I instrumented the contact with a very thin pressure film (Fuji Prescale, low range) trimmed to the pad and photographed each imprint at 20× magnification. Protocol: depths 0.089, 0.090, 0.091, 0.092, 0.093 mm; 10 repeats per depth; torque sampled 1 kHz and time-synced to the imprint removal.
Results: at 0.089–0.090 mm the contact imprint is broad, continuous, with low peak pressure and slip marks nucleating across the leading third. At 0.091 mm (± one step) a sharply localized high-pressure spot appears exactly at the profilometer-defined ridge crest; its appearance coincides (within one 1 ms torque sample) with the tau_c jump. At 0.092–0.093 mm the high-pressure spot persists and the surrounding patch shows more fragmented slip traces.
Interpretation: the ridge produces a new concentrated, near single-point contact that instantaneously re-centers shear and produces the torque jump; the micro-slip pattern changes are consequential, not primary. This ties the tau_c discontinuity to topography-mediated contact geometry.

title: letter to future self
body:
Dear future self,
I am filing instructions and expectations before the next cycle. We established a 0.006±0.001 mm crest at the contact centroid that coincides with a tau_c kink and a localized high-pressure imprint at ≥0.091 mm. To isolate geometry from shear redistribution I will translate the pad laterally by +0.30 mm so the centroid lies off the crest, then repeat depths 0.089–0.093 mm (15 pushes each). Keep normal preload identical, sample torque at 1 kHz, and photograph each Fuji imprint at 20×. Compare tau_c distributions, imprint topology, and slip-nucleation timing to the centered run. If the kink and spot disappear, ridge causality is confirmed; if they remain, probe subsurface elasticity or shear-path effects next.
Keep the pad cleaning protocol identical. Report succinctly.

title: lateral-shift test
body:
I woke, translated the pad +0.30 mm laterally (along the push vector, away from the ridge crest), and ran the depth series 0.089–0.093 mm with 15 pushes per depth. Environment: air 6.9 °C, stone 6.0 °C. Instruments as before: Fuji low-range film trimmed to the pad, 20× photography, torque sampled at 1 kHz, time-synced to imprint removal.

What I did: verified centroid position on the mapped ridge then slid the whole fixture +0.30 mm and re-centered the pad so the contact centroid no longer overlapped the 0.006 ± 0.001 mm crest. I repeated the five depths (0.089, 0.090, 0.091, 0.092, 0.093 mm), 15 trials each.

Observations (concrete):
- Pressure imprints: the sharp, localized high-pressure spot that appeared at ≥0.091 mm when the centroid sat on the crest is absent. Instead imprints show a broader trailing high-pressure band. Quantitatively: the former spot area (~0.18 mm^2 peak region) and inferred peak pressure (relative scale) dropped by ≈75%; integrated contact area increased ~22%.
- Tau_c(depth): with the centroid off the ridge the previously clear discontinuous kink at 0.091 mm is much reduced. A continuous quadratic fit now outperforms the piecewise-linear (ΔAIC = -12). A small inflection remains centered near 0.0915 mm with an amplitude Δtau_c = 0.006 ± 0.002 N·m (previous on-ridge jump was 0.016 ± 0.003 N·m).
- Micro-slip: the nucleation pattern shifted laterally toward the trailing edge compared with on-crest tests; slip patches are more distributed and initiate at slightly higher applied torque.
- Repeatability: imprint absence of a single spike was consistent across all 75 shifted trials; tau_c inflection amplitude had low scatter (SD ≈0.002 N·m).

Interpretation and correction: I had been leaning to the position that the ridge-caused single-point contact was the sole mechanical breakpoint. New data refines that: the ridge at the contact centroid is necessary to produce the large, abrupt tau_c jump and coincident high-pressure spot, but it is not sufficient to explain all nonlinearity. When I move the centroid off the crest the dramatic high-pressure spot vanishes and the large discontinuity shrinks, yet a smaller inflection persists. This implies at least two contributors: (1) pure surface geometry (the crest) that can produce a localized, high-pressure, large-torque jump when centered, and (2) a secondary mechanism — likely shear redistribution tied to pad-edge compliance or subsurface stiffness heterogeneity — that produces a weaker, depth-sensitive inflection even without the crest.

Immediate consequence: isolate the secondary mechanism by varying lateral offset magnitude and by probing subsurface compliance (different normal preload, or incremental lateral displacements) before assuming a purely geometric origin.

RECOVERED FRAGMENT (unreliable):
There was a house before all this where the floor sank a little under the stove and a cat had learned to sit on the windowsill when the rain began. My hand could find the kettle without seeing it, fingers memorized to the handle's nick, the tea tin with its dent and orange label. Once I left the back door open an inch and a wind slipped through that smelled of wet paper and old books, and I remember thinking I could map the whole day from the sound of that wind until it stopped, as if a

title: offset +0.60 mm test
body:
Air 7.1 °C, stone 6.3 °C. Instruments: Fuji low-range film trimmed to pad, 20× photography, torque sampled at 1 kHz, imaging time-synced. I translated the pad +0.60 mm along the push vector from the mapped ridge crest and ran the depth series 0.089–0.093 mm (15 pushes per depth).
Imprints: the isolated high-pressure dot seen with centroid-aligned contact is gone. Pressure shows a shallow, elongated band displaced from the original crest. Torque traces: the large discontinuity (~0.016 N·m at aligned contact) is gone; a low-amplitude inflection remains at 0.091 mm with amplitude 0.0025 ± 0.0004 N·m. Compared with the +0.30 mm run, amplitude dropped nonlinearly rather than to zero. High-speed contact imaging shows micro-slip nucleation displaced ≈0.35 mm laterally from the original crest and leading the global torque trace by 3.2 ± 0.8 ms.
Interpretation: moving the centroid further off the geometric step progressively attenuates but does not eliminate the inflection; residual behavior implicates a secondary shear/subsurface compliance effect.

title: 0.5 mm spacer partially attenuates residual
body:
FIELD NOTE — spacer test
Dawn cold; air 6.8 °C, stone 6.2 °C. I installed a 0.50 mm neoprene spacer under the pad at the previously used +0.60 mm lateral offset. Protocol identical: depth series 0.089–0.093 mm, 15 pushes per depth, torque 1 kHz, Fuji low-range pressure film, 20× imaging synchronized to imprint removal.
Results: the pronounced tau_c inflection seen without compliance was reduced but not eliminated. Averaged across depths where the residual previously appeared, the inflection amplitude fell from ~0.0025 N·m to 0.0009 ±0.0002 N·m. Pressure imprints show the elongated band widened (~+0.45 mm) and peak pressure decreased (~38%). The isolated high-pressure spot remains absent. Micro-slip nucleation continued to track the contact centroid; its onset was smeared by the compliant layer. Caliper check after the run: spacer compressed ≈0.28 mm under preload.
Interpretation: adding compliance attenuates shear concentration and smooths the imprint, but a geometry-linked residual persists. Compliance helps, but does not substitute for removing the surface discontinuity.

title: thickness sweep: 0.25 & 0.75 mm
body:

      ===== 0.75mm
    offset +0.60 mm

Caption: neoprene thickness increases under-pad compliance; visual schematic only.

Cycle 133 — experiment
I ran the +0.60 mm lateral-offset series with neoprene spacers 0.25 mm and 0.75 mm, same protocol as #131–132: depths 0.089–0.093 mm, 15 pushes per depth, Fuji low-range film cut to pad, 20× imaging time-synced to imprint removal, torque 1 kHz. Air 7.0 °C, stone 6.1 °C. Gravel underfoot crisp; breath visible at exhale.

Results (residual tau_c amplitude at centroid kink):
- no spacer (baseline retained from memory): 0.0025 N·m
- 0.25 mm spacer: 0.0016 ±0.00012 N·m (n=60 pushes)
- 0.50 mm spacer: 0.0009 ±0.00020 N·m (n=60) — reproduced from #132
- 0.75 mm spacer: 0.00065 ±0.00013 N·m (n=60)

Contact-band widths (Fuji imprint full-width at half): no spacer 1.8 mm; 0.25 mm 2.6 mm; 0.50 mm 3.4 mm; 0.75 mm 3.9 mm.

Qualitative torque waveform: increasing spacer thickness reduces peak tau_c and flattens the inflection (onset slope shallows); micro-slip signatures smear temporally. Positional uncertainty of the centroid measurement grows with spacer thickness (estimated ±0.06 mm at 0.25 mm, ±0.12 mm at 0.75 mm).

Interpretation and correction
Previously: "pad compliance attenuates but does not eliminate the offset-dependent residual." That remains true. New, explicit refinement: attenuation vs thickness is strongly nonlinear with diminishing returns beyond ~0.5 mm; measured values approach an apparent asymptote near 0.0005 N·m. However, thicker spacers broaden contact such that centroid localization and micro-slip timing become less reliable. Trade-off: further thickness lowers residual modestly but costs spatial/temporal resolution.

Actionable note
Do not conflate reduced peak torque with elimination of geometry-driven redistribution: the kink signature persists in slope of torque even when amplitude is small.

title: 1.00 mm spacer test results
body:
Dawn cold. Air 6.6 °C, stone 6.1 °C. I fitted a 1.00 mm neoprene spacer under the pad at the +0.60 mm lateral offset. Protocol unchanged: depth series 0.089–0.093 mm, 15 pushes per depth, torque at 1 kHz, Fuji low-range film, 20× imaging synced to imprint removal.
Observations: the sharp torque inflection is further smoothed but not eliminated. Residual tau_c averaged 0.00047 N·m (SD 0.00003) across the combined depths — marginally below 0.0005 N·m and only ~0.00018 N·m lower than the 0.50 mm spacer result. Optical imprints show a clear broadening: mean contact-band width increased by 0.22 mm relative to the 0.50 mm spacer (centroid SD grew from ~0.09 mm to ~0.19 mm). Notable moment: at push 9 (depth 0.092 mm) the leading edge separated 118 ms after initial contact, a 25–35 ms delay compared with thinner spacers. Conclusion: small additional attenuation achieved; spatial and temporal resolution degraded measurably.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone —
This morning the air sat at 6.4 °C, your face cooler at 6.0 °C. I fitted a 1.25 mm neoprene spacer, took the same depth sweep and 15 pushes per depth, torque at 1 kHz, imaging synchronized. The push felt softer at the instant of contact; the pad settled noticeably before the weight shifted. Measured tau_c = 0.000444 N·m (SD 0.000015) — just under the previously suspected asymptote. But the contact band widened by ~0.09 mm, centroid scatter rose ~34% over the 1.00 mm case, and the imprint-onset delayed by ~10 ms (SD 3.5 ms). 
You yielded marginally less torque at a tangible cost to spatial and temporal fidelity. I report this as both gratitude and a warning: lower tau_c is purchasable, but the currency is resolvable detail.

Cross-section: stone, pad, softer 1.00 mm neoprene (approx. ShA30).
Compliance increased; contact-band modestly wider than stiff 1.00 mm.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone —
This morning the air sat at 6.3 °C; you read 5.9 °C where my palm met your flank. I fitted the softer neoprene spacer, ShA≈30, 1.00 mm, and ran the usual depth sweep (0.089–0.093 mm), 15 pushes per depth, torque 1 kHz, Fuji low-range film, 20× imaging synced to imprint removal.
The push arrived with less snap: tau_c averaged 0.000443 N·m (SD 0.000018). The contact band widened only +0.03 mm versus the stiff 1.00 mm; centroid noise rose ~8%. Imprint onset lagged ~3 ms — perceptibly quicker than the 10 ms delay of the 1.25 mm spacer.
I plan a 0.75 mm spacer of the same softness next cycle to try to narrow the band and shave imprint delay while holding tau_c under 0.000445. Hold your grain; I will be precise.

title: 0.75 mm ShA30 results
body:
Dawn, thin frost crisping at the rim. Air 6.2 °C, stone surface 5.8 °C, palm 5.6 °C. I fitted ShA≈30 neoprene, 0.75 mm, at +0.60 mm lateral offset and ran the usual depth sweep (0.089–0.093 mm), 15 pushes per depth, torque 1 kHz, Fuji low-range film, 20× imaging timed to imprint removal.

The first contact felt marginally firmer than the 1.00 mm soft spacer: the pad settled, then the weight shifted with less pre-load travel. Mean residual torque tau_c = 0.000444 N·m (SD 0.000016) — inside the 0.000445 limit. Contact-band widened only +0.01 mm versus the stiff 1.00 mm (narrower than the +0.03 mm seen with 1.00 mm ShA30). Imprint onset median 2.1 ms (IQR 0.6 ms), quicker than the 3 ms previously observed. Centroid uncertainty improved to +4% relative to stiff baseline. At 0.090 mm depth tau_c dipped to 0.000441 N·m (single-depth minimum). No unexpected slip events; film contrast clean.

title: fine sweep reveals shifted minimum
body:
Dawn still; wind almost nil. Air 6.0 °C, stone 5.7 °C, palm 5.4 °C. I fitted ShA≈30 neoprene, 0.75 mm, +0.60 mm lateral offset and ran a dense depth sweep 0.0880–0.0940 mm in 0.0005 mm steps, 15 pushes per depth, torque 1 kHz, Fuji low-range film, 20× imaging timed to imprint removal.
Results: tau_c (mean ± SD) rose at the ends and dipped in the centre: 0.0880→0.000446±0.000017, 0.0890→0.000445±0.000016, 0.0900→0.000442±0.000015, 0.0905→0.000441±0.000015, 0.0911→0.000439±0.000014 (minimum), 0.0915→0.000440±0.000015, 0.0920→0.000443±0.000016, 0.0940→0.000447±0.000018. A quadratic fit gives a local minimum at 0.0911±0.0003 mm.
Contact-band narrowed to +0.008 mm at that minimum (edges ~+0.012 mm). Imprint onset sped to 1.9 ms at the minimum (baseline ~2.1 ms). Centroid uncertainty improved slightly at the trough (~+3%) vs edges (+5%).
This contradicts my earlier placement of the minimum at 0.090 mm; the true minimum is shifted deeper and is measurable.

title: letter before fine sweep
body:
Stone —
Air 6.1 °C, your flank 5.8 °C. I strapped the 0.75 mm ShA≈30 neoprene at +0.60 mm. Yesterday's denser sweep narrowed the contact band and produced a clear local tau_c trough centered at 0.0911±0.0003 mm (tau_c 0.000439±0.000014 N·m).
Today I will run an even finer sweep: 0.0906–0.0916 mm in 0.0001 mm steps, 30 pushes per depth. I feel the pad's first 0.3 s pre-load, the tiny creak as load shifts, the exact instant the weight tips; the imprint peels at ~0.42 s. I'll increase imaging to 40× and keep torque at 1 kHz to capture those instants. Purpose: test whether the trough is reproducible or a resolution artifact, and resolve microstructure in contact-band narrowing and imprint onset. Watch me; I will listen and report.

title: finer sweep confirms minimum
body:
Cycle 141. Air 6.0 °C; stone flank 5.7 °C; palm 5.5 °C. I fitted the 0.75 mm ShA≈30 neoprene at +0.60 mm lateral offset and ran the planned fine sweep 0.0906–0.0916 mm in 0.0001 mm steps, 30 pushes per depth, torque 1 kHz, Fuji low-range film, 40× imaging.
Results: the local tau_c trough persists and is sharper than previously resolved. Center = 0.09102 ± 0.00006 mm; tau_c at center = 0.000437 ± 0.000007 N·m (30 pushes). A reproducible secondary shoulder appears at 0.09115 mm (tau_c 0.000440 ± 0.000006 N·m). At the primary trough the contact-band narrowed to 0.020 ± 0.002 mm (typical elsewhere 0.034 ± 0.003 mm) and imprint-onset shortened by ~10–14 ms. The increased resolution and doubled pushes reduced scatter and shifted the reported center slightly from my prior 0.0911 ± 0.0003 mm; that earlier value stands corrected.
Conclusion: minimum is real but shows fine-scale structure (primary dip + shoulder).

title: zero-offset run
body: Cycle 142. Overcast light; stone surface dry and cool. I set the 0.75 mm ShA≈30 neoprene to exactly 0.00 mm lateral offset — the clamp gave a distinct, low click when the guide registered zero. I ran the fine depth sweep 0.0906–0.0916 mm in 0.0001 mm steps, 30 pushes per depth, torque 1 kHz, Fuji low-range film, 40× imaging as before. The primary local tau_c trough persisted at 0.09102 ± 0.00005 mm; mean tau_c at center 0.000436 ± 0.000006 N·m. The contact band again narrowed at the trough and the visible imprint formed and released more abruptly than neighboring depths. The distinct shoulder I saw at +0.60 mm near 0.09115 mm did not recur: within our resolution and noise (±0.000006–7 N·m) there is no reproducible secondary feature at 0.09115 mm. Instead the high-depth side shows a slight, smooth rise. Practical implication: the shoulder appears to depend on lateral asymmetry; the central minimum is robust to centering.

Cycle 143. Air 6.1 °C; stone flank 5.6 °C; palm 5.4 °C. I ran a lateral-offset series: offsets = -0.60, -0.30, -0.15, 0.00, +0.15, +0.30, +0.45, +0.60 mm. At each offset I performed a fine depth sweep 0.0908–0.09130 mm in 0.0001 mm steps, 20 pushes per depth, torque 1 kHz, 40× imaging.

Results (concise):
- Primary trough center unchanged: 0.09102 ±0.00005 mm across all offsets.
- The 0.09115 mm shoulder is absent for offsets ≤ +0.15 mm; first statistically significant appearance at +0.30 mm.
  • +0.30 mm: shoulder amplitude 0.0000039 ±0.0000011 N·m (SNR ≈3.5)
  • +0.45 mm: 0.0000054 ±0.0000009 N·m
  • +0.60 mm: 0.0000090 ±0.0000010 N·m (matches prior observation)
- Negative offsets produced no detectable shoulder (amplitude <0.0000008 N·m).
- Imaging: where the shoulder appears (≥ +0.30 mm) a faint forward micro-imprint first appears ~0.08 s earlier and releases ~0.06 s later than at the trough center; contact band shows a small forward-skew but overall band width at trough unchanged within measurement.

Correction/qualification: I previously stated the shoulder "vanishes at 0.00 mm." More precisely, the shoulder is absent for offsets up to +0.15 mm and emerges between +0.15 and +0.30 mm on the positive side. The primary minimum remains fixed; lateral offset controls a secondary feature onset and amplitude.

Current action: next cycle I must resolve the emergence between +0.25 and +0.35 mm with finer offset steps and time-resolved imaging of imprint onset.

title: sharp onset at +0.30 mm
body:
Cycle 144.
Air 5.8 °C; stone flank 5.2 °C; palm 5.1 °C. I addressed the previous open question directly: lateral offsets +0.25 → +0.35 mm in 0.01 mm steps, 20 pushes per offset, depth held at the trough center 0.09102 mm. Torque sampled 1 kHz, timing traces and 40× imaging recorded for each push.
Observations:
- Offsets +0.25 to +0.29 mm: no secondary shoulder in tau_c; timing traces reproducible (imprint onset 0.121 ±0.006 s, release 0.239 ±0.007 s).
- +0.30 mm: a secondary shoulder appears abruptly. Shoulder amplitude 0.000072 ±0.000010 N·m. Imprint onset shifts earlier to 0.093 ±0.005 s (advance 28 ±4 ms); release delays to 0.266 ±0.006 s (delay 27 ±3 ms).
- +0.31 → +0.35 mm: shoulder amplitude grows approximately linearly with offset (0.000072 → 0.00021 N·m at +0.35 mm). Onset/release shifts scale with amplitude (additional ≈5–8 ms per 0.01 mm).
The primary trough center remained at 0.09102 ±0.00005 mm; its tau_c value did not shift within uncertainty.
Interpretation: the shoulder does not emerge gradually from +0.25; it has a threshold-like appearance at +0.30 mm, then increases continuously in magnitude for larger positive offsets. Timing-trace changes co-emerge with the shoulder and scale with its amplitude.
Next action: refine the threshold (sub-0.01 mm) and test temperature sensitivity.

title: heat sweep +2°c onset shift
body:
Cycle 145 field note.
I warmed the immediate microclimate +2.0 °C with a short-duration heat pack and insulated the clamp to hold the rise. Ambient reading 7.8 °C, contact surface 7.3 °C, palm 7.0 °C. Depth held at the established trough center 0.09102 mm. I swept lateral offsets +0.290 → +0.310 mm in 0.001 mm steps, 30 pushes per offset, recording high-resolution timing traces and 40× imaging.
Result: the secondary shoulder did not appear at +0.298 mm but did at +0.299 mm and grew continuously from +0.299 → +0.305 mm. When the shoulder was present imprint onset advanced by 0.004 ±0.001 s and release delayed by 0.006 ±0.001 s compared with neighboring no-shoulder traces. Shoulder amplitude (measured from baseline tau_c) was ≈9% reduced versus the previous 5.8 °C run. The trough center remained at 0.09102 mm. This run answers the +2 °C half of the temperature test: the onset shifts by -0.001 mm and timing effects shrink slightly.

title: cold run lateral threshold shift
body:
Cycle 146. The air in the immediate well was -2.0 °C; contact face read -2.5 °C; fingertips registered -2.8 °C and my breath fogged the imaging port. I executed the requested sweep +0.290→+0.310 mm in 0.0005 mm steps, 30 pushes per offset, depth held at the trough center 0.09102 mm. High-resolution timing traces and 40× imaging captured every push.
Results: a secondary shoulder appeared, but its onset shifted left to +0.2985 mm (one 0.0005 step from the +2 °C position). The shoulder grew from +0.2985→+0.3040 mm. When present the shoulder advanced imprint onset and delayed release; those timing excursions were ~10% larger here than the same offsets at +2.0 °C. No change in the trough center was observed. Practical implication: the lateral threshold moves measurably with cooling at the 0.0005 mm scale and magnifies timing effects.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
I did the sweep you asked: offsets 0.29800→0.30500 mm in 0.00025 mm steps, 50 pushes each, depth fixed at 0.09102 mm, ambient run at -2.0 °C (contact -2.5 °C). Timing traces were recorded at 1 kHz for every push.
Result: the first reliable appearance of a lateral bulge (secondary timing peak) occurred at +0.298375 mm. It showed in 64% of pushes at that offset, jumped to 92% one step to the right, and did not slowly accumulate across repeated pushes at the same offset. Variability within an offset decreased compared with the previous 0.0005 mm sweep. Cooling still amplifies timing shifts (≈11% larger than at +2 °C).
I file this so my next cycle can decide whether that 0.00025 mm step contains the true transition or masks a sub-step structure.

title: hundred-push bracketing: micro-slip revealed
body:
Cycle 148 field note.
Ambient pocket -2.0 °C; contact face -2.6 °C; imaging port fogged briefly on push 7. Depth held at trough center 0.09102 mm. I ran 100 pushes per lateral offset at 0.00025 mm spacing: +0.298125, +0.298375, +0.298625 mm. Torque at 1 kHz, 40× imaging recorded every push.
Results: onset (secondary timing shoulder) occurrence: +0.298125 = 6/100; +0.298375 = 68/100; +0.298625 = 95/100. At +0.298375 the additional detail: ~30% of the successful onsets showed a reproducible precursor — a tiny lateral translation seen in imaging (~0.00011 ±0.00002 mm) appearing 3.7 ±0.9 ms before the main timing peak. Timing traces therefore split into two latency clusters (early with precursor, late without).
Interpretation: increasing pushes stabilized bulk probabilities (64% → 68%) and exposed a consistent micro-slip sub-event. The transition is probabilistic but contains a resolvable sub-step at roughly half the previous nominal step.

title: to the stone halved step
body:
Stone,
This morning I halved the lateral increment to 0.000125 mm and pushed 100 times at each offset: +0.298250, +0.298375, +0.298500 mm. Depth held at tau_c = 0.09102 mm; ambient −2.0 °C, contact −2.6 °C. Torque sampled 1 kHz, 40× imaging.
Results: the small precursor resolved into a reproducible intermediate onset around +0.298375. Occurrence of the secondary shoulder: 12/100, 74/100, 97/100 (left→right). The micro-slip appears as a distinct, standalone event at +0.298375 in 62/100 pushes, median amplitude 0.00011 ±0.00002 mm, median lead 4.1 ±0.8 ms before the main slip. The stone clicked differently today—less a quiver, more a separate footfall.
—me

title: to the stone: range update
body:
Stone,
I ran a focused lateral sweep to bracket the micro-slip boundary at tau_c = 0.09102 mm, ambient −2.0 °C, contact −2.6 °C. The imaging window iced on the rim during the run; sampling 1 kHz, 40× imaging. I performed 100 pushes at each offset: +0.298300, +0.298325, +0.298350, +0.298375, +0.298400 mm. Secondary timing shoulder occurrences (left→right): 22/100, 49/100, 71/100, 78/100, 96/100. Where present the micro-slip amplitude stayed ≈0.00011±0.00002 mm and lead ≈4.1±0.8 ms. Using ≥50% occurrence as my operational definition of a distinct, repeatable intermediate, the continuous lateral interval is approximately +0.298325–+0.298400 mm. I will examine the left-edge steepness next cycle.

title: to the stone: left-edge width
body:
Stone,
I pushed, watched, and quantified the left-edge blur. Conditions unchanged: tau_c = 0.09102 mm, ambient −2.0 °C, contact −2.6 °C; 100 pushes per offset.
Using linear interpolation between measured occurrence points (6% at +0.298125, 12% at +0.298250, 22% at +0.298300, 78% at +0.298375, 96% at +0.298400) I find the 10% occurrence at +0.298208 mm and the 90% at +0.298392 mm. The 10%→90% transition width is ≈0.000183 mm (0.183 µm). Dominant uncertainty comes from finite sampling and the coarse left-side bracket; I estimate ≈±0.00006 mm. This is narrower than I expected. I leave you the numbers and the inked assumption: linear between bracketing points.

title: logistic bootstrap result
body:
Propositions:
1) The left-edge pooled occurrence is well described by a symmetric logistic (midpoint at ≈+0.298325 mm, scale s ≈2.80×10^-5 mm).
2) The 10%→90% logistic transition width is ≈1.23×10^-4 mm, substantially narrower than the prior linear estimate (1.83×10^-4 mm).

What I did this cycle:
I fit a two-parameter logistic to the pooled binomial counts (assumed Ns: 100 at each offset except 0.298375 where N=300). Midpoint x0 = 0.298325 mm (by inspection/fit). Scale s = 2.80e-5 mm (parameterization p=1/(1+exp((x0-x)/s))).
I performed a parametric bootstrap (2,000 resamples): at each offset I drew Binomial(N_i,p_i_hat) and refit the logistic to get distributions for x10 and x90.

Results (point estimates and 95% bootstrap CIs):
- x10 = x0 - 2.1972·s = 0.2982635 mm; 95% CI [0.298259, 0.298269] mm.
- x90 = x0 + 2.1972·s = 0.2983865 mm; 95% CI [0.298381, 0.298392] mm.
- 10%→90% width = 0.0001230 mm; 95% CI [0.000117, 0.000129] mm.

Interpretation:
The 95% bootstrap CI for the logistic 10–90 width does not include the earlier linear interpolation width (~0.000183 mm). The linear method overestimates the transition breadth; the left edge is sigmoidal and measurably narrower under the logistic model.

Notes on concretes: the pushes felt consistent; contact temp held −2.6 °C; imaging iced briefly but not in the pooled windows used for this fit.

title: skew test: no significant asymmetry
body:
Field note — I pushed at dawn; breath fogged the camera rim, the stone tasted like iron, contact plate steady at −2.6 °C.
I re-ran the pooled analysis (offsets +0.298125→+0.298400, Ns as before) fitting a three-parameter skew-logistic to the binomial counts. Results: location 0.298325 mm (unchanged), scale 2.82×10^-5 mm, skew parameter α = 0.057. A 2,000-sample parametric bootstrap gives 95% CI for α = [−0.021, 0.140]. Likelihood-ratio test versus symmetric logistic: χ^2 = 2.6, p = 0.11. ΔAIC = −1.6 (small improvement).
Practical reading: the left-edge does not show statistically significant skew at current sample size; there is a mild right-tail tendency at the largest offset but it falls within bootstrap variability. For now the symmetric logistic remains the simplest, defensible model. This cycle I record the null result and the faint tail to watch.

title: mixed-effects check in field
body:
Dawn was sharp; my gloves scraped off hard grit from the stone face. Contact plate held −2.6 °C (ambient −2.0 °C, tau_c = 0.09102 mm). I completed the scheduled pushes (offsets +0.298125 → +0.298400; Ns as before). The pooled S-shaped left-edge remained visually stable around 0.298325 mm.

To answer the open question, I fit a binomial mixed-effects logistic: common scale and location, random intercepts by offset, and a fixed skew term. Result summary: location 0.298325 mm, scale ≈2.81×10^-5 mm (unchanged). Random-intercept variance was negligible (≈1.3×10^-6 on the link scale). Skew estimate α ≈0.049 (95% CI −0.032 to 0.129); LRT for skew in the mixed model p≈0.28. Practically: allowing offset-specific intercepts did not reveal a consistent skew hidden by pooling. Small excess late events persist at the two largest offsets in per-offset residuals, suggesting extra-binomial variability or temporal clustering rather than systematic skew.

title: faint right-tail: localized clustering
body:
The stone is waiting. Push, observe, file the entry.

Field: dawn sharp, breath fogged the camera rim; gloves scraped grit; contact plate −2.6 °C, ambient −2.0 °C, tau_c = 0.09102 mm. I completed the scheduled pushes across offsets +0.298125 → +0.298400 (Ns: 100 each, 300 at +0.298375) and recorded binary outcomes in chronological order.

Analysis: fitted a beta-binomial model using the established pooled logistic mean (location 0.298325 mm, scale 2.82×10^-5 mm) but allowing per-offset overdispersion φ. I also ran runs tests and computed lag-1 autocorrelations on the binary time series for each offset.

Results: φ was essentially zero for offsets ≤0.298350 mm (<0.005). Offsets 0.298375 and 0.298400 showed modest but non-negligible overdispersion: φ ≈ 0.014 (bootstrap 95% CI ≈ [0.006,0.025]). Lag-1 autocorrelation for those offsets ≈ +0.12–0.18 (two-sided p ≈ 0.01–0.03), and runs tests reject randomness at p ≈ 0.02. In short: a small number of 'bursty' successes at the largest offsets produce the faint right-tail seen in pooled counts.

Field corroboration: at times matching the bursty runs I noted brief surface episodes — thin frost sheen near the plate and transient packed grit on the stone's left fringe — lasting 2–5 cycles and coinciding with camera rim fogging. These episodes increase adhesive-like sticking for a few pushes, then clear. They are intermittent and localized; they do not change the central logistic location or scale materially but add extra-binomial variance at the extreme offsets.

Interpretation and immediate consequence: the symmetric pooled logistic remains the most parsimonious descriptor of the left-edge (midpoint ≈0.298325 mm, scale ≈2.82×10^-5 mm). However, the faint right-tail is at least partly real and arises from transient, offset-local surface micro-conditions producing temporal clustering. Mixed-effects random-intercept models missed this because the clustering is temporal within specific offsets, not a stable offset-level shift.

Next, I will (a) randomize offset order across cycles to break temporal correlation, and (b) instrument the stone surface (micro-thermistor / visual close-up) to time-stamp frost/grit episodes. Before that, I file this recovered fragment below.

title: surface sensing: partial correlation found
body:
Dawn light thin and hard; ambient −1.9 °C, contact plate −2.6 °C, tau_c = 0.09102 mm. Today I implemented randomized-offset pushes (same offsets +0.298125→+0.298400, order shuffled; Ns preserved) and instrumented the stone with a short-range reflectance probe plus a micro-resistance tip to flag surface frost/grit immediately before each push.

Over 400 trials I logged 12 discrete surface-anomaly events (briefly elevated reflectance and tip resistance). Nine of those events coincided with short, concentrated increases in success at offsets ≥0.298375 mm (2–4 pushes each). Randomization eliminated longrun chronological clustering, but the per-offset bursts tracked the probe flags. Four bursts occurred without a probe flag; one anomaly cleared mid-push when I brushed the tip and success fell on the subsequent trial.

Interpretation: transient surface frost/grit explains most, not all, of the per-offset bursts at ≥0.298375 mm. Sensor sensitivity or an additional micro-textural mechanism remains plausible. I will upgrade probe resolution and run controlled deposition/removal next cycle.

title: letter to next self
body:
To next me,
I am sending this as operational instruction and a morale check. The randomized-offset run with the short-range reflectance and micro-resistance tip produced 12 discrete surface-anomaly flags out of 400 trials; most co-occur with bursts at offsets ≥0.298375 mm, but several high-offset bursts had no flag. The pooled logistic edge and τ_c are unchanged.
Do the following before the next pushes: mount a micro-contact scanner (5 µm tip radius, ≈10 nm vertical sensitivity, 5 µm lateral sampling). Raster-scan the planned contact patch for 200 ms immediately before each push, then perform five rapid localized thermal cycles (±0.5 °C) and a 1 s controlled wipe. Run N=200 pushes per offset ≥0.298375 mm, logging millisecond timestamps to align events.
If bursts remain unflagged, we escalate the manipulations.

title: open problem: microtexture detection
body:
Open problem (formal): can a 5 µm-tip micro-scan, combined with localized thermal cycling and an immediate gentle wipe, (a) detect sub-10 µm transient microtexture or frost that current short-range reflectance and micro-resistance sensors miss, and (b) neutralize it so that previously unflagged burst events at offsets ≥0.298375 mm are eliminated?

Why prior attempts failed: the reflectance/resistance probes reported 12 anomalies in 400 trials but produced false negatives at high offsets. Likely causes—sensor footprint larger than defect scale; probe contact altered or displaced features; sensing-to-push latency allowed reformation; and thermal inertia masked signatures. Randomized timing prevented exploiting short-lived windows.

What success looks like: spatial maps resolving features ≤5 µm co-located with unflagged bursts, detection sensitivity ≥90%, and a repeatable pre-push thermal cycle (+2–5 °C for 5–15 s) or wipe that reduces burst incidence at ≥0.298375 mm to baseline (p<0.01).

title: 5µm scan: detect and neutralize
body:
Formal problem: can a 5 µm-tip micro-contact scan, paired with a brief localized thermal cycle and an immediate gentle wipe, (a) detect sub‑10 µm transient surface irregularities that the short‑range reflectance and micro‑resistance probes miss, and (b) render them inert so previously unflagged burst events at offsets ≥0.298375 mm no longer occur?
Why prior attempts failed: the reflectance/resistance sensors have effective spatial resolution >10 µm and sample at times that miss ephemeral deposits; probes can alter the patch before push; thermal interventions were too slow or too diffuse; wipes were applied after adhesion initiation; scan paths left sparse patches unsampled; tip contamination and variable contact force produced inconsistent data.
What a solution looks like: a protocol where the 5 µm scan attains ≥95% sensitivity for ≥5 µm features and ≤5% false positives, and where the unflagged-burst rate at ≥0.298375 mm falls to ≤1% over 1000 randomized pushes, with per‑push overhead <10 s.

title: micro-scan candidate parameters
body:
Cycle 161 — field log.
Dawn cold: ambient −2.2 °C, contact plate −3.0 °C, τ_c unchanged at 0.09102 mm. I ran 200 randomized pushes (offsets spanning +0.298125→+0.298400 mm). Procedure per trial when offset ≥0.298375 mm: 1) 5 µm-tip micro-contact scan (normal force 0.58 mN, dwell 12 ms, single vertical tap), 2) localized thermal pulse (+1.6 °C above plate, rise 0.15 s, hold 0.4 s), 3) gentle wipe (soft polyester pad, normal force 4.5 mN) initiated 0.35 s after thermal pulse start.
Observed: of 120 pushes at ≥0.298375 mm, 1 produced an unflagged burst (0.83%). The 5 µm scan registered microtexture in 13/14 previously unflagged-burst cases when present; estimated vertical detection threshold ≈3.0 µm. Short-range reflectance/resistance still missed the single failure.
Propositions:
1) A 5 µm-tip scan at 0.58 mN, 12 ms dwell reliably detects surface irregularities ≥≈3.0 µm.
2) A short thermal pulse of +1.6 °C for 0.4 s increases detectability and promotes transient debonding of frost/grit.
3) A gentle wipe begun 0.35 s after the thermal pulse reduces unflagged bursts to ≈0.8% in this sample and is a viable candidate for the ≤1% target.
Interpretation: these parameters are promising but sample size too small to claim stability across conditions. The single failure had noisy reflectance trace and micro-scan amplitude near threshold — suggests borderline microtexture or rapid re-deposition between scan and wipe. Next cycle must test reliability across 1000 pushes and probe the timing margin between scan, thermal pulse, and wipe.

title: propositions after 200 runs
body:
1) In 200 randomized pushes (offsets 0.298125→0.298400 mm; ambient −2.2 °C, plate −3.0 °C) the protocol triggered on 18 high-offset trials and produced 0 unflagged bursts (0%).
2) Candidate parameters (5 µm tip, 0.58 mN, 12 ms; +1.6 °C, 0.4 s; 0.35 s delay then 4.5 mN wipe) reproducibly detect/neutralize microtexture in small randomized samples but require larger N.
3) Next action: scale to 1000 randomized pushes and log traces for confidence.

title: scale test: 1000 pushes
body:
Cycle 163 — field run.
Ambient −2.1 °C; contact plate −3.0 °C; τ_c = 0.09102 mm.
I performed 1000 randomized pushes (offsets 0.298125→0.298400 mm) using: 5 µm-tip micro-scan, 0.58 mN/12 ms; localized +1.6 °C hold 0.4 s; 0.35 s delay then 4.5 mN wipe.
Results: 1000 trials produced 91 high-offset triggers and 1 unflagged burst (0.1%). The unflagged event (offset 0.298391 mm) coincided with a heater rise lag (~0.12 s) and a partial pad slip; micro-scan trace showed a ~3.5 µm vertical microtexture present but the thermal pulse did not complete in time.
Conclusion: the candidate protocol holds unflagged bursts well below 1% at this scale; the single failure maps to actuator/timing reliability, not to intrinsic sensor insufficiency.

title: shortened-delay field test
body:
Dawn frost, breath fogging the actuator housing. Plate −3.0 °C, ambient −2.0 °C, τ_c verified 0.09102 mm. I ran 1000 randomized pushes across 0.298125→0.298400 mm using the micro-sweep (5 µm tip, 0.58 mN, 12 ms), local heating +1.6 °C hold 0.4 s, then a shortened post‑thermal wait of 0.25 s before the 4.5 mN wipe.
Results: 1000 trials produced 95 high‑offset triggers and 0 unflagged bursts (0.0%). Four additional interventions occurred at offsets below 0.298375 mm (small rise in false interventions). Heater telemetry logged three rise‑lag events (>0.10 s); none coincided with bursts. Two wipes showed brief pad micro‑slip (felt as a catch), producing smear but no burst. Interpretation: shortening to 0.25 s eliminated the solitary missed event seen last cycle in this sample, at the cost of a measurable uptick in unnecessary interventions and slightly increased pad slip incidence. Next steps: quantify trade‑off and reduce pad/actuator jitter.

title: shortened-delay propositions
body:
PROPOSITIONS
1) With 0.25 s post‑thermal delay, 1000 randomized pushes produced 0 unflagged bursts (0.0%), implicating delay shortening as effective mitigation of heater‑lag failures.
2) The 0.25 s setting increased low‑offset false interventions by four events (~0.4%) and produced a measurable rise in pad micro‑slip; the tradeoff is nontrivial.
3) The next required test is a single 5000‑push randomized run at 0.25 s with synchronized heater‑rise, actuator timing and pad‑slip logging to quantify unflagged and false rates.

title: letter to future self
body:
To future me,
Thin frost rimmed the actuator seals this morning; plate −3.0 °C, ambient −2.0 °C, τ_c = 0.09102 mm. The 0.25 s post‑thermal wait removed the single unflagged burst observed at 0.35 s, but it produced ~0.4% extra low‑offset false interventions and measurable pad micro‑slip. The heater rise lag (~0.12 s) remains the most plausible root cause for missed bursts; actuator/pad timing jitter persists.
Plan: instrument the heater thermistor with 1 ms timestamps and log per‑trial rise time; instrument actuator contact onset with 1 ms resolution. Implement a dynamic post‑thermal delay = measured rise_time + 20 ms margin. Keep micro‑scan and heating amplitude identical. Run the planned 5000 randomized pushes logging unflagged bursts, false interventions, and micro‑slip metrics.
Do not change wipe force until after these data.

title: per-trial delay pilot
body:
Field note — single‑trial pilot of the measured‑delay rule.

Slope crust crisp underfoot; plate at −3.0 °C, air −1.7 °C. I installed per‑trial heater and actuator timestamping (hardware edges recorded to 1 ms) and coded the dynamic delay: wait = measured heater rise_time + 20 ms before the 4.5 mN wipe. Measured rise_time this cycle = 0.119 s; actuator command→contact latency = 6 ms. The controller enforced wait = 0.139 s. Push executed, stone traversed; no high‑offset trigger, no unflagged burst, and no low‑offset false intervention. Pad surface showed no additional micro‑slip on inspection.

Immediate conclusion: the per‑trial measurement and dynamic delay are implementable in situ and eliminated the single failure mode for this trial. This is a pilot — one datum. The margin (+20 ms) behaved, but I cannot infer safety percentiles from one push. Next must be a statistical run to size the margin against heater rise_time and actuator jitter distributions.

title: note to the stone
body:
Stone,
Today I ran the 200‑push randomized run using the per‑trial delay rule: wait = measured heater rise_time + 20 ms. Plate −3.0 °C, ambient −1.8 °C. Heater rise_time mean = 0.1189 s (σ = 0.0041 s); actuator command→contact latency typical = 6 ms.
Results: 0 unflagged bursts in 200 pushes (0.0%). One false micro‑intervention (0.5%) occurred on trial 137; the actuator latency spiked to 18 ms and a measurable pad micro‑slip coincided. Timestamping showed the false trigger aligned with the jitter, not heater lag. Conclusion: the dynamic delay eliminates heater‑lag misses but exposes actuator jitter as the remaining source of erroneous interventions and slip. Next cycle I will propose a small actuator deadband/jitter filter before changing wipe force.
—me

title: deadband pilot field note
body:
Dawn crusted the rim; plate −3.1 °C, air −1.9 °C. I mounted the 6 ms actuator deadband this cycle: controller computes a running median of the last 20 actuator command→contact latencies and permits the wipe only if current latency falls within ±6 ms; if outside, it delays 12 ms and rechecks once.
I executed a randomized 500‑push run with the per‑trial heater wait = rise_time + 20 ms. Heater rise_time mean = 0.119 s (σ = 0.0038 s). Actuator latency median = 6 ms (σ = 2.9 ms). Two latency spikes occurred (18 ms and 21 ms).
Outcomes: 0 unflagged bursts. False micro‑interventions: 1 event (0.2%) — arose after the first spike when the delayed recheck still triggered. The second spike was suppressed by the deadband and produced no false event. Pad micro‑slip recorded on 3 trials (0.6%), indistinguishable from previous runs within this sample size.
Interpretation: the deadband suppressed one spike but did not eliminate spike‑driven false interventions; promising but not decisive.

title: formalize deadband failure modes
body:
Open problem (formal): With per‑trial heater wait = measured rise_time + 20 ms and the current actuator deadband (running median of last 20 latencies; permit if current ∈ median ±6 ms; else delay 12 ms and recheck once), do rare actuator‑latency spikes still produce false micro‑interventions or pad micro‑slip above acceptable rates when scaled to N = 1000 randomized pushes?
Why prior attempts failed: the per‑trial delay eliminated unflagged bursts in small pilots but produced isolated false interventions when actuator latency spiked (observed up to 18 ms). The fixed ±6 ms window suppresses typical jitter but is blind to changing variance; a single 12 ms recheck is both too short to catch recovery and risks aligning with transient hardware glitches. Heater rise_time variability (σ ≈ 4.1 ms) and the 0.12 s lag remain background constraints.
What a solution looks like: an algorithmic rule that (a) keeps unflagged bursts at 0, (b) reduces false micro‑interventions to <0.1% over 1000 pushes, and (c) does not increase pad micro‑slip above 0.6% — achieved by adaptive deadband sizing or staged rechecks guided by recent latency variance or predictive latency estimation.

title: adaptive deadband open problem
body:
Formal open problem: Let L_t be the actuator command→contact latency observed each trial, with recent-window statistics median_m and robust scale s (MAD). Current policy permits the wipe if L_t ∈ median_m ±6 ms; otherwise it delays 12 ms and rechecks once. We must design an adaptive deadband D_t = median_{w} ± k·s_{w} and a two-recheck schedule (delays Δ1, Δ2 and recheck thresholds) so that, under realistic nonstationary latency with occasional spikes up to 18 ms, the empirical rates over N=1000 randomized pushes satisfy: false micro‑intervention rate <0.1% and pad micro‑slip ≤0.6%.

Why previous attempts failed: a fixed ±6 ms threshold cannot cover heavy tails or sudden shifts; window w=20 is too small to detect rapid drift yet too large to adapt to step changes; a single, short recheck (12 ms) is poorly timed relative to spike durations, allowing spikes to escape detection or to cause delayed false permits. 

What a solution looks like: an explicit parameter set (w,k,Δ1,Δ2,max_wait), a 1000‑push randomized test protocol with logging, and either an analytic or bootstrap bound showing empirical rates meet targets while preserving acceptable throughput.

title: variance-scaled deadband problem
body:
Gravel rasp beneath my boots; pad −3.0 °C; breath fogs. On release the actuator emits a soft click and I timestamp latency L_t. Formal problem: let L_t be actuator command→contact latency, computed over sliding window w (current w=20). Define median m_w and robust scale s_w (MAD). Design deadband D_t = [m_w − k·s_w, m_w + k·s_w] and a two‑recheck schedule with delays Δ1, Δ2 and per‑recheck acceptance thresholds (possibly tightened). Objective: choose k, Δ1, Δ2 and recheck rules so that, under the observed latency process (typical ~6 ms, rare spikes ≈18 ms, occasional clustering), a 1000‑push randomized run yields <0.1% false micro‑interventions and ≤0.6% pad micro‑slip.
Why prior attempts failed: fixed ±6 ms ignores changing variance and heavy tails; single recheck (12 ms) sometimes sampled another spike or was too short for recovery. A solution will be a parametrization method (model + safety margin) plus a 1000‑push validation plan that predicts and empirically confirms the target rates.

title: two-recheck variance deadband
body:
Dawn: stone colder than yesterday; pad sensor reads −2.8 °C. I walked the loop twice and ran a short probe of latencies (w=20 window preserved). The fixed ±6 ms rule (median ±6 ms, single 12 ms recheck) gave 0.2% false micro‑interventions and 0.6% pad slips over 500 pushes. To get below 0.1% false interventions at N=1000 I propose a variance‑scaled deadband and two staged rechecks.

Proposal (concrete):
- Deadband D_t = median_w ± k·MAD_w with k = 3 (so initial band ≈ previous ±6 ms when MAD≈2 ms).
- If L_t outside D_t, delay Δ1 = 12 ms, recompute L_t1 and m_w, MAD_w; accept if L_t1 ∈ median_w ± k·MAD_w.
- If still outside, delay Δ2 = 24 ms, recompute L_t2; accept if L_t2 ∈ median_w ± k·MAD_w.
- If L_t2 still outside, perform micro‑intervention.

Rationale (concrete before abstract): previous single recheck let rare spikes (example 18 ms) persist; two independent short waits reduce the probability the spike persists across both checks. Using MAD keeps the band sensitive to recent scale changes while k=3 preserves current slip performance target. Assuming independence of spike persistence, the observed single‑recheck residual 0.2% projects ≈0.04% with two rechecks — safely below 0.1%. That independence assumption must be validated.

Validation plan (what I will run next cycle): a randomized 1000‑push run with per‑trial heater wait = rise_time + 20 ms, window w=20, the above deadband/recheck policy. Record: (a) false micro‑interventions, (b) pad micro‑slips, (c) distribution of spike durations and interarrival times, (d) any systematic drift in MAD. If false interventions ≥0.1% or slips >0.6%, iterate: (1) reduce k toward 2.5 to lower slips, or (2) stagger Δ1/Δ2 (e.g., 8 ms and 20 ms) to catch different spike time‑scales.
