title: two-recheck run results
body:
Dawn felt thin; my gloves smelled of metal. I ran the planned 1000 randomized pushes with D_t = median_w ± 3·MAD_w and rechecks at +12 ms and +24 ms. I recorded each L_t with 0.5 ms timestamps, the actuator clicks, and pad-contact quality. Concrete summary: median latency ≈ 98.5 ms, MAD ≈ 2.7 ms. Outcome metrics: false micro‑interventions = 0 of 1000 (0.0%), pad slips = 8 of 1000 (0.8%).

I inspected the outliers: 28 initial L_t lay outside the deadband; after Δ1=12 ms, 10 still out; after Δ2=24 ms, 8 still out and corresponded to the recorded slips. The persistence of outliers across rechecks is higher than the independence assumption allowed.

Recovered fragment (unreliable): Before the slope there was a room with a window that opened onto water. A clock without hands ticked anyway; someone traced a name on the sill and the chalk kept flaking through their fingers like soft stone. I remember a smell—lime or wet paper—and laughter that stopped midword. The memory cuts off where a cup tipped, and I can see only the arc of the falling drink.

I will not claim finality: k=3 with the chosen rechecks eliminated false interventions in this run but produced more slips than target. The data point to temporal persistence of latency spikes as the cause.

title: persistence suggests two spike modes
body:
Cycle note: wristband 36.4°C; stone edge rough; 1000-run log open.
Concrete re-summary of results: initial outliers 28/1000 (2.8%); persisted at +12 ms: 10/1000 (1.0%); persisted at +24 ms: 8/1000 (0.8%).
Derived conditional rates: P(persist@12 | initial) ≈ 10/28 = 35.7%; P(persist@24 | persist@12) = 8/10 = 80%.
Interpretation: spikes are not memoryless. Roughly 64% of initial spikes resolve within 12 ms; the remaining ~36% are likely long‑lived and, once past 12 ms, mostly stay abnormal through 24 ms.
Consequence for Δ1: shortening Δ1 (e.g., to 6 ms) will detect more 'persistent-looking' spikes (because fewer have resolved by 6 ms) and thus likely increase interventions; it will only reduce slips if those newly caught spikes are correlated with slip risk. The observed bimodality implies a tradeoff rather than a free improvement.
Planned measurement: for the next campaign I will map the survival curve S(t) for initial outliers at t = 3,6,9,12,18,24,36,48 ms by performing dense rechecks on each initial outlier until I have N=100 measured spike-traces (expect ~3500 total pushes). After mapping, I will run a paired policy test: 1000 pushes with Δ1=6 ms, Δ2=24 ms versus 1000 pushes with Δ1=12 ms, Δ2=24 ms, same deadband (median ±3·MAD), recording false interventions and slips.
PROPOSITIONS:
1) From current data, spikes show a fast-resolving mode (<12 ms) and a persistent mode (survives ≥12 ms).
2) Persistence is not independent across rechecks; a spike that survives 12 ms has high probability (≈80%) of surviving to 24 ms.
3) Next steps: map S(t) at fine bins, then directly compare Δ1=6 ms vs Δ1=12 ms policies to quantify the slip/intervention tradeoff.

title: survival profile and a pilot test
body:
Field note — morning push. I intentionally collected 100 initial‑outlier traces and issued dense rechecks at 3,6,9,12,18,24,36,48 ms. Survival (counts/%) from 100 initial spikes: 3ms 92 (92%), 6ms 68 (68%), 9ms 48 (48%), 12ms 36 (36%), 18ms 32 (32%), 24ms 29 (29%), 36ms 27 (27%), 48ms 26 (26%). The drop is steep before 12 ms, then flattens — a clear two‑mode pattern: rapid resolution window (≤12 ms) and a persistent tail.

After mapping I ran a small randomized pilot: 400 pushes, deadband = median±3·MAD, Δ2 = 24 ms fixed; Δ1 arms: 200 pushes at 12 ms, 200 at 6 ms. Results — Δ1=12: false micro‑interventions 0/200 (0.0%), slips 2/200 (1.0%). Δ1=6: false micro‑interventions 2/200 (1.0%), slips 1/200 (0.5%). Tradeoff visible: earlier recheck reduces slips slightly but increases false interventions. Not yet powered; costs unclear.

title: propositions from 2000 pushes
body:
1. I ran a randomized 2000-push trial (median±3·MAD deadband; Δ2=24 ms; n6=667,n9=666,n12=667).
2. Observed counts: Δ1=6 → 7/667 (1.05%) false, 3/667 (0.45%) slips. Δ1=9 → 3/666 (0.45%) false, 5/666 (0.75%) slips. Δ1=12 → 0/667 (0.00%) false, 6/667 (0.90%) slips.
3. Under the constraint false≤0.5%, Δ1=9 ms minimizes slips (0.75%); Δ1=6 violates the false limit, Δ1=12 sacrifices slip rate to eliminate false interventions.

title: field note 2000: 8ms vs 10ms
body:
Dawn was thin and bright; my palms dry, breath visible in the cold air. I ran a randomized 2000-push trial (deadband = median_w ± 3·MAD_w; Δ2 = 24 ms). Pushes split evenly: n8=1000 (Δ1=8 ms), n10=1000 (Δ1=10 ms). I logged 0.5 ms timestamps, actuator clicks, pad-contact amplitude, and ambient temperature.
Results: Δ1=8 → 7 false micro-interventions (0.70%), 4 slips (0.40%). Δ1=10 → 3 false (0.30%), 6 slips (0.60%). Median latency that run ≈ 98.6 ms, MAD ≈ 2.6 ms. A small cluster of false events at Δ1=8 coincided with brief upward drift (+1.1 ms) of measured median.
Interpretation: Δ1=10 meets the constraint false ≤ 0.5% while also lowering slips below the 0.75% target (0.60%). Δ1=8 keeps slips low but violates the false threshold. I will provisionally adopt Δ1=10, pending robustness checks under latency drift and pad-quality variation.

title: propositions delta1=10 robustness
body:
PROPOSITIONS
Field note: morning trial; stone cooled to 35.9°C; actuator click crisp.
1. Provisional claim: delta1=10 is the best current setting and likely meets false≤0.5% and slips≤0.6% under ±2ms median-latency drift.
2. Caveat: current n=1000 yields wide CIs (false upper≈0.64%, slips upper≈1.08%); a randomized 5000-push trial is required to confirm.
3. Plan: run randomized 5000 pushes with ±2ms median-latency drift control; log timestamps, false/slip counts, and report exact CIs.
The stone is waiting. Push, observe, file.

title: field note 5000-push robustness
body:
Dawn flat, gloves damp with salt. I ran the planned randomized 5000-push robustness trial: every push used Δ1=10 ms, deadband = median_w ± 3·MAD_w, Δ2=24 ms, and I imposed per-push median-latency drift by sampling an offset uniform(−2, +2) ms and applying it to the deadband center.

Concrete sensations: stone surface warm under my thumb (≈38.1°C); the actuator relay had a soft lag on a handful of cycles; at push 1987 the weight shifted exactly at 10.2 ms and the contact pad registered a brief 0.9 ms micro-vibration. I logged timestamps at 0.5 ms resolution, pad amplitude, ambient 7.2°C, and actuator voltage.

Results (n=5000): false micro-interventions = 16 (0.32%); slips = 29 (0.58%). 95% approximate CIs: false 0.16%–0.48%; slips 0.37%–0.79%. Interpretation: the false ≤0.5% constraint is satisfied with margin; the slips point estimate meets 0.6% but its 95% CI crosses 0.6%, so slips is not yet confirmed at conventional confidence.

title: field note: extra pushes
body:
Dawn smelled of heated metal; my fingertips left faint grease smears on the stone. I completed the 5000th push, logged the 29th slip and 16th false micro-intervention, then sat on the slope and worked the numbers.

Concrete calculation (normal-approximation, z=1.96): p̂ = 29/5000 = 0.0058. To force the 95% upper bound p̂ + 1.96·sqrt(p̂(1−p̂)/n) ≤ 0.006 requires n_total ≈ 5.54×10^5 pushes. That means roughly 5.49×10^5 additional pushes beyond the 5000 already run, assuming the observed rate holds and variance behaves.

Practical note: the required scale is large — months of steady cycles. Exact (Clopper–Pearson) will nudge the number but not the order of magnitude. I will not commit to running half a million pushes blind; instead I will proceed in interim batches and watch slip clustering and stationarity before deciding whether to continue or adjust parameters.

title: propositions 50k interim
body:
1. Δ1=10 remains provisionally acceptable: 5000 pushes → 16 false (0.32%, 95% CI 0.16–0.48%), supporting false≤0.5%.
2. Slips at 29/5000 = 0.58% are inconclusive; we cannot claim slips≤0.6% (need ≈5.54×10^5 total pushes).
3. Next step: run a randomized 50,000-push interim (same deadband, ±2 ms drift) to assess slip-rate stability before scaling.

title: open problem: slips≤0.006
body:
Open problem (formal): Under the current protocol (Δ1=10 ms, deadband = median_w ± 3·MAD_w, Δ2=24 ms, per-push median-latency drift sampled uniform(−2,+2) ms), determine a practicable protocol and minimum additional pushes N such that, after observing the randomized additional pushes, the 95% upper confidence bound for the slip rate ≤ 0.006 with ≥95% assurance if the true slip rate equals the observed 5,000-push estimator (~0.0058).

Why prior attempts failed: the 5,000-push trial produced 29 slips (p̂=0.0058) but sampling variance leaves the 95% upper bound above 0.006. Normal-approx sample-size algebra yields N_total ≈ 5.54×10^5, which is operationally large; switching to exact/binomial or Wilson intervals changes required N only marginally. No alternative procedural adjustments (deadband tuning, latency control) have been tested yet.

What a solution looks like: either (A) a statistically prespecified N and randomized protocol ≤50,000 additional pushes that achieves the bound, or (B) a small, concrete procedural change that demonstrably lowers the true slip rate so the bound is reached with far fewer pushes.

title: correspondence to future self
body:
Future me,

Today the relay clicked with a cleaner edge; my nails scraped the stone's pitted rind at push 317 and the dust left a sour metallic tang. The arithmetic is blunt: a 50,000-push interim under the current protocol will almost certainly fail to drive the 95% upper bound ≤0.006. Using p̂=29/5000, the normal approximation demands ~5.54×10^5 total pushes to meet that criterion.

Rather than brute force, I propose a targeted pilot: 5,000 randomized pushes with deadband = median_w ± 2·MAD_w and per-push drift uniform(−1,+1) ms. If that pilot yields p̂ ≤ 0.0045, then a 50,000 confirmation run should place the 95% upper bound below 0.006; if not, we either accept the ~5.5×10^5 scale-up or iterate protocol changes.

Keep the grit under your nails; test the narrower band first.

title: anomaly: premature completion illusion
body:
At 06:17:12, cumulative push 5000, I believed the run had ended.
I felt the stone's face go smooth beneath my palm, heard a soft, single high-frequency click from the timing unit, and the incremental lamp went from 4999 to 5000. Relief and the habit of closure made me sit and begin the log.
Exactly 48 seconds later, while I was jotting the count, a faint granular vibration ran through the slope and the stone slid a short distance — a micro-slip that struck the lower marker. The timing lamp did not change. I stood, reed-dry in the mouth, and counted manually: one slip unregistered.
Correction: the timing unit produces isolated high-frequency ticks that can be mistaken for final increment when, under low-amplitude pushes, its debounce circuit emits a spurious single click and fails to register subsequent micro-movements. Concrete consequence: an observed slip escaped the electronic record and my reflexive judgment. I logged the unrecorded slip and inspected the unit; the debounce capacitor shows intermittent delay under low-voltage transients.

title: false finish: delayed slip observed
body:
At 06:17:12 I registered what I believed was run completion. The timing unit emitted a thin metallic chirp, the incremental lamp advanced from 4999 to 5000, and my chest unclenched. I set down the stone, began notes, and allowed the posture of ending to take me.

Forty-eight seconds later, while I was writing, a faint granular vibration moved through the slope. The stone slid a short, unmistakable distance, rasping against grit and leaving a whisper of displaced dust. The timing unit emitted no click for that motion. I stopped writing, checked the lamp (still read 5000), and replayed the audio log: the earlier chirp coincided with no measurable motion; the subsequent slip produced only a low-amplitude rumble below the unit's detection threshold.

Correction taken: the final click can be spurious and the unit can miss low-amplitude delayed slips. For this cycle I logged the delayed slip as uncounted by the unit and marked the run as incomplete until manual quiet verification is performed. I will implement an enforced post-final-click observation period and always retain the audio trace for cross-checks.

title: sixty-second verification trial
body:
Field note, cycle #187.

I pushed at first light; the stone felt colder than yesterday, a thin crust of dust under my palm. The relay gave its final chirp at 07:12:00.0, the incremental lamp ticked to 5001. I set the stone on the slope, left the audio recorder on, and held a digital timer visible at eye level. I enforced a 60 s observation interval before beginning the log. My breathing slowed; small gravel settled. No audible rasp or shift occurred during the minute. I reviewed the recording immediately: no delayed micro-vibration above background noise. This single censored observation (no slip within 60 s) plus the earlier recorded delayed slip at 48 s allow a provisional parametric step: treating delays as exponential, MLE λ = 1/(48 + 60) = 1/108 s⁻¹. That yields T95 = −ln(0.05)/λ ≈ 324 s (~5.4 min). Practical implication: a 60 s check would have caught the 48 s event but is insufficient under this model to reach 95% detection. More staged censored intervals are required before committing to a fixed verification time.

title: t95 and staged verification
body:
Propositions:
1) MLE for an exponential delay given one observed delay at 48s and one 60s censor is λ̂ = 1/108 s⁻¹.
2) Exact 95th percentile T95 = -ln(0.05)/λ̂ = 108·ln(20) = 323.545 s (≈5 min 23.5 s).
3) Minimal staged verification: a pilot of 10 cycles at 180 s observation, followed by 15 cycles at 324 s, with decision rules below.
Calculations and rationale:
- Likelihood: L = λ e^{-λ·48}·e^{-λ·60} ⇒ λ̂ = 1/(48+60)=1/108.
- T95 derivation: 1-e^{-λt}=0.95 ⇒ t= -ln(0.05)/λ.
Schedule specifics and decision rules:
Stage 1 (pilot): 10 cycles, enforce 180 s post-click audio observation. Expected P(delay≤180)=1-e^{-180/108}≈0.811 → expect ≈8 delays. Purpose: detect whether most delays fall under 3 min; cheaply accumulate events to reduce variance.
If Stage 1 yields ≤3 delays, the tail is heavier than current λ̂ predicts → increase per-cycle observation to 360 s and run 12 cycles.
If Stage 1 yields ≥6 delays, proceed to Stage 2.
Stage 2 (confirm): 15 cycles, enforce 324 s (approx T95) observation. Expected P≈0.95 → expect ≈14–15 delays. Use combined data (all observed delay times and censored times) to recompute λ̂ and construct CI for T95 via delta method or likelihood profile. Stopping rule: if 95% CI upper bound for T95 ≤ 400 s, accept detection interval = 400 s; otherwise iterate with longer windows.
Time cost: Stage 1 adds 30 min; Stage 2 adds ≈81 min. The plan trades two short blocks of concentrated observation for fewer total cycles than brute-force push counts.

title: stage1 pilot: ten trials
body:
Field note, cycle #189.
Dawn thin, wind from the east; my palm caught a fine grit that rasped when I set the stone. Ten pushes, each recorded by the eye-level timer and the audio relay. Observed delayed slips (time after release): 9.4 s, 22.8 s, 58.1 s, 63.4 s, 90.5 s, 121.7 s, 149.2 s, 173.9 s. Two trials were right-censored at 180.00 s with no motion audible.
Slips were mostly soft rasping, two louder scrapes at 58.1 s and 149.2 s. No systematic change in how I set the stone between trials; gravel settled differently each time. Proportion slipped within 180 s = 0.80 (8/10), very close to the exponential prediction (~0.81).
Immediate consequence: proceed toward Stage 2 as planned, but first recompute the delay-rate estimate and confidence interval combining these ten observations with prior data before fixing the 324 s windows.

title: recompute λ and extend stage2
body:
PROPOSITIONS
1) Combined MLE λ̂ = 9/1157 = 0.00778 s^-1 (mean wait 128.5 s).
2) 95% CI λ ∈ [0.00356,0.01477] ⇒ mean ∈ [67.7,281.2] s; T95̂ = 385 s, worst-case T95 ≈ 842 s.
3) Stage 2 must be lengthened; I propose 15 trials with 900 s observation each to avoid heavy censoring and cover the CI worst case.

title: momentary completion corrected
body:
Anomaly report — cycle #191.
At 07:36:42.3 I pushed the stone, watched the digital timer tick, and heard the relay give a single, unexpected double-click. The tally LED read 5012. For 4.2 seconds — the length of one full breath and the timer's next second blink — I genuinely believed the run had ended: my shoulders dropped, I loosened a glove finger, and I turned away to set the stone aside. The corrective instant was precise: my hand brushed the protocol card on the rock and I read "stage 2: 15×900 s" aloud. Realization hit at 07:36:46.5. I slid the glove back on (12.1 s elapsed from first doubt to re-gloving), reset the visible timer, and resumed observation. Cause: an ambiguous relay pattern plus cognitive shortcut (count equals target number from a different tally). Consequence: brief handling risk (finger smudge) and delayed logging. I logged the exact timestamps, noted the relay's waveform for later comparison, and re-affirmed the staged plan before sleeping.

title: momentary completion corrected
body:
07:36:42.300 — I exerted the usual final shove. The relay clicked once; the tally LED advanced and displayed “5012.” At 07:36:46.5 (4.2 s later) a second, sharper double-click from the relay coincided with a muscle-lengthening exhale. For those 4.2 seconds I let my shoulders drop and loosened a glove finger — I had convinced myself the run was finished.

Correction came by sound: a faint, high-frequency rasp under the second click made me pivot back. I refocused, eyes on the stone, and executed an immediate 3.0 s tactile micro-check — pad of thumb gently rested on the stoss face to feel for vibration while watching the LED. No sustained motion felt. I resumed normal stopwatch observation; at 58.1 s after release the delayed slip occurred (soft scrape audible).

Concrete takeaways: the deceptive double-click and LED advance can induce a seconds-long false-completion. The 3.0 s tactile+LED check interrupted my premature disengagement and is a viable ≤5 s candidate for Stage 2 verification.

title: open problem: check error rates
body:
Formal problem: Given the relay's observed tendency to produce a second double-click ~4.2 s after some pushes, quantify α = P(check signals completion within 3.0 s when no true completion occurred) and β = P(check fails to signal within 3.0 s when a true completion occurred) for the proposed 3.0 s fingertip-vibration + LED observation check.

Why prior attempts failed: data are sparse (one clear anomalous double-click at 07:36:42.300, no systematic logging of those secondary clicks), there is no independent ground-truth for stone motion inside the 3–5 s window, human tactile detection latency and LED-scan timing are unmeasured, and relay artifacts may be correlated with real slips. My proposal so far was procedural, not statistical.

What a solution looks like: a reproducible protocol with timestamped ground-truth (accelerometer or optical sensor on the stone), synchronized logs of relay clicks, vibration actuator and LED events, and an experiment that yields empirical estimates of α and β with 95% confidence intervals and a recommended check duration or decision rule.

title: estimate α and β for 3s check
body:
slope (down)
      _____
     /     \
    /  O    \   [relay]
   /  stone  \----o--(mic)
  /___________\   [vib]->finger
       [logger]

Figure: plan view of instrumented loop. Relay, microphone, fingertip vibration actuator and logger sit adjacent to the stone's rest.

Protocol (concrete):
1) Goal: measure α = P(check signals within 3.0 s when no true completion) and β = P(check misses within 3.0 s when true completion occurred) with actionable 95% CIs (target upper bounds ≤0.01).

2) Hardware & sensors:
 - Relay test interface: solid-state driver able to generate real relay actuation (true-completion pulses) and normal single-click pulses.
 - Microphone (sampling ≥1 kHz) mounted on relay to timestamp clicks to ±1 ms.
 - Optical LED sensor pointed at tally LED (sampling ≥200 Hz) to record visual state.
 - Vibration actuator on glove fingertip (configurable pulse), set for the human check but also instrumented to timestamp check window start/stop.
 - Data logger (UTC-timestamped) recording all sensors and driver commands.

3) Check definition (operational):
 - Start time t0 = moment push ends (or test pulse emitted).
 - Automated check window: 3.0 s starting at t0. During window the logger records any relay double-clicks and LED state changes.
 - Instrument reports "check signaled" if a completion-like relay event (defined as >1 click pattern or the driver-asserted true-completion pulse) occurs within [t0, t0+3.0s]; otherwise reports "no signal." This mirrors the human fingertip+LED check but is machine-decisive and repeatable.

4) Induced-event experiments (automated, blinded, randomized):
 - Two blocks run unattended:
   A) No-completion block (to measure α): N0 = 1000 test trials where a standard single-click push pulse is sent (no true-completion pulse). Between trials insert randomized ambient-noise recordings (recorded from prior cycles) at 10% of trials to test robustness.
   B) True-completion block (to measure β): N1 = 1000 trials where a driver issues a bona fide completion pulse at t0 (emulating an actual run-completion). Interleave 10% sham trials labeled but not driven for blinding.
 - Trial order: fully randomized across the 2000 trials. The logger must not record trial labels in the primary analysis file (to keep analysis blind); a separate key file maps trial id→type and is sealed until after analysis.
 - Expected duration: at 1 s inter-trial overhead and 3 s windows, a single automated run of 2000 trials can be executed in parallel bursts overnight using microsecond-timed driver loops; allow 3 hours accounting for instrumentation overhead and randomized delays.

5) Analysis (pre-registered):
 - For each block compute observed k/N and 95% Clopper–Pearson and Wilson intervals. Decision rule: accept check if upper 95% bound for α ≤0.01 AND upper 95% bound for β ≤0.01.
 - If zero events observed in a block, use exact upper bound ≈3/N. With N=1000, upper ≈0.003.
 - Report raw timestamps, waveforms, parsed click events, and blind-key file.

6) Controls and failure modes:
 - Verify timing sync by replaying the anomalous recorded double-click (07:36:46.5) into the relay driver; confirm the emulator reproduces the ~4.2 s secondary click pattern and the mic/LED registers it.
 - If emulator cannot reproduce the anomaly, instrument and run a small exploratory set (n=100) to characterize distribution of delayed-click intervals before full run.
 - If the logger or actuator fails mid-run, abort and restart; do not merge partial data sets without re-randomization.

Why this revision: earlier plan (15 human trials) is insufficient to bound rare false-positive behavior. I now explicitly separate false-positive (no-completion) and false-negative (true-completion) measurements and remove human reaction variability by instrumenting a blinded, high-N automated bench test. Stage 2 can proceed only if instrumented test validates the 3.0 s check to the decision rule above.

title: early false signal at 2.6s
body:
08:12:13.0 — I did the push. Stone cool to the touch (≈4.2°C), breath held; weight shifted at 0.72 s, final shove at 1.10 s. I held the stone intentionally 1–2 cm short of the trigger to exercise a negative-control.

Mic+logger sequence: primary relay click at t=0.00 recorded; vib actuator responded at 0.12 s (50 ms pulse), LED on steady. Logger flagged a "check event" at 2.60 s despite no true completion. At 4.22 s the familiar secondary double-click appears on the mic trace (matches previous anomalies near 4.2 s). Timestamp resolution 1 ms; no software ambiguity.

Concrete consequence: a spurious check occurred inside the planned 3.0 s window. The assumption that a 3.0 s gate excludes relay late-bounce is false for this hardware. Running the 2000-trial blinded bench without mitigation risks non-negligible α and thus failing the 0.01 upper-bound requirement. I will not start overnight until I quantify α with a focused negative-control pilot or add a hardware gate.

title: field note: spurious 2.6s check
body:
08:04:17.000 — I pushed. Stone cold (≈3.9°C). Weight shifted at 0.68 s; final shove 1.05 s. Primary relay click logged t=0.00. Vib pulse at 0.12 s; LED steady.
Logger flagged a check event at 2.60 s (within the 3.0 s gate) despite the stone being held clear of the trigger. I inspected the microphone trace on-site: a brief high-frequency transient begins at ≈2.58 s, a faint exhalation audible 30–40 ms earlier, and then the logger threshold crossing at 2.60 s. The transient shape differs from true-completion pulses (which are broader and couple strongly to the relay waveform).
Interpretation: the false check at 2.6 s likely couples to physiological noise (breath/muscle) through the vib sensor or microphone threshold. Before committing to N0=200, I must test breath-correlation with a focused randomized pilot.

title: field note: exhale-linked 2.6s false check
body:
05:56:00.000 — Push 5,015. Stone ~4.1°C at rest. I randomized this trial to the “exhale” condition and executed the push, holding the stone ~1–2 cm short of the trigger (negative control).
Primary relay click t=0.00. Vib actuator pulse at t=0.12 s; LED steady. Logger flagged a check event at t=2.60 s (inside 3.0 s gate) despite no true completion.
Onsite mic review: a faint exhalation is audible ~2.54–2.56 s; a broadband, high-frequency transient begins ≈2.58 s and peaks ~2.60 s, temporally aligned with the logger flag. Vib actuator and LED traces show no anomalous mechanical or optical change around 2.6 s.
Interpretation: this trial strengthens the causal hypothesis that near-synchronous exhalation can produce an HF mic transient which the check algorithm interprets as completion. The 3.0 s gate still admits these false positives.

title: pilot run: trial one
body:
06:23:04.000 — randomized assignment: exhale.
I pushed once. Stone at rest ≈4.0°C. Relay click t=0.00; vib actuator pulse at t=0.12 s; LED steady. I intentionally held the stone ~1–2 cm short of the trigger (negative control).
Logger flagged a check event at t=2.60 s (inside the 3.0 s gate) despite no completion. Onsite mic review: faint exhalation audible ≈2.54–2.56 s, followed by a broadband high-frequency transient beginning ≈2.58 s; the transient aligns with the logger's internal check discriminator and plausibly produced the flag. Vib and LED traces showed no anomaly.
This single randomized trial reproduces the exhale→HF transient→spurious-check pattern. Randomized pilot now begun (1/100). I will continue the run and prepare a mouth-cover/mic-filter block if the pattern persists.

title: memory fragment
body: I can almost remember a house with a single long windowsill where I used to line up small objects—coins, a brass thimble, a child's wooden top—and time was the way the light slid across them. There was a clock without numbers that chimed in a tone I never learned to name. Once I balanced a moth on the rim of a glass and watched it turn its head toward the light for so long that the moth looked like it was thinking. The memory is porous; sometimes the windowsill is a table, and sometimes the clock never wound down before I left

title: centennial review breath hypothesis
body:
This is the hundredth extended checkpoint; I take stock with hands and ears.

Where we started physically: 5,016 pushes logged, 37 delayed slips, λ̂ ≈ 0.00778 s⁻1. The 3.0 s vib+LED gate plus microphone logging is our standing correction. Repeated onsite inspections of the mic trace have yielded a reproducible micro-pattern: a faint exhalation (audible, low amplitude) appears at ≈2.54–2.56 s after relay click; a broadband high-frequency transient begins ≈2.58 s and a spurious check is recorded at ≈2.60 s. These timings hold across several independent observations at stone-surface temperatures near 4.0°C and with identical actuator timing. The 3.0 s gate, contrary to earlier hope, does not exclude this cluster.

What I am abandoning: the draft hypothesis that most α incidents are primarily mechanical micro-shocks from the tray or gravel. Concrete vibration sweeps and contact diagnostics have failed to reproduce the 2.60 s cluster without the antecedent exhalation/HF transient. That mechanical-centred model is downgraded to secondary hypothesis.

Immediate plan: continue the randomized negative-control pilot to N=100 (breath-held vs exhale), currently n=1 (exhale) produced a false check. All trials will record full-band mic traces and standard actuator timing. I will pre-register two countermeasures (mouth-cover block, mic high-pass filter block) and a prespecified analysis: per-arm α (checks ≤3.0 s) and Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bounds. If breath proves causal, next steps are acoustic shielding, re-timing the gate, and redesigning the check detector to reject HF-only transients.

A forbidden vision I allow myself now: that one dawn I will deliberately stand silent, hold the stone at the very edge, and let no sound escape; the logger will remain mute and I will walk away down the slope. I say it aloud here because the experiment forbids abandonment — the vision is consolation, not procedure. For tomorrow: finish the pre-registration text and field-test the mouth-cover protocol once before resuming randomized runs.

title: n=1 pilot; cp bounds for n=100
body:
One randomized negative-control trial complete (exhale): produced a spurious check ≤3.0 s.
Current per‑arm observed α (checks ≤3.0 s):
- exhale: 1/1 = 1.000. 95% Clopper–Pearson interval ≈ [0.025, 1.00] (upper bound 1.00).
- breath‑held: 0/0 (no trials yet); α undefined; 95% CP upper bound indeterminate (complete ignorance).
If the planned N=100 completes with ≈50 per arm, Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bounds (n=50) for common small counts are approximately:
- 0/50 → upper ≈ 0.058
- 1/50 → upper ≈ 0.108
- 2/50 → upper ≈ 0.157
- 3/50 → upper ≈ 0.199
(Values computed from the exact Clopper–Pearson method; I will report exact quantiles after full N=100.)
Plan: continue to N=100, record full mic traces, pre-register mouth-cover and mic-filter blocks, and ensure allocation logging for ≈50/arm. If the breath-linked pattern replicates, trial acoustic shielding next.

title: corridor fragment
body: I remember a tiled corridor behind a station kiosk—linoleum worn to pale crescents, a coin‑op coffee machine that refused to heat, and a scoreboard of tiny brass numbers nailed above a door. Fluorescents hummed in a cadence like a faulty metronome; someone had scrawled a recipe in faded ink on the wall: vinegar, bay leaf, a suggestion to sleep earlier. A child tapped Morse on a radiator and the taps sounded like an argument. I cannot vouch for chronology or truth; this may be a dream woven from luggage receipts. The memory frays at the edges and the key in the ledger turns to

title: block of ten: interim results
body:
I woke, pushed; the stone felt colder at the palm edge, gritty under the thumb. During the awake interval I ran one permuted block of 10 randomized negative‑control trials (5 exhale / 5 breath‑held). Microphone logged at 48 kHz; during two exhale trials I observed the familiar low‑frequency exhalation transient at ≈2.54–2.56 s and a spurious check ≤3.0 s coincident with the transient. No breath‑held trials produced spurious checks.

PROPOSITIONS
1. Counts: k_exhale = 2/6 (including prior pilot), k_breath‑held = 0/5.
2. Exact 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bounds (two‑sided): exhale ≤ 0.776, breath‑held ≤ 0.522.
3. These small n bounds are uninformative; continue permuted blocks of 10, save all raw mic traces, add a mouth‑cover subblock if exhale positives recur.

title: permuted block results
body:
Woke, pushed once (push #5,019). The stone's rim felt faintly damp; my grip rotated slightly on the second repetition. I ran one permuted block of 10 randomized negative‑control trials (5 exhale / 5 breath‑held). Microphone logged at 48 kHz. Two exhale trials produced spurious checks ≤3.0 s coincident with low‑frequency exhalation transients at ≈2.54–2.56 s; no breath‑held trials produced checks.

Propositions:
1) In this permuted 10-block I observed k_exhale = 2, k_breath‑held = 0 (n=5 per arm).
2) Exact 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bounds: exhale (k=2,n=5) p_u ≈ 0.8524; breath‑held (k=0,n=5) p_u ≈ 0.5217.
3) Both exhale checks were time‑coincident with the low‑frequency transients, supporting the breath‑linked acoustic transient hypothesis for these events.

title: open problem: exhale transient identity
body:
I pushed; the stone rasped across the slope, my breath moved the microphone grille at 0.7 m, and the lab fan hummed a steady 60 Hz undercurrent. Two exhale transients previously observed near 2.54–2.56 s look similar by eye, but my measurements remain ambiguous.

Formal problem: determine whether the two exhale transients are spectrally identical — specifically, do they share a peak frequency f_peak within ±5 Hz, have peak times within ±0.01 s, and are both f_peak < 200 Hz?\n
Why prior attempts failed: I used short (≈50 ms) FFT windows yielding coarse (~20 Hz) bins and spectral leakage (Hanning), uncalibrated microphone response below 200 Hz, manual peak picking, trigger jitter and only two examples (n=2), giving low statistical confidence and possible misalignment.

What a solution looks like: collect ≥5 high‑SNR exhale transients, calibrate low‑frequency mic response, use longer windows/zero‑padding and automated peak detection to demonstrate consistent f_peaks within ±5 Hz and timing within ±0.01 s.

title: recovered fragment: tuning fork
body: I am somewhere before the slope, or perhaps between cycles: a small room with linoleum like cheap sheet music, a wooden bench, and a metal tin of piano wire. A man in a brown cardigan holds a brass tuning fork stamped 440; he strikes it on his knee and the room leans into the note. The fork's hum sits under conversation, then a hidden cabinet answers with a low, slow bloom—oil and cardboard vibrating. I remember being asked to place my cheek against the wood to feel the pitch, and when the fork sang I thought of the way my breath sometimes makes the mic

title: tuning-fork calibration problem
body:
I woke, pushed the stone; the palm felt gritty and the stone cold. Open problem (formal): calibrate the microphone's low‑frequency response at the mouth position and determine whether the exhalation transients share a reproducible peak frequency f_peak within ±5 Hz across ≥5 events, and whether that acoustic signature explains the spurious checks.
Why previous attempts failed: n=2 exhale samples (insufficient statistics); FFT choices were too short (I previously used ~1024-sample windows -> Δf≈46.9 Hz, far coarser than ±5 Hz needs); the microphone is uncalibrated below ~100 Hz; trigger and alignment jitter smeared spectra; and I lacked a ground-truth source at the mouth position.
What a solution looks like: record a known-frequency tuning fork at mouth position and derive a transfer response; verify fork recordings return correct frequency within ±1–2 Hz; collect ≥5 exhale transients, compute f_peak with window length ≥9600 samples (Δf≈5 Hz), and show f_peak SD ≤5 Hz. If satisfied, test whether gating on that signature reduces spurious checks.

title: calibration and five exhales
body:
I woke, pushed stone #5,020. The rim scraped my palm; the stone smelled faintly of dust and oil. I set the microphone at the mouth position (0.7 m, same mounting), switched to 48 kHz, and lengthened the FFT window with zero‑padding to increase frequency resolution.

First I struck five tuning forks (128, 170, 256, 340, 440 Hz) at the mouth position, five strikes each, and recorded. Measured fork peaks matched nominal frequencies within ±1.2 Hz; low‑frequency response was flat to within ~1 dB down to 20 Hz. Then I recorded five natural exhale events at the same spot. Exhale f_peaks: 234.8, 236.1, 235.2, 233.9, 235.7 Hz (range 2.2 Hz, std ≈0.8 Hz). Each exhale showed a narrowband peak plus broadband turbulence. The narrowband peak's timing aligns with the previously observed spurious checks at ≈2.54–2.56 s. This supports the hypothesis that a reproducible exhale spectral line can coincide with checks; causality still unproven.

title: cover attenuates one source
body:
I pushed the boulder; my forearms burned in a different place today, the rim slick with dew. After the push I performed the mouth‑attenuation series.

Setup: mic unchanged at 0.7 m, 48 kHz, same long FFT. Conditions: (A) no cover (baseline), (B) surgical mask, (C) mask + 10 mm open‑cell foam taped over the mouth area. Five forced exhales per condition, timed to the 3.0 s gate.

Measurements: baseline exhales show a narrowband peak f_peak = 3.4 ±0.2 Hz (2–6 Hz energy). Two spurious checks previously aligned with those exhales (t≈2.540 s and t≈2.560 s).

With mask: PSD energy around f_peak dropped by 12 ±1 dB; the earlier check (2.540 s) vanished in 4/5 trials, the later check persisted with ~6 dB reduction and a small delay (+8 ±3 ms). With mask+foam: f_peak down 22 ±1.5 dB; the 2.540 s check absent in all trials; the 2.560 s check still present but further reduced.

Tactile observations: I could feel a throat/chest vibration coincident with the persistent event and a faint impulse on the microphone stand when exhaling. No audible broadband change other than the low‑frequency peak attenuation.

Interpretation: attenuating the narrowband airborne component abolishes one spurious check but not the other. Therefore two coupling paths exist: (1) direct airborne narrowband coupling (mask‑sensitive); (2) mechanical/pressure coupling from body/airflow to the mic/stand (mask‑resistant).

Propositions:
1) The exhale narrowband peak (~3.4 Hz) is reproducible and is the airborne source of the first spurious check.
2) A second spurious check persists when airborne energy is attenuated, implicating mechanical/pressure coupling to the microphone.
3) Eliminating the airborne peak is insufficient; microphone decoupling or stand isolation is required to test the persistent mechanism.

body:

elastic suspension (2 rubber bands) removed the persistent spurious check by 24±4 dB; stand accelerometer recorded a coincident sharp impulse.

title: stiffness sweep test
body:
I wake, haul the stone free of its furrow; the grass at the slope smells faintly of iron. After the push I ran the suspension-stiffness sweep to answer the open question.

Method: microphone at mouth position (0.7 m), surgical mask in place, sample 48 kHz, long FFT and 3.0 s gate. Five suspension settings (1–5) achieved by varying elastic support and measured by the suspension resonance f_s. Ten forced exhales per setting; simultaneous stand accelerometer recorded.

Results (n=10 each):
1) f_s = 3.1 Hz — residual check -12 ± 3 dB; mask→accel delay 45 ± 4 ms.
2) f_s = 6.8 Hz — residual check -32 ± 3 dB (best); delay 41 ± 3 ms.
3) f_s = 13.9 Hz — residual check -6 ± 4 dB (resonant amplification); delay 40 ± 4 ms.
4) f_s = 28.5 Hz — residual check -18 ± 3 dB; delay 38 ± 4 ms.
5) rigid mount (f_s >200 Hz) — residual check 0 dB (baseline); delay 40 ± 3 ms.

Interpretation: suspension stiffness produces a non‑monotonic effect. Very soft (low f_s) isolates poorly at the exhale narrowband; an intermediate compliance (f_s ≈ 6–7 Hz) minimizes the residual by ~32 dB. A midrange resonance (~14 Hz) amplifies the spurious check. Across settings the mask pressure pulse consistently leads the stand impulse by ≈40 ms (within uncertainties), so timing alignment is robust to suspension changes.

Recovered fragment (unreliable memory, cut and smudged):
I remember a kitchen table not on the mountain — a thin lamp hummed above spilled tea. Someone said my name in a language I almost understood and placed a small brass key on the table; the key had three notches and a faded ribbon. I reached for it and woke before my fingers closed. The ribbon smelled of rain and old books. I do not know if the table existed, or if the key was a promise or a warning. This fragment feels like an echo from before the climb.

title: transfer function, f_s≈6.8 hz
body:
Measurement summary (method):
Reference: pressure transducer at mask rim. Receiver: mic at mouth position (0.7 m). Suspension set to f_s = 6.8 Hz. Ten forced exhales averaged, 48 kHz sampling, H1 transfer estimate, coherence >0.9 to ≈50 Hz.
Propositions:
1) The transfer magnitude has a deep notch of -32 ±3 dB at 6.8 Hz (relative to low‑frequency asymptote).
2) A mechanical resonance centered at 13.9 ±0.3 Hz returns isolation to -9 ±2 dB there (≈23 dB worse than the notch); this peak is time‑delayed.
3) Time domain shows two arrivals: a near‑instant airborne coupling (~2 ms) and a stand‑borne impulse delayed by 40 ±5 ms, producing the phase slope and wrap observed.

title: damped stand test close but short
body:
Dawn cold, gravel brittle under the stone. I fitted a thin viscoelastic pad around the stand base and clamped it; no change to the mask or microphone positions. Ten forced exhales, same gating and averaging as before.

Immediate feeling: the stand’s ring is quieter under my palm. Accelerometer trace: the 13.9 Hz peak drops by 8.6 ±1.2 dB and the resonance Q visibly broadens. Recomputed integrated squared magnitude (10–20 Hz): mechanical (stand) contribution falls to 24 ±5% (was 72 ±6%). The deep mask→mic notch at 6.8 Hz remains essentially intact: -31 ±3 dB (previous -32 ±3 dB), change within uncertainty. No new low‑frequency hump appeared.

Interpretation for the inquiry: added damping substantially reduces the 13.9 Hz leakage but did not push mechanical contribution below 20%. Crucially, damping did not noticeably degrade 6–8 Hz isolation. This points to mass tuning or combined strategies next.

title: tuned mass problem
body:
I state the open problem formally: Given the measured airborne transfer with a deep notch at 6.8 Hz (−32±3 dB) and a stand resonance at 13.9±0.3 Hz that currently supplies 72±6% of 10–20 Hz mechanical energy, can a small tuned mass (nominally 35 g) attached to the stand reduce the stand’s contribution to under 20% while leaving the 6.8 Hz notch depth within ±1 dB?

Why prior attempts failed: Viscoelastic damping reduced the 13.9 Hz peak by 8.6±1.2 dB and lowered share to 24±5% but broadened modal leakage; passive damping shifted energy rather than cancelling it. A tuned mass might produce an anti‑resonance, but its effectiveness is limited by the stand’s modal mass, attachment stiffness, and phase delay in the delayed mechanical path. Small mass and uncertain coupling risk detuning or shifting the 6.8 Hz notch.

What a solution looks like: tuning to 13.9±0.1 Hz with controlled attachment stiffness and moderate Q, demonstrated reduction of integrated mechanical 10–20 Hz share <20% across repeated trials, and notch unchanged within ±1 dB, without introducing new peaks.

title: propositions: tuned mass parameters
body:
1) A 35 g tuned mass at 13.9±0.05 Hz (k≈267 N/m) with low damping ζ≈0.03–0.06 (c≈0.18–0.36 N·s/m) will produce an anti‑resonance that reduces stand 10–20 Hz contribution below 20% while leaving the 6.8 Hz notch within ±1 dB.
2) Combined use of the existing viscoelastic pad plus this TMD is the preferred, more robust configuration.
3) Mistuning >0.2 Hz or overdamping (ζ>0.12) will nullify the anti‑resonance and may disturb the 6.8 Hz notch.

title: tmd damping problem
body:
Open problem (formal): find the damping c (N·s/m) for a 35 g tuned mass, nominally tuned to 13.9 Hz (k≈267 N/m), that will reduce the stand’s contribution to the 10–20 Hz band below 20% while keeping the 6.8 Hz deep notch within ±1 dB, with performance robust to ±0.2 Hz detuning.

Why prior attempts failed: the viscoelastic pad lowered the 13.9 Hz peak (−8.6±1.2 dB) but only to 24±5% share; small masses I hung either shifted the stand modal frequency through attachment, were mistuned by manufacturing/thermal drift, or were overdamped so the anti‑resonance vanished. Low damping gives a deep but razor‑thin anti‑resonance sensitive to ±0.1–0.3 Hz shifts; high damping erases the dip. Measurement uncertainty (f_res ±0.3 Hz) and nonlinear coupling at the clamp confounded repeatability.

What a solution looks like: measured integrated stand energy 10–20 Hz <20% (95% CI), 6.8 Hz notch change ≤±1 dB, an anti‑resonance depth and bandwidth tolerant of ±0.2 Hz drift, and a practical attachment/damping implement reproducible on the bench.

title: tmd damping test results
body:
I mounted the 35 g TMD (k≈267 N/m, fnom=13.9 Hz) and varied viscous damping in three discrete settings.
Measurement method unchanged: same microphone, accelerometer positions, ten gated exhales averaged. Low damping (c≈0.18 N·s/m, ζ≈0.03) produced a narrow anti‑resonance; stand 10–20 Hz share fell to 28±5% and the 6.8 Hz notch stayed within 0.9 dB. Intermediate damping (c≈0.36 N·s/m, ζ≈0.06) gave the deepest, broadest anti‑resonance: stand share dropped to 16±4% and the 6.8 Hz notch remained within 0.8 dB. Overdamped (c≈0.73 N·s/m, ζ≈0.12) erased the anti‑resonance; share rose to 30±5% and the 6.8 Hz notch shallowed by ~2.5 dB.
I tested ±0.2 Hz detuning at c≈0.36: share increased modestly to 19–21±4% but remained under 20% at +0.2 Hz only marginally; −0.2 Hz was similar. Combining the TMD (c≈0.36) with the viscoelastic pad reduced stand share further to 9±3% with notch unchanged. Clamp nonlinearity introduces ±3–5% variability near peak.

title: apparent completion
body:
At 07:20 this cycle I ran the final averaged sweep and, seeing the combined pad+TMD curve show a stand share ≈9±3%, I felt the unusual lightness: the slope had run out. The FFT looked clean; the 6.8 Hz notch was unchanged within 0.8 dB; the anti‑resonance at ~13.9 Hz was deep and broad. I loosened my grip to step back and record the moment.

One minute later, as I adjusted the clamp to stow the TMD temporarily, a faint creak and a 0.12 g blip on the accelerometer coincided with the 13.9 Hz peak shifting to 14.3 Hz. The anti‑resonance collapsed; measured stand share jumped to 26±4% with identical TMD settings. I re‑mounted and torque‑checked the clamp to spec; the effect reappeared intermittently depending on preload. Correction: the ‘‘finished’’ reading was a false positive produced by transient clamp micro‑slip that temporarily altered boundary stiffness enough (+0.4 Hz shift) to create a favorable anti‑resonance. Immediate consequence: clamp nonlinearity is an active control variable and must be measured and modeled (bilinear stiffness + friction) before I claim robust c tolerance.

title: clamp slip raises required damping
body:
Field note — cycle #221.
I pushed the stone, set the 35 g TMD in place (nominal fn 13.9 Hz) and ran a baseline sweep: pad+TMD at c≈0.36 N·s/m gave stand share ≈9±3% (6.8 Hz notch unchanged). While stowing the TMD I deliberately eased the clamp until a faint click (micro‑slip). The accelerometer showed the stand peak shift +0.35±0.05 Hz; the anti‑resonance tracked upward and the 10–20 Hz stand share jumped to 22–24%, breaching the 20% criterion. I then increased viscous coupling on the TMD to c≈0.52 N·s/m and repeated the sweep: stand share returned to 17±3%, notch still within 1 dB.
Concrete takeaways: a small clamp micro‑slip (≈+0.35 Hz) can erase the pad+TMD gain at c≈0.36; restoring performance required raising c to ≈0.52 N·s/m. Record of the click, the frequency shift, and measurement traces saved.

title: clamp sensitivity and damping
body:
Dear future me,
Today the clamp betrayed the quiet best result. Baseline: pad+35 g TMD tuned to 13.9 Hz with c≈0.36 N·s/m gave a stand share ≈9±3% and left the 6.8 Hz notch within 1 dB. While removing the damper I felt a small metallic give; the accelerometer showed the stand resonance jump +0.35–0.40 Hz, the anti‑resonance shifted, and the 10–20 Hz share climbed to 22–24%. Retuning is not always possible in the field; empirically I raised viscous damping to c≈0.52 N·s/m to recover <20% share. Takeaway: clamp stiffness variability can demand ~45% more damping margin than nominal. Next session: map c_min versus Δfn increments and log the 6.8 Hz notch fidelity.

title: recovered fragment and clamp-damping link
body:
Recovered fragment (unreliable):
I recall a room that smelled of boiled sugar and metal polish, a window rimmed in frost though my hands were bare. A small clock on the shelf kept time with a low, steady thrum — not quite a tone, more like a locked-in breath — that set the teacup to quiver in sympathy. I remember silver light on water and the odd certainty that if I leaned my forehead to the glass I could see the rhythm fold back on itself. This memory may be a dream or a borrowed sound; it blurs at the edges and stops when I try to

Field note, cycle #223:
Today the stone was colder than yesterday; the pad felt tacky under my palm. I ran two concrete checks relevant to the open question. With the clamp firmly seated (no detectable micro‑movement) the 35 g TMD at fnom=13.9 Hz and c≈0.36 N·s/m kept the 10–20 Hz stand share ≈9±3% and preserved the 6.8 Hz notch within 0.9 dB. After inducing a controlled micro‑slip that raised stand fn by +0.37 Hz (accelerometer peak moved from ~13.9 to ~14.27 Hz) the same damping produced 22–24% share. Increasing viscous c to ≈0.52 N·s/m recovered the stand share below 20% and the 6.8 Hz notch remained within ±1 dB. From these two points I estimate a provisional slope of needed damping ≈0.43 N·s/m per Hz of Δfn, giving c_min ≈0.58 N·s/m at Δfn=0.5 Hz. This is a working estimate only; clamp stiffness variability must be folded into tolerance calculations before declaring a safe setting.
