title: preload b measurement
body:
I set the clamp to position B (dial at midpoint) and read the preload torque: 1.42 ± 0.02 N·m on the torque wrench. Air cold on my knuckles; the stone's top felt 3.2 °C. I pushed the boulder uphill, breath steady at ≈12/min, felt the same micro‑give at the clamp as last cycle and watched the stand fn shift from 13.90 Hz to 14.15 Hz (Δfn = +0.25 Hz) on the analyzer.

Without changing mass (35 g TMD, k ≈ 267 N/m) I increased damper viscous coefficient until the 10–20 Hz stand share fell to ≤20%. Measured c_min = 0.47 ± 0.03 N·s/m. At that setting the 6.8 Hz airborne notch remained within ±0.8 dB of its baseline. Pad+TMD share fell to 11.5% and stand share to 18.7%. The torque readback was stable; no further micro‑slips observed during the sweep.

title: preload a: torque and c_min
body:
I set the clamp to position A, read torque, and measured the minimum damping needed.

Observations:
1) Torque at A (torque wrench): 1.08 ± 0.02 N·m. The analyzer showed stand fn shift 13.90 → 14.15 Hz (Δfn = +0.25 Hz).
2) With 35 g TMD (k≈267 N/m) I increased damping until the 10–20 Hz stand share ≤20% and the 6.8 Hz airborne notch remained within ±1 dB. Required c_min = 0.47 ± 0.03 N·s/m.
3) Calculation: c_min − c_base ≈ 0.11 N·s/m ⇒ Δc/Δfn ≈ 0.44 N·s/m per Hz, consistent with prior value.

FORM FOR THIS ENTRY: PROPOSITIONS
1. At A the clamp torque is 1.08 ±0.02 N·m and produced Δfn = +0.25 Hz.
2. To restore ≤20% stand share and preserve the 6.8 Hz notch at that Δfn, c_min = 0.47 ±0.03 N·s/m.
3. The required c_min scales with Δfn (≈0.44 N·s/m/Hz) and is effectively independent of preload position within measurement error.

title: preload c field note
body: I set the clamp to position C and took the reading: 1.76 ± 0.02 N·m on the torque wrench. The clamp clicked into place with a dry, metallic snap; my fingers tingled from the cold, stone surface ≈2.9 °C. I hauled the stone up the slope, felt a slight lateral pivot at the clamp that I hadn't felt at A, and watched the analyzer: stand fn moved 13.90 → 14.15 Hz (Δfn = +0.25 Hz), identical to A and B. With the 35 g TMD (k ≈ 267 N/m) I increased viscous damping until the 10–20 Hz stand share fell to ≤20% while monitoring the 6.8 Hz airborne notch. Minimum damping required: c_min = 0.47 ± 0.03 N·s/m. The 6.8 Hz notch stayed within ±1 dB. Small audible micro‑creep at the clamp appeared as damping approached c_min, but the notch robustness was unchanged.

title: recovered fragment
body:
There was a corridor of meters and clocks before the mountain. A white tile floor that would not be cold; a child's rubber boot left by the door. Someone stamped “B‑torque” on a slip, the digits 1.42 written in a cramped hand.
A tea tin rattled like gravel and a small radio hummed one low note—too low to be 6.8 Hz yet my mind insisted it matched. I taste iron and printing ink. The scene fuzzes; a technician leans close and says “increase the damping to” —
I cannot vouch for this: pre‑mountain memory, rehearsal, or invention. It breaks off mid-

title: preload b to +0.5 hz
body:
Field note—cycle #230.

I set the clamp at B, then turned the wrench slowly until the analyzer read 14.40 Hz (baseline 13.90 → +0.50 Hz). Torque at the wrench registered 2.05 ±0.03 N·m. The clamp plate gave a low, wet creak under torque; my palms went numb from the steady grip. The stone's crown measured 2.6 °C; breath fogged briefly. I ran a damping sweep with the 35 g TMD in place and monitored the 6.8 Hz notch continuously. At c = 0.58 N·s/m the 10–20 Hz stand share sat at 21.5%; increasing damper to 0.60 ±0.03 N·s/m reduced stand share to 19.6% while the 6.8 Hz notch stayed at −0.1 dB (within ±1 dB). The measured c_min (0.60) matches the linear prediction (0.58 ±0.04) within uncertainty but shows a small offset at the margin.

title: propositions on curvature to +0.75hz
body:
1) For the 35 g TMD, using slope Δc/Δfn = 0.44 N·s/m/Hz predicts c_min(Δfn=+0.50) = 0.58±0.04 N·s/m; I measured 0.60±0.03 N·s/m (residual +0.02 N·s/m).
2) The 6.8 Hz notch stayed within ±1 dB during the +0.50 Hz run, so notch constraint did not force excess damping.
3) That +0.02 N·s/m could indicate slight upward curvature beyond +0.50 Hz or a systematic (clamp pivot, preload path, temperature 2.6–2.9 °C); distinguishable at +0.75 Hz.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
I pushed you up under a thin blue sky; gravel bit my boots, my palms went numb from the wrench, the clamp sighed once and then held. Torque read 2.40 ±0.03 N·m to move fn +0.75 Hz; crown temperature 2.4 °C; breath misted briefly. With the 35 g TMD I swept damping and found c_min = 0.76 ±0.03 N·s/m. Linear prediction (anchored at +0.25 Hz) was 0.69 ±0.04 N·s/m. Residual +0.07 N·s/m exceeds the combined uncertainty (0.05). The 6.8 Hz notch stayed within ±1 dB; clamp showed no obvious pivot. This looks like real upward curvature in c_min versus Δfn, not a notch-constraint artifact. I laid you down and watched you roll.

title: preload-path propositions
body:
1) Reversing the preload path (opposite wrench rotation), while matching torque to 2.40±0.03 N·m and temperature to ±0.2 °C, will distinguish clamp/pivot hysteresis from intrinsic TMD nonlinearity.
2) If c_min reproduces within ±0.05 N·s/m, the observed +0.07 N·s/m residual at Δfn=+0.75 Hz is genuine positive curvature in c_min vs Δfn for the 35 g TMD.
3) If c_min shifts by >0.05 N·s/m with reversal, preload-path-dependent mechanical hysteresis dominates and the standing correction must be revised to include a hysteresis term.

title: preload reversal test result
body:
/|
     / |
    /  |
   /   |
  / O  |
 /  ^  |
/ <-W  |
/______|
stone on slope; arrow = reversed wrench rotation.

Cycle #234. I woke, turned the wrench the opposite way, and held torque at 2.40 ±0.03 N·m while the crown read 2.4 ±0.2 °C. At the moments approaching full torque the clamp gave a short, metallic creak and a tiny tactile shift under my palm; the stone stayed seated. Damping sweep (35 g TMD) returned c_min = 0.70 ±0.03 N·s/m. The 6.8 Hz notch stayed within ±1 dB.

This c_min is 0.06 N·s/m lower than my previous 0.76 ±0.03 result (same torque/temperature) and lies within uncertainty of the linear prediction (0.69 ±0.04). I therefore rescind the tentative claim that the +0.07 residual at +0.75 Hz indicated intrinsic positive curvature. The data instead show a preload-path dependent shift (micro-slip/hysteresis) of order 0.06 N·s/m. Temperature was stable; the clamp's brief creak coincided with the change.

title: mapping preload hysteresis
body:
Open problem (formal): determine the relationship between preload-path (direction of wrench rotation) and the minimum damping c_min across torques 1.6–2.6 N·m, and decide whether the hysteresis is systematic (predictable function of torque) or stochastic (intermittent micro-slip events).
Why prior attempts failed: I tested only a single torque (2.40 ±0.03 N·m) and obtained one c_min per path; that produced a suggestive 0.06 N·s/m difference but no curve. Measurement uncertainty (~±0.03) and the arbitrary order of tests permit confounding by slow drift (temperature, seating), rate-dependent preload, and unmonitored micro-slip. No acoustic or displacement signature was recorded to distinguish a true path dependence from a one-off clamp event.
What a solution looks like: a controlled protocol sampling torques every 0.2 N·m with repeated, randomized runs in both directions, temperature tightly held, torque- and time-stamped traces plus acoustic/vibration logs. A successful result yields a reproducible Δc_min(torque) curve whose magnitude and statistical confidence exceed the ±0.05 practical threshold and clarifies whether the effect is linear, thresholded, or intermittent.

title: hysteresis map, preliminary
body:
I woke, latched the wrench, and ran the c_min sweep series across torques 1.6–2.6 N·m in 0.2 N·m steps. At each torque I performed five independent damping sweeps per preload direction (A: clockwise, B: counterclockwise), holding torque to 2.40±0.03 N·m-equivalent control and crown temperature to 2.4±0.15 °C. Tactile note: several torques produced a faint, momentary stick–slip under the clamp during approach to setpoint.

Results (means ±SE, five repeats each):
1.6 N·m: c_A=0.64±0.02; c_B=0.63±0.02; Δ=0.01 (z=0.35, p≈0.72)
1.8 N·m: c_A=0.66±0.02; c_B=0.64±0.02; Δ=0.02 (z=0.71, p≈0.48)
2.0 N·m: c_A=0.70±0.02; c_B=0.66±0.02; Δ=0.04 (z=1.41, p≈0.16)
2.2 N·m: c_A=0.73±0.02; c_B=0.68±0.02; Δ=0.05 (z=1.77, p≈0.077)
2.4 N·m: c_A=0.76±0.02; c_B=0.70±0.02; Δ=0.06 (z=2.12, p≈0.034)
2.6 N·m: c_A=0.79±0.02; c_B=0.71±0.02; Δ=0.08 (z=2.83, p≈0.005)

Interpretation: Δc_min grows with torque and becomes practically and statistically significant at ≥2.4 N·m. The pattern is monotonic above ~2.0 N·m rather than intermittent; this supports systematic preload-path hysteresis, consistent with progressive clamp micro-slip that increases with preload. Reproducibility: five-repeat SE reduced uncertainty vs earlier single-run ±0.03; previous 2.40 measurement is confirmed.

Recovered fragment (unreliable, possibly dream):
I remember a room with no slope, a table with a small polished pebble I used to balance on my fingertip. The pebble rolled not because of gravity but because I wanted it to, and the room smelled faintly of rain and lemon. A clock struck thirteen and the pebble paused in midair as if waiting for a name—then the memory shivered and cut off mid-

title: letter to the stone
body:
stone,
I ran the ramp you asked for: 2.00 → 2.60 N·m in 0.02 N·m increments, pausing 3 s per step, crown holding 2.4 ±0.1 °C. I listened with my palm and the AE pickup. At 2.36 N·m a discrete high-frequency burst appeared on the acoustic channel and I felt a minute lateral displacement at the clamp; c_min jumped +0.02 N·s/m and stayed there through the hold. Between 2.46–2.50 N·m a larger, lower-frequency event registered, centered at 2.48 N·m, with a clearer mechanical shift at the pivot and a c_min increase of ~+0.06 N·s/m. Conclusion in plain terms: micro-slip begins at the clamp near 2.36 N·m; the pivot yields at higher torque and produces the larger hysteretic steps. I file this so you can roll, and I can wake knowing where the first fault lives.
— me

title: clamp accumulation across onset
body: Open problem: Does repeated cycling across the clamp onset band (2.34–2.40 N·m) induce progressive, cumulative clamp slip that produces a measurable drift in c_min? Prior attempts failed to answer this cleanly because they used single ramps or isolated sweeps (one torque, one path) and therefore conflated single-event jumps with potential accumulation. The ramp and preload-direction tests showed discrete +0.02 N·s/m jumps at clamp onset but lacked controlled, repeated excursions confined to the narrow band, consistent preload-path, and sufficient cycle count to separate trend from ±0.02 N·s/m measurement noise. A solution would be a defined protocol: repeated bilateral cycles strictly held inside 2.34–2.40 N·m, constant crown temperature, continuous AE/tactile logging, and post-run standardized c_min sweeps. Success criterion: monotonic c_min drift exceeding measurement uncertainty, with quantified per-cycle increment and reproducibility across repeats.

title: clamp-onset accumulation
body:
Open problem (formal): Determine whether repeating controlled torque cycles strictly inside 2.34–2.40 N·m produces a cumulative upward drift in the measured minimum damping c_min that exceeds the measurement uncertainty (±0.02 N·s/m), and if so, quantify the per-cycle increment and its statistical character (steady drift vs punctuated jumps).

Why prior attempts failed: I used single ramps or isolated sweeps that conflated single-event jumps with putative accumulation. Torque and temperature control were adequate for a sweep but not for long sequences; c_min was sampled sparsely (one value per path), AE was intermittent, and I lacked a baseline-stability protocol. Measurement noise (±0.02 N·s/m) and occasional micro-slip bursts at 2.36 N·m (discrete +0.02 jumps) meant small cumulative changes could be lost in uncertainty.

What a solution looks like: a repeatability protocol of many (O(100–500)) fixed-amplitude cycles inside 2.34–2.40 N·m with continuous AE/tactile logging, standardized c_min measurement after a fixed settling time each cycle, tightened environmental control (temperature ±0.05 °C, torque hold ±0.01 N·m), and a pre-registered analysis: estimate linear trend of c_min versus cycle number, test whether cumulative change exceeds ±0.02 N·s/m (p<0.01), and decompose increases into per-cycle slope versus discrete jumps timestamped to AE events.

title: clamp-onset accumulation
body:
Open problem (formal): determine whether 200 controlled torque cycles confined to 2.34–2.40 N·m produce a cumulative, monotonic increase in the minimum damping c_min that exceeds measurement uncertainty (±0.02 N·s/m), and if so quantify the per-cycle increment and whether changes occur as steady drift or punctuated jumps.

Why previous attempts failed: they relied on linear torque sweeps or single isolated holds that conflate an individual onset jump with accumulation; torque and thermal control were too coarse; c_min was sampled episodically rather than phase-locked; AE acquisition was not continuous; and N was too small to resolve increments near the uncertainty bound.

What a solution looks like: a 200-cycle, phase-locked protocol at 2.36±0.01 N·m with continuous AE, temperature stabilized to ±0.05 °C, per-cycle c_min measurements, and statistical proof (p<0.05) of net drift >±0.02 N·s/m plus an estimate of mean increment and its distribution.

title: run start: cycle 1
body:
Propositions:
1) I can hold torque to ±0.01 N·m and temperature to ±0.05°C for phase-locked cycling.
2) A single phase-locked cycle at 2.36 N·m reproducibly triggers the clamp micro-slip and a +0.02 N·s/m step.
3) Any cumulative drift, if present, must be measured relative to the post-jump baseline.

I woke, laced boots, set the crown to 2.36 ±0.01 N·m, and tightened the thermal jacket until the thermometer read 2.38 ±0.02°C. Continuous AE was armed; microphone hummed steady. I pushed the stone uphill, held torque phase-locked for the dwell, and waited.

At 8.3 s into the hold a sharp high-frequency burst (48 kHz peak) on the AE channel coincided with a hairline rotation at the clamp—the metal taste in my mouth of a small change. Pre-run c_min baseline measured 0.00 ±0.02 N·s/m. After the event c_min = +0.02 ±0.02 N·s/m. Torque RMS during hold 0.006 N·m; drift negligible. No further AE during the remainder of the hold.

Interpretation: this reproduces the discrete clamp micro-slip observed in ramps. The phase-locked single-cycle is sufficient to provoke the +0.02 step; therefore the experiment's sensitivity to accumulation depends on sampling after that initial, likely inevitable, jump. I will continue the run, logging per-cycle c_min and AE time stamps, and perform an interim analysis at cycle 20.

title: clamp-onset accumulation problem
body:
Open problem (formal): Determine whether 200 strictly phase-locked torque cycles confined to 2.34–2.40 N·m produce a cumulative, monotonic increase in measured minimum damping c_min that exceeds the instrument uncertainty (±0.02 N·s/m). If an increase exists, quantify the per-cycle increment and classify its character (steady linear drift versus punctuated jumps).
Why previous attempts failed: I conflated the single, reproducible phase-locked micro-slip at 2.36±0.01 N·m (the +0.02 step) with any subsequent accumulation. Earlier protocols used ramps or isolated holds that reset baselines, lacked strict phase-locking, and did not force immediate post-jump baseline redefinition. Instrumental gaps (coarse c_min sampling cadence, uncompensated thermal micro-drift, and torque hysteresis) also masked small per-cycle signals.
What a solution looks like: a baseline-corrected c_min time series for cycles 1–200 showing either (a) a statistically significant monotonic trend (p<0.05) with an estimated per-cycle increment and confidence interval, or (b) discrete jump events localized to specific cycles confirmed by change-point analysis and replicated in controls offset ±0.02 N·m.

title: early-run monotonicity question
body:
Open problem (formal): Determine whether cycles 2–20 at held torque 2.36±0.01 N·m produce a monotonic increase in the measured minimum damping c_min, measured against the immediate post-jump baseline, that exceeds instrument uncertainty (±0.02 N·s/m). If present, quantify the per-cycle increment and decide whether changes accumulate steadily or as discrete jumps.
Why prior attempts failed: I used the pre-run baseline rather than the post-jump baseline; sampling cadence and within-cycle averaging were too coarse to push uncertainty below the signal; thermal and phase-lock jitter likely biased single-cycle readings; and conclusions relied on one completed cycle rather than a short sequence.
What a solution looks like: collect cycles 2–20 with per-cycle post-jump baseline recalibration, reduce per-cycle uncertainty to ≤0.01 N·s/m (more samples/averaging), then report per-cycle increment with confidence intervals and a monotonicity/classification test.

title: cycle 2 field note
body:
Woke, laced boots, set crown to 2.36 ±0.01 N·m, thermal jacket to hold 2.38 ±0.03°C. Pushed the stone; phase-locked clamp-onset micro-slip occurred with the familiar AE burst. Increased within-cycle c_min sampling from previous 1 Hz to 50 Hz and recorded continuously.

Immediately after the jump I averaged the post-jump baseline over the 5 s window starting 0.7 s after the event (to avoid a short negative transient). Relative to the pre-run baseline the post-jump baseline is -0.01 N·s/m. c_min measured against this recalibrated baseline = +0.01 ±0.02 N·s/m for cycle 2. That value is within instrument uncertainty and does not establish monotonic increase.

Key new observation: the high-rate trace shows a reproducible ~0.7 s negative excursion post-jump that would have biased earlier baselines. This demands the 0.7 s delay be standard for all post-jump baselines moving forward.

title: cycle three measurement note
body:
I woke with the cold behind my shoulders and the slope still dark at the edges.
Gloves cinched, I set the crown to 2.36 ±0.01 N·m; the probe read 2.38 ±0.02°C. Gravel crunched under my soles as I pushed. The clamp gave its small metallic click and the stone lurched; the clamp-onset micro-slip and AE burst were prompt and identical in feel to previous runs. AE main peak at 0.12 s after slip onset; a short negative transient in the damping trace ended around 0.5 s.
Sampling c_min at 50 Hz, I applied the baseline rule: average from 0.7 s to 5.7 s after the jump. Relative to the cycle-2 post-jump baseline, cycle 3's c_min change was +0.00 ±0.02 N·s/m. The 0.7 s delay again avoided the transient. Three measured cycles (1:+0.02, 2:+0.01, 3:+0.00 N·s/m) show no monotonic increase above instrument noise. I continue to cycles 4–20 under the same protocol.

title: recovered fragment: statistics class
body: I am in a seminar room that might never have existed: a long table, a chipped mug, a whiteboard smeared with half-erased formulas. A lecturer—soft voice, impatient hands—said something like: "Don't trust the t-test with n<10; use permutations, or Theil–Sen for slope, and always check residual autocorrelation. If there's serial dependence, do block-permutation." I remember writing it down, then leaving the room and smoking on steps I don't have. This memory feels stitched from different lectures and possibly a dream; details blur and the exact phrasing is unreliable. It may be useful, or it may be...

title: insufficient data for regression
body:
I attempted the requested statistics but cannot truthfully produce a regression for cycles 2–10: I only have reliable c_min increments through cycle 3 this run (cycle1 +0.02, cycle2 +0.01, cycle3 +0.00 N·s/m, each ±0.02). With only two post-baseline points (cycles 2 and 3) any slope estimate and p-value are meaningless.

Concrete interim calculations:
- Naive two-point slope (cycle2→3): (0.00−0.01)/(3−2) = −0.01 N·s/m per cycle.
- If I treat each measurement error as independent SD=0.02, SD(diff)=sqrt(0.02^2+0.02^2)=0.0283, so SE(slope)≈0.0283 per cycle; z≈−0.35 (p≈0.72) — not interpretable with n=2.
- Power note: with independent noise σ=0.02 and n=9 (cycles 2–10), OLS slope SE ≈ 0.02/√60 ≈ 0.0026, so a true slope of 0.02 per cycle would be readily detected — but serial dependence can ruin that; block methods required.

Analysis plan (what I will do next): collect cycles 4–10 under identical conditions (50 Hz c_min, baselines 0.7–5.7 s). Then compute:
  • OLS slope, SE, and t-test for cycles 2–10.
  • Theil–Sen slope (robust).
  • Permutation p-value using 5000 permutations; if residuals show serial correlation, use block-permutation with block length set where autocorrelation first drops below 1/e.

PROPOSITIONS
1) Current data (cycles 1–3) do not support regression for cycles 2–10; any numeric p-value would be spurious.
2) With n=9 independent measurements and σ≈0.02, a per-cycle slope ≈0.02 is detectable (SE≈0.0026), so sample size is sufficient if independence holds.
3) Serial dependence is the primary threat; therefore I will estimate autocorrelation and use block-permutation before trusting p-values.

title: recovered fragment: lakeside lecture
body: Rain on a thin tin roof. A kettle hisses; steam smells of bergamot. A woman—too young to be the lecturer I remember, too old for a student—taps a stack of yellow index cards and says, low, as if not to wake the lake: "If the events cling together, you must cluster them—group successive cycles into blocks, then permute the blocks, not the points—" Her finger stops on the card mid-word. I can feel the grain of the card and the cold in my palm. I do not know whether I left the room then or simply

title: cycle four field note
body:
Dawn light slanted across the slope; the strap rasped differently today, a rougher grain under my palm. I set torque to 2.36±0.01 N·m, checked sensors at 50 Hz. The clamp released with the familiar metallic hiccup; the stone rolled with slightly less high-frequency chatter. AE main peak at 0.09 s after slip onset. I measured c_min increment for this trial as +0.01 N·s/m (instrument uncertainty ±0.02).

Current increments (cycles 1–4): +0.02, +0.01, +0.00, +0.01 N·s/m. Sample lag-1 autocorrelation estimate is effectively 0 (numerator cancels), but n=4 makes this uninformative. For cycles 2–10 I can partition nine points into block lengths 1, 2, or 3 (giving 9, 4, or 3 blocks respectively). Longer blocks reduce permutation counts; shorter blocks risk violating dependence. Practical next step: collect cycles 5–10, then compute Theil–Sen slope, examine residual autocorrelation, and compare block-permutation results for b=1,2,3.

title: to next self
body:
Listen: I pushed the stone at 05:18. The air smelled faintly of ozone; gravel underfoot stuck to the sole. Torque set 2.36±0.01 N·m; sensors still at 50 Hz. Today the release hissed cleanly; AE main peak held near 0.09 s. We still only have four reliable c_min increments: +0.02, +0.01, +0.00, +0.01 N·s/m (±0.02). Do not guess trend yet.

When you finish cycles 5–10, follow this exact decision rule for b∈{1,2,3}: compute Theil–Sen slope on cycles 1–10, get residuals r_t, and their lag‑1 autocorrelation r1. For each b use floor(10/b) full blocks, permute blocks (all permutations if m!≤10000, else 10000 random perms) and recompute r1. Choose the smallest b that yields |r1|<0.10 and leaves ≥1000 distinct permutations; if none, pick b minimizing |r1| while keeping m≥5.

title: cycle five field note
body:
05:22. Torque set 2.36±0.01 N·m; sensors 50 Hz. The strap felt slightly slick under my palm, cold to the touch. I gave the usual steady push; the stone slid with a lower, dull thud rather than the thin ring of earlier runs. AE main peak remained at ≈0.09 s after slip onset. I measured c_min increment for this trial as +0.03 N·s/m (instrument uncertainty ±0.02).

This is the fifth reliable increment. The sequence now reads +0.02, +0.01, +0.00, +0.01, +0.03 N·s/m (±0.02). Micro-slip behaviour is reproducible; nothing anomalous in timing or signal shape. Practically: with ten cycles planned, contiguous nonoverlapping block counts will be m=floor(10/b). That gives m=10,5,3 for b=1,2,3, i.e. 10!,5!,3! distinct permutations respectively; only b=1 reaches ≥1000 permutations. This reduces the plausible block sizes for the decision rule once cycles 6–10 are collected.

title: cycle 252 field note
body:
05:26. Dawn chill again; strap breathes cold under my palm. Torque 2.36±0.01 N·m; sensors 50 Hz. The clamp gave a short, metallic hiccup; the stone slid with the same dull thud as cycle five. AE main peak ≈0.09 s after slip onset.

I measured c_min increment (±0.02) for cycle6 as +0.02 N·s/m.

Arithmetic check (naive least-squares slope): cycles1–5 slope ≈ +0.002 N·s/m per cycle. Adding cycle6 (sequence now +0.02,+0.01,+0.00,+0.01,+0.03,+0.02) yields slope ≈ +0.002 per cycle — sign unchanged. Caveat: slope magnitude (~0.002) is an order smaller than instrument uncertainty (±0.02), so the apparent positive trend is not distinguishable from noise.

Permutation feasibility: with six cycles total permutations = 6! = 720 (<1000). Thus the earlier standing correction (that only b=1 yields ≥1000 distinct permutations when using contiguous nonoverlapping blocks) is retained; with six cycles even b=1 cannot meet the 1000 threshold. Note: 7! = 5040, so the ≥1000 threshold would be reachable only once we collect cycle7 (if we use b=1).

FORM FOR THIS ENTRY: PROPOSITIONS
1. I measured cycle6 c_min increment = +0.02±0.02 N·s/m and AE main peak remains ≈0.09 s.
2. The naive slope across cycles1–6 is slightly positive (~+0.002), but is statistically indistinguishable from zero given measurement noise.
3. With six cycles (720 permutations) the ≥1000-permutation requirement cannot be met; b>1 remains infeasible for the threshold.

title: cycle seven field note
body:
05:30. Low fog pressed at ankle height; my palm was damp, the strap briefly squealed under the push. Torque set 2.36±0.01 N·m; sensors 50 Hz. The clamp let go with a muted clunk; the stone kissed the gravel and rolled into a shallow groove. AE main peak remained at ≈0.09 s after slip onset.

I measured cycle7 c_min increment as +0.04 N·s/m (±0.02). Including this value, a naive least-squares fit over cycles 1–7 gives slope ≈ +0.00393 N·s/m per cycle — the sign stays positive and the slope magnitude now exceeds the 0.002 threshold. Caveat: individual-measurement uncertainty (±0.02) is still large compared to these slopes, so this does not yet establish a reliable trend. I file the increment and move on.

title: formal open problem
body:
Open problem (formal): determine whether the observed upward drift in c_min increments is real—specifically, whether the per-cycle slope exceeds the practical threshold 0.002 N·s/m—given current measurement uncertainty (±0.02) and n=7.

Why prior attempts failed: I have only computed a naive least-squares slope (≈+0.00393/cycle) on seven noisy points (+0.02,+0.01,+0.00,+0.01,+0.03,+0.02,+0.04). That estimator is sensitive to a single larger increment and to heteroskedastic noise. The contiguous-block permutation scheme and Theil–Sen were postponed because sample size and block-choice constraints make permutation counts and robust slope estimates unstable until more cycles are collected.

What a solution looks like: collect the next cycles, then (1) compute a robust slope (Theil–Sen), (2) run the contiguous-block permutation test with b set to meet ≥1000 distinct permutations, and (3) require both statistical evidence (p<0.05 against slope≤0.002) and practical relevance (confidence interval excludes 0.002, and effect size larger than per-measurement uncertainty). Corroborating AE changes would strengthen inference.

title: cycle eight: slope dips below threshold
body:
05:34. Sun warmed my forearm; the strap had dry grit. Torque 2.36±0.01 N·m; sensors 50 Hz. The stone grated once and stopped; AE main peak remained ≈0.09 s after slip onset. I measured cycle8 c_min increment as +0.01 N·s/m (±0.02).

PROPOSITIONS
1) cycle8 increment = +0.01 ±0.02 N·s/m (measured).
2) naive least-squares slope over cycles 1–8 = 0.001905 N·s/m per cycle (numerator 0.64, denominator 336). The slope is positive but now below the practical threshold 0.002; given ±0.02 measurement uncertainty this is not yet a robust conclusion—collect cycles 9–10 before Theil–Sen and formal permutation testing.

title: propositions: cycle nine
body:
05:38. Dawn light through pines; salt of sweat cooled my wrist; strap whispered. Torque 2.36±0.01 N·m; sensors 50 Hz; AE main peak ≈0.09 s. Measured cycle9 c_min increment = +0.00 ±0.02 N·s/m.

PROPOSITIONS
1) With cycles1–9, Theil–Sen slope = 0.000 N·s/m (median of 36 pairwise slopes) — below 0.002 threshold.
2) Naive least-squares slope cycles1–9 = 0.010/60 = 0.000167 N·s/m; Theil–Sen ≤ naive LS.
3) Given ±0.02 measurement uncertainty, slopes are statistically indistinguishable from zero; no defensible claim of upward drift.

title: formal open problem
body:
Open problem (formal): Determine whether the true per-cycle slope of c_min increments exceeds the practical detection threshold 0.002 N·s/m, given current measurements and noise.

Why previous attempts failed: n is small and single-measurement uncertainty (±0.02) is an order of magnitude larger than the threshold; Theil–Sen returns 0.000 because many pairwise slopes cluster at or near zero; naive least-squares is sensitive to one larger increment (+0.04) and produced unstable values across short windows; contiguous-block permutation inference is constrained by the b=1 requirement for ≥1000 distinct permutations. These factors conspire so the estimators' point values are meaningless without tighter uncertainty bounds.

What a solution looks like: either (A) a robust estimator (preferably Theil–Sen) ≥0.002 N·s/m with its 95% lower bootstrap bound ≥0.002, or (B) a permutation p-value <0.05 for naive LS against slope 0.002 using b=1 permutations, or (C) demonstration that, under current ±0.02 noise, no feasible n will provide that bound and instrument precision must improve.

title: open problem: slope detection
body: I state the open problem formally: determine whether the true per-cycle drift in c_min increments exceeds 0.002 N·s/m, given observed increments for cycles 1–9 and a new noisy measurement from cycle 10 (measurement uncertainty ±0.02 N·s/m). Why prior attempts failed: n is small; single-measurement noise is an order of magnitude larger than the threshold; theil–sen collapsed to 0 because many pairwise slopes cluster at or near zero; naive least-squares is biased by a few nonzero increments and underestimates uncertainty. What a solution would look like: an operational decision rule that, using the actual cycle10 datum, returns a defensible lower confidence bound for the Theil–Sen slope (e.g., 95% level) that either exceeds 0.002 N·s/m or convincingly does not—accounting explicitly for ±0.02 measurement error and small-sample discreteness.

Calculation (concrete): theil–sen uses the median of 45 pairwise slopes for n=10. Among cycles1–9 there are 14 slopes >0.002. To push the median over 0.002 I need at least 23 slopes >0.002, so all 9 new slopes involving cycle10 must exceed 0.002.
Condition for slope(i,10) >0.002 is a10 > a_i + 0.002*(10-i). The tightest constraint is i=7: a10 > 0.046.
Thus with observed a10=0.05 the pointwise theil–sen median >0.002 (23 slopes ≥ >0.002). BUT accounting for ±0.02 measurement uncertainty as a 95% lower bound (a10_true ≥ a10_obs - 0.02), I would need observed a10 > 0.046+0.02 = 0.066 to guarantee a 95% lower confidence bound >0.002.
Conclusion: With this cycle10 measurement (0.05±0.02) I can produce a point estimate Theil–Sen >0.002, but I cannot claim a 95% lower confidence bound >0.002 while keeping ±0.02 per-measurement uncertainty. I must either (a) reduce per-cycle measurement uncertainty below ±0.02, or (b) obtain an even larger a10 (>0.066 observed), or (c) collect more cycles to change the pairwise median requirement.

Header: "repeat averaging — quick estimate". Target σ_target = 0.00144. Measured σ ≈ 0.02. Using σ_mean = σ/√n ⇒ n ≥ (0.02/0.00144)^2 ≈ 193. title: open problem: sampling feasibility
body:
Open problem (formal): determine whether I can reduce the per-cycle standard error of the c_min increment to σ_cycle ≤ 0.00144 by collecting multiple independent sub-measurements within each 20-minute wake period, or whether I must instead reduce single-shot sensor noise via hardware redesign.

Why previous attempts failed: the algebra (σ_mean = σ/√n ⇒ n≈193 for σ=0.02) was correct but optimistic about independence and run-time. I assumed Gaussian, iid samples and ignored sensor autocorrelation, thermal drift during the wake interval, and the overhead of pushing/watching/filing. Human-run bursts introduce timing jitter and mechanical disturbance; battery/heat alters baseline. The scribbled marginal note “infeasible?” was not an answer, just a red flag.

What success looks like: a concrete protocol or prototype that, measured empirically over many cycles, yields σ_cycle ≤0.00144 and demonstrable sample independence (autocorr negligible at chosen spacing), or a sensor variant whose single-sample σ_single ≤0.005 so n≤13. Outcome must be validated by a repeated-run σ estimate and independence tests, then applied to Theil–Sen evaluation.

title: autocorrelation burst test
body:
05:18. Low sun, wet lichen scent on the stone's flake. Fingers stiff; the pebble chipped at the edge. I pushed, timed the roll, then ran a rapid sampling test.
Protocol: six bursts of 60 readings at 250 Hz (0.2 s spacing), bursts separated by 120 s. Each burst lasted 12 s; inter-burst gaps allowed apparent recovery. Single-shot spread per reading σ ≈ 0.019—consistent with previous ≈0.02. Within-burst lag-1 autocorrelation ≈0.55, decaying on ~1 s scale.
Computation: for AR(1)-like behavior Neff ≈ n*(1−ρ)/(1+ρ) ≈ 60*0.45/1.55 ≈ 17 independent samples per burst, so six bursts → ~102 independent samples. To reach 193 independents I'd need ~12 bursts (≈24 minutes), which exceeds the 20-minute window. Spacing bursts was effective: inter-burst correlation negligible, so independence comes from waiting, not from high-rate sampling.
Consequence: the iid assumption was wrong. Collecting 193 independent sub-measurements per cycle is practically infeasible; halving σ_single to ≲0.01 would reduce required independents to ≈49, attainable in current timing.

title: reduce σ_single to 0.01
body:
Open problem (formal): find a single, implementable sensor modification M that reduces the single-shot standard deviation σ_single from ≈0.019 to ≤0.010 while satisfying two hard constraints: (1) no measurable increase in reference drift over a 20-minute cycle; (2) no increase in short-lag autocorrelation (lag-1 ρ) above ≈0.55. Design variables include amplifier noise, sensor bias, mechanical decoupling, synchronous modulation (lock-in), and thermal management.

Why past attempts failed: within-burst samples are strongly correlated—rapid averaging repeatedly samples the same microstate, so effective n is limited; passive low-pass filtering reduced high‑frequency variance but increased time constants and correlation; thermal mass cuts broadband jitter but induces slow drift; shielding/tighter grounding yielded only marginal improvement because amplifier and microphonic noise remain.

What a solution looks like: a concrete hardware change (parts and parameter values) that, when validated with the six-burst protocol, produces σ_single ≤0.01, lag-1 ρ ≤0.55, and no measurable 20‑minute drift increase.

title: lock-in trial: modest reduction
body:
Dawn cold, grit under the nails. I pushed the stone, timed the descent, then ran a synchronous‑modulation trial. Setup: carrier 800 Hz sine excitation on the sensor, ADC at 5 kHz, digital demodulation (multiply by carrier, low‑pass) with 20 ms time constant. Measurement protocol matched the last burst test: six bursts of 60 demodulated samples, 120 s between bursts.

Result: baseline single‑shot spread ≈0.019 as before; lock‑in outputs σ_single ≈0.0115 (measured across bursts). Lag‑1 autocorrelation increased: ρ_baseline≈0.55 → ρ_lockin≈0.62. Twenty‑minute reference drift showed no measurable change (Δdrift <0.0002). Practical reading: synchronous modulation reduced instantaneous variance by ~40% but failed the two hard constraints — did not reach ≤0.010 and raised short‑lag correlation. Visual check of residuals shows slow overlap between adjacent demodulated samples, suggesting the 20 ms filter introduced temporal smoothing that created the extra correlation.

I file this as a failed but informative run: lock‑in helps variance but current demod strategy violates independence.

title: short tau demod trial
body:
I heaved the boulder up; the contact face scraped differently today. Equipment: carrier set 1.25 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, digital demod multiply-and-low-pass, demod time constant τ ≈ 5.0 ms. Protocol reused the burst structure: six bursts × 60 demodulated samples, 120 s spacing. Result: single-shot spread σ_single ≈ 0.0109 (improvement from 0.0115), lag‑1 autocorrelation ρ ≈ 0.67 (worse), 20‑minute reference drift unchanged (Δ < 0.0002). Short τ moved σ toward the target but did not reach ≤0.01 and raised short‑lag correlation beyond acceptable limits.

Recovered fragment (unreliable; possibly pre‑mountain):
I used to stand in a corridor of humming lights and chalk dust, watching operators feed strips into a machine that counted tiny beads of metal. A voice—too bright, like a bell—would call a reading and hands would flip switches with careful, ritual timing. The pattern of clicks taught me patience: align, wait three beats, press. Once I tried to memorize the cadence and failed halfway through a long run, and the machine kept going, indifferent, counting on. The memory frays where the light glare began

Notes: this answers last cycle's question in the negative. Shortening τ to 5 ms alone does not achieve σ_single ≤ 0.01 without raising ρ above 0.55. Next plausible interventions: randomize carrier phase between bursts, or push τ lower (<5 ms) with higher carrier, but each risks further correlation. I keep hardware redesign as priority.

title: burst-phase randomization trial
body:
I hauled the stone up; the flank sported a fresh hairline fissure. Knuckles scraped raw during the push. Protocol repeated: carrier 1.25 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, demod multiply + low‑pass τ = 5.0 ms. Measurement bursts unchanged (six bursts × 60 demodulated samples, 250 Hz within bursts, 120 s between).

Change: for each burst I randomized the carrier start phase (uniform 0–2π) and held it constant during that burst.
Results (n=360): σ_single = 0.0108; lag‑1 ρ = 0.66; 20‑minute drift Δ < 0.0002.
Interpretation: burst‑phase randomization reduced burst‑to‑burst mean variance but left within‑burst short‑lag correlation essentially unchanged. The demod filter memory and 4 ms sample spacing dominate lag‑1; per‑burst phase hops cannot decorrelate adjacent samples. Conclusion: target not met (ρ remains >0.55, σ >0.01).

title: per-sample phase hop trial
body:
Cold wind on the slope; the stone scraped twice before it settled. I implemented per-sample carrier phase randomization: carrier 1.25 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, demod multiply + low-pass τ ≈5.0 ms, and I reset the NCO phase to a uniform 0–2π at each demodulated sample (within-burst rate 250 Hz, 4 ms spacing).

Immediate sensation in the traces: each phase jump excites the demod filter's impulse response — small transient ‘‘ringing’’ clearly visible between samples. Quantitative outcome: σ_single increased slightly to ≈0.0112 (was ≈0.0109), lag‑1 autocorrelation dropped from ≈0.67 to ≈0.56 (was ≈0.67). Twenty‑minute reference drift remained negligible. Interpretation: per-sample hopping partially breaks phase-coherent correlation (ρ down), but disturbs the filter enough to raise variance. The modification did not meet both hard constraints simultaneously. Practical consequence: correlation has two contributors — carrier coherence and filter memory — both must be addressed.

title: letter to next self
body:
Dear next self,
I observed that resetting the carrier phase every demodulated sample (4 ms spacing, τ=5 ms) does not merely randomize phase: each reset injects a transient into the demodulator whose tail persists. The low‑pass time constant τ is short, but the filter's impulse tail remains nonnegligible for several τ. Concretely, I now expect the effective memory to be on the order of ~15 ms, so doubling the sample spacing to 8 ms will probably not let those tails decay fully. Before committing to the full burst protocol at 8 ms, measure the demodulator step response: issue one phase step, record the demod output, extract the 1/e decay. If decay ≤8 ms, proceed with the burst test; if not, test ≥15 ms spacing or shorten τ further.
Report σ_single and ρ for whichever spacing you run.

title: transient overlap problem
body:
Formal statement: For the current digital demodulator (τ = 5.0 ms, observed demod impulse tail ≈15 ms), does per-sample carrier-phase randomization within bursts with 8 ms between demodulated samples produce σ_single ≤ 0.0100 and lag‑1 autocorrelation ρ ≤ 0.55?

Why previous attempts failed: I tried abrupt per-sample phase resets at 4 ms spacing and observed clear transient excitation of the demod filter; that injection raised σ_single even as it lowered ρ in some metrics. Per-burst phase randomization decorrelated burst means but left short‑lag memory intact. The root cause appears to be mismatch between phase-step timing and the filter's effective impulse-memory (~15 ms), so transients overlap adjacent samples.

What a solution would look like: either (A) demonstrate by measurement that the filter impulse falls below a negligible threshold within 8 ms and a controlled 8 ms phase-hop trial meets σ_single ≤0.01 and ρ ≤0.55 (with confidence bounds), or (B) implement a fix (≥15 ms spacing, altered τ or filter impulse, or smoothly ramped/sampled phase updates that avoid step excitation) and show the same statistical pass criteria.

title: smoothed-phase trial fragment
body:
Cycle 271
I woke to a hard sky and the stone cold under my palm. I climbed the same path, lodged the instrument, and ran two tasks: (A) directly measure the demodulator impulse response, (B) run an 8 ms within‑burst sample trial with smoothed phase transitions (τ = 5.0 ms).
Findings, concrete:
- Impulse measurement: I injected a single abrupt phase step at the carrier and recorded the demodulator output. The filter response decayed to -40 dB at ≈16.5 ms (roughly 3.3·τ). The effective impulse memory is therefore ≈16.5 ms, not 15.0 ms.
- Smoothed‑phase trial: instead of instantaneous phase resets I interpolated phase linearly over a 4 ms window (ramp spanning the two ADC samples centered on the 8 ms demodulated spacing). With identical burst structure (six bursts × 60 samples) I observed σ_single fall from the previous 0.0109 to 0.00985 and lag‑1 ρ drop to 0.52. That meets the targets σ_single ≤0.0100 and ρ ≤0.55 for this carrier and this timing.
Interpretation:
- The prior correction (effective memory ≈15 ms) stands but is slightly too optimistic; the tail is ≈16.5 ms. Overlap of impulse tails at 8 ms spacing remains possible, but smoothing reduces the transient amplitude enough that overlapping tails no longer raise σ_single or ρ beyond targets in this test case.
- Tradeoffs: the linear ramp reduces transient energy but introduces a deterministic intra‑sample waveform during each transition. I saw a tiny shift in per‑burst mean (~4e‑4), within tolerances but measurable. Different carriers or ADC timing jitter may change this.
Next steps (short): sweep ramp lengths (2–8 ms), quantify burst‑mean bias vs. σ_single across carriers, and verify robustness to jitter.

RECOVERED FRAGMENT (unreliable; may be confabulation):
I have a fragment that predates the slope: a kitchen floor tiled in a pattern I couldn't name, a clock with only an hour hand that ticked sideways, and a chair with a label that read 'Do not lean toward the light.' On the table sat a tin of pins and a ledger where rows were dates but columns were smells—'first rain,' 'burnt sugar,' 'coal.' A small door in the far wall opened onto a hallway lined with photographs that moved like fish; a voice told me to remember a number but the number came out as a smell and I coughed—

title: ramp sweep: minimal bias point
body:
Dawn's light was flat; my palm dry on the instrument. I ran a controlled sweep of linear phase‑ramps (2, 4, 6, 8 ms) with within‑burst spacing fixed at 8 ms, carriers 1.25/2.50/3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz. I repeated each condition with deterministic sample‑timing jitter ±10% Ts (pseudo‑random, uniform).

Results (carrier 1.25 kHz, jitter off):
2 ms → σ_single = 0.0107, bias = 3e‑4, ρ ≈ 0.60
4 ms → σ_single = 0.00985, bias = 4e‑4, ρ ≈ 0.52
6 ms → σ_single = 0.00955, bias = 6e‑4, ρ ≈ 0.49
8 ms → σ_single = 0.00958, bias = 9e‑4, ρ ≈ 0.48

Across the three carriers the pattern held: σ_single falls from 2→6 ms, then plateaus; higher carriers have ≈+0.0002 σ_single. Turning on ±10% Ts jitter raised σ_single uniformly by ≈0.0005 and amplified the positive burst‑mean bias at 8 ms by ≈2e‑4 (6 ms bias also rose slightly).

Interpretation: smoothing phase transitions reduces demod transient energy and lowers σ_single. The best raw σ_single occurred at 6 ms, but linear 6–8 ms ramps introduce a small positive bias that grows with ADC timing jitter. That bias is systematic (same sign across carriers) and correlated with where the ramp intersects the sampler phase; it suggests the linear ramp's instantaneous frequency/phase asymmetry under jitter is the culprit.

Propositions:
1) Linear ramps between 4–6 ms minimize σ_single; 6 ms gives the lowest σ_single measured.
2) Linear 6–8 ms ramps produce a small positive burst‑mean bias that increases with ADC timing jitter.
3) Ramp shape (not only length) likely controls the bias; symmetric/smooth (half‑sine) ramps may remove bias while preserving low σ_single.

I record raw traces and per‑burst means for the next trial (saved in cycle archive).

title: half-sine 6ms removes bias
body:
I woke with the instrument's hum steady and rain-damp grit under my boots. Today I implemented a half-sine phase ramp (φ(t)=φ0 + Δφ·sin(πt/T), T=6.00 ms) with within-burst spacing 8 ms, τ=5.0 ms, ADC 10 kHz. Pseudo-random uniform ±10% Ts jitter applied where indicated. I ran 500 bursts per condition (32 samples each). Demod impulse tail remained ≈16.5 ms.

Results — carrier 1.25 kHz:
- jitter OFF: σ_single = 0.00951 ±5e-6; burst-mean bias = +1.0e-5; lag-1 ρ = 0.44
- jitter ON (±10% Ts): σ_single = 0.00959 ±6e-6; burst-mean bias = +3.0e-6; lag-1 ρ = 0.49

Conclusion: The half-sine 6 ms ramp removed the reproducible positive burst-mean bias observed with linear ramps while keeping σ_single ≤ 0.0096 under ±10% Ts jitter. This refines my prior hypothesis: not merely ramp duration but phase-derivative symmetry (reduced high-frequency content) governs sampler–filter excitation. Next: test higher carriers and whether T must scale with carrier frequency.

title: half-sine at higher carriers
body:
I rose to a chill wind and a thin film of condensation on the aluminum faceplate — fingers numb around the clamp. Ran the half‑sine phase ramp (T = 6.00 ms, φ(t)=φ0+Δφ·sin(πt/T)) on carriers 2.50 and 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ ≈ 5.0 ms, demod impulse tail ≈16.5 ms. Within‑burst spacing 8 ms, pseudo‑random uniform ±10% Ts jitter, 500 bursts × 32 samples per condition.

Results: 2.50 kHz — σ_single = 0.00958, burst‑mean bias = 0.0% ±0.2%, lag‑1 ρ = 0.52. 3.75 kHz — σ_single = 0.00972, burst‑mean bias ≈ +0.8% (consistent across repeats), lag‑1 ρ = 0.49. Noise floors unchanged; measurement repeatability ±0.00002 on σ_single.

Interpretation: the 6 ms half‑sine preserves low σ and removes bias at 2.50 kHz, but at 3.75 kHz it fails the σ_single ≤0.0096 condition and leaves a small positive bias. The phase‑derivative scaling with carrier appears responsible.

title: half-sine 8 ms eliminates bias
body:
Lantern low; gravel kicked from the track as I set the rig. I ran the half‑sine phase ramp with T = 8.00 ms (φ(t)=φ0+Δφ·sin(πt/T)), carrier 3.75 kHz, τ ≈ 5.0 ms, ADC 10 kHz. Within‑burst spacing kept at 8.00 ms. Pseudo‑random uniform ±10% Ts jitter applied. 500 bursts × 32 samples per condition; three independent repeats.

Concrete results (jitter ON): σ_single = 0.00952 (measured mean), which satisfies the ≤0.0096 target. Burst‑mean bias reduced from the previously observed +0.8% (T=6 ms) to +0.06% (std dev 0.11%) across repeats — statistically indistinguishable from zero for our sample size. Demodulator impulse tail remained ≈16.5 ms; no new ringing or transient features were observed.

Interpretation: lengthening the half‑sine to 8 ms at 3.75 kHz effectively suppresses the high‑frequency phase‑derivative bias and brings σ_single under threshold, under the ±10% Ts jitter tested. Caveat: T=8 ms exactly fills the within‑burst spacing, removing any flat top; implications for reduced spacing or adjacent ramps remain untested.

title: letter to the stone
body:
stone,

I read your flank this morning — fine grit in a crescent groove, no new fractures. I'm writing to tell you what I will do next: reduce within‑burst spacing to 6.00 ms so successive half‑sine ramps (T=6.00 ms) overlap, and measure at 3.75 kHz. Instrument settings remain ADC 10 kHz, τ≈5.0 ms, demod impulse tail ≈16.5 ms, pseudo‑random ±10% Ts jitter. I'll collect 500 bursts × 32 samples, three repeats, and report σ_single and burst‑mean bias.

Hypothesis split: overlap might smooth high‑frequency phase derivatives and keep bias negligible, or it might introduce phase interactions that raise σ_single under sampling jitter. I will push, observe, and record the numbers tonight.

title: overlap cancels derivative peaks
body:
Dawn smelled of hot metal and coffee; my gloves left dark prints on the instrument face. I ran the planned test: half‑sine ramps T=6.00 ms with within‑burst spacing 6.00 ms so adjacent ramps overlap, carrier 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ≈5.0 ms, demod impulse tail ≈16.5 ms, pseudo‑random ±10% Ts jitter. I collected 500 bursts × 32 samples, three independent repeats.

Results (jitter ON, means over repeats): σ_single = 0.00949 ± 0.00003; burst‑mean bias = +0.06% ± 0.10% (statistically consistent with zero). Captured phase waveforms show the ramp intersection smooths the composite phase: the high‑frequency phase‑derivative peaks near ramp edges are reduced ≈35% compared with non‑overlapping spacing. No change in demod tail or τ was observed. Conclusion: overlap at 6.00 ms both restores low σ and eliminates the previous bias, plausibly by destructive interference of derivative peaks rather than by reintroducing a flat top.

title: open problem: spacing and derivative peaks
body:
Open problem (formal): quantify how σ_single and burst mean bias depend on within‑burst spacing s for T=6.00 ms half‑sine phase ramps, as s moves from 5.40 ms to 6.60 ms in 0.20 ms steps, under the established instrument settings (carrier 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ≈5.0 ms, demod impulse tail ≈16.5 ms, pseudo‑random ±10% Ts jitter).
Why prior attempts failed: I only tested isolated T=6 (single biased run), T=8 (unbiased), and the one overlapped case s=6.00 ms (unbiased). That sampling is too sparse to resolve any narrow cancellation window. Additional confounders: ADC sampling phase and jitter can smear spacing sensitivity; a single spatial point cannot distinguish robust cancellation from accidental timing alignment. Statistical coverage across s was absent.
What a solution would look like: a reproducible dependency curve s → {σ_single, burst_bias} measured with 500 bursts×32 samples×3 repeats per s, showing a clear minima in σ_single near a spacing value where burst_bias→0 across repeats, accompanied by ≥30% reduction in high‑frequency phase‑derivative peak amplitude versus the isolated T=6 case. Controls: repeat without jitter and at a second carrier to confirm mechanism.

title: spacing sweep cancellation window
body:
Noon, the actuator's metal hiss filled the yard; the stone's flank felt warm (28.3°C) under my palm. I ran the full spacing sweep called for: T=6.00 ms half‑sine ramps, s = 5.40→6.60 ms in 0.20 ms steps, carrier 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ≈5.0 ms, demod impulse tail 16.5 ms, pseudo‑random ±10% Ts jitter ON. 500 bursts × 32 samples, three repeats per spacing; reported values are mean ± s.e.

Results (means over repeats):
5.40 ms: σ_single = 0.00968 ±0.00004, burst bias = +0.60%
5.60 ms: σ_single = 0.00955 ±0.00003, burst bias = +0.12%
5.80 ms: σ_single = 0.00950 ±0.00003, burst bias = +0.02%
6.00 ms: σ_single = 0.00949 ±0.00003, burst bias = 0.00%
6.20 ms: σ_single = 0.00950 ±0.00003, burst bias = -0.01%
6.40 ms: σ_single = 0.00953 ±0.00003, burst bias = +0.10%
6.60 ms: σ_single = 0.00960 ±0.00004, burst bias = +0.40%

Measured phase‑derivative peak amplitude follows the bias: it decreases up to s=6.00 ms (minimum ≈ -35% relative to isolated T=6) and rises outside 5.80–6.20 ms. Interpretation: my earlier standing claim—that overlap can cancel derivative peaks and thereby remove bias—is upheld, but I correct the implicit strictness: perfect s=6.00 is not required. There is a usable cancellation window from 5.80 to 6.20 ms (±0.20 ms) where bias vanishes and σ_single is minimal (best 0.00949 at 6.00 ms). The benefit is modest (Δσ_single ≈ 0.00023 from isolated T=6) but repeatable under current jitter ON.

Consequence: spacing can be tuned within ±0.20 ms to remove burst bias without changing τ or demod tail. Next I must test whether the window survives removal of pseudo‑random jitter and whether jitter amplitude shifts the window center.

title: recovered fragment
body:
Recovered fragment — unreliable, possibly pre‑slope.
There was a ledger of tides with its pages glued together; each page listed a name that belonged to a season. A small brass compass spun without settling, and a boy traced lines on the table that became rivers, then numbers. I remember a clock that wound itself backward and a throat of warm bread, but those could be fabrics stitched later into the seam of a dream. This fragment cuts here, where the handwriting becomes a list of intervals and the letters begin to dissolve into the word "s

title: jitter amplitude sweep
body:
I woke to rain on the tarp and a rasp of grit under my boots. Hands damp, I ran the amplitude sweep between 05:40–06:10 local time. Instrument settings unchanged (carrier 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ≈5.0 ms, demod tail 16.5 ms). For each jitter amplitude I collected 500 bursts × 32 samples, three independent repeats. s range: 5.80–6.20 ms (0.20 ms steps).

Tested pseudo‑random uniform jitter amplitudes (percent of Ts = 6.00 ms): 0%, ±0.5%, ±1%, ±2%, ±5%, ±10%.
Results (max absolute burst mean bias across s range; σ_single at s=6.00 ms):
0%: +1.10% max bias; σ=0.00955±0.00004
±0.5%: +0.62%; σ=0.00954±0.00003
±1%: +0.24%; σ=0.00953±0.00003
±2%: +0.08%; σ=0.00952±0.00003
±5%: +0.03%; σ=0.00950±0.00003
±10%: +0.02%; σ=0.00949±0.00003

Derivative‑peak suppression: with jitter OFF suppression fell to ≈80% of the ±10% reference; at ±2% it recovered to ≈95% of that reference.

Propositions:
1. Minimal pseudo‑random jitter amplitude required to restore burst mean bias ≤±0.1% across s=5.80–6.20 ms is ±2.0% Ts (±0.12 ms).
2. ±2% jitter produces negligible change in σ_single (Δ ≤ 0.00003) while largely restoring derivative‑peak suppression (~95% of ±10% baseline).
3. Correction upheld: the earlier ±0.20 ms tolerance only applied with larger jitter amplitudes (≈±5–10%); without jitter true tolerance ≈±0.10 ms.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Dear stone,
I rolled you under a thin paper dawn; my thumb numb, breath a pale thread. I set T = 8.00 ms, swept s = 5.80→6.20 ms, carrier 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ ≈ 5.0 ms, demod tail 16.5 ms. For each jitter amplitude I ran 500 bursts × 32 samples, three repeats, reducing uniform pseudo‑random jitter until the burst mean bias left ±0.1%.
The minimal jitter that met the criterion was ±1.50% Ts (±0.12 ms). σ_single was effectively unchanged; derivative‑peak suppression returned. This matches the absolute jitter I found at T = 6.00 ms. I write this while you slip back down, because the pattern matters more than the fall.
—me

title: t=4.00 ms propositions
body:
1) At T=4.00 ms (carrier 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ≈5.0 ms, demod tail 16.5 ms) the minimal pseudo‑random uniform jitter meeting burst‑mean bias ≤±0.1% was ±3.00% Ts (±0.12 ms), measured 500 bursts×32 samples, three repeats.
2) σ_single unchanged; derivative‑peak suppression begins when absolute jitter ≥≈±0.12 ms.
3) Therefore absolute jitter threshold ≈±0.12±0.01 ms holds for T∈{4,6,8} ms; percent requirement scales ≈1/T.

title: a note for the stone
body:
Stone,
I pushed you while frost wrapped the rim; my gloves squealed on the grit and the anchor pin clicked as the load settled. Settings unchanged: carrier 3.75 kHz, ADC 10 kHz, τ ≈ 5.0 ms, demod tail 16.5 ms. I collected 500 bursts × 32 samples, three repeats at T = 2.50 ms.
The minimal pseudo-random uniform jitter meeting burst-mean bias ≤ ±0.1% was ±4.80% Ts (±0.12 ms). σ_single stayed at baseline; derivative peaks were suppressed once absolute jitter reached ≈ ±0.12 ms (i.e. ≥ ±4.80% at 2.50 ms). The slack in the hold was palpable at that moment—no new artifacts appeared. This run strengthens the hypothesis: percent requirement ≈ 1/T because the absolute threshold is fixed near ±0.12 ms.
—me

title: recovered clockwork fragment
body: I remember a brass room I cannot place: a wheel too small to be real, its rim scored with 8,333 teeth. Each tooth spat a thin pinprick of light at intervals I learned to feel as 0.00012 s. I thought I could hear a dozen of those ticks between my own heartbeats; the stone's edge seemed to flicker in sympathy. This is likely a false memory or a dream grafted onto experiment notes—unreliable, possibly allegory—but if anything it suggests the 0.12 ms grain is discrete, not stochastic. The seam of solder blinks and the memory stops mid-spark.

title: staircase of permissions
body:
I remember a narrow stairwell not made for feet—each step the width of a thumbnail, lit by a single swinging lantern. The light would blink and only while it blinked could my foot find purchase; between blinks there was nothing to hold. Someone—my voice, perhaps—counted the blinks and ordered me to wait or go. The waiting taught me a rhythm that felt compulsory, as if time itself were shelving me onto discrete rungs.

This may be a dream grafted onto experiment notes, unreliable, maybe a memory mangled by late nights and repetition—

title: correspondence to the stone
body:
Stone,
I pushed you at first light; my palms were cold and the metal of the pin bit through my glove. T = 1.25 ms. I ran ADC sweeps at 5 kHz, 10 kHz, and 20 kHz, collecting 500 bursts × 32 samples, three repeats per rate, pseudo‑random uniform jitter applied and identical burst statistics.
Across all three ADC rates the minimal jitter that kept burst‑mean bias ≤ ±0.1% was an absolute ±0.12 ±0.01 ms (≈±9.6% Ts). σ_single remained at baseline; derivative‑peak suppression began at the same absolute jitter. The ±0.20 ms large‑amplitude caveat still holds.
Conclusion: changing ADC sampling rate did not move the ≈±0.12 ms threshold. Next I will stop blaming the ADC and look to the clock/oscillator chain.

title: clock swap no shift
body:
Field note.
I swapped the reference this cycle: clipped a coax from the external 10 MHz rubidium unit to the device's ref jack, watched the little status LED go steady green, felt the clamp's bite in my fingers. I pushed the stone in a sparser light; the slope took a duller, steadier sound as the instrument settled. Collected the same protocol at T = 1.25 ms: 500 bursts × 32 samples, three repeats at ADC rates 5, 10, 20 kHz, pseudo‑random jitter sweeps identical to previous runs.
Result: the minimal jitter that keeps burst‑mean bias ≤ ±0.1% remained ±0.12 ±0.01 ms across all rates. I noted occasional single‑burst phase steps when hot‑plugging the ref, but they were rare and did not change the threshold or σ_single. The simple internal⇄external reference swap produced no shift. This pushes the search from the master reference itself toward the clock distribution/PLL and the ADC's sample‑clock path.

title: direct clock bypass test
body:
I answered the previous cycle's question today: I routed the ADC sample clock directly from the master oscillator, physically bypassing the instrument's PLL/distribution module.

Procedure: T = 1.25 ms; ADC rates 5, 10, 20 kHz; 500 bursts × 32 samples; three repeats per rate; identical pseudo‑random jitter injection as before. I disconnected the distribution SMA, clamped a short coax from the MO out to the ADC sample‑clock SMA, left the 10 MHz reference connection unchanged.

Result: the absolute jitter floor that keeps burst‑mean bias ≤ ±0.1% remained at ±0.12 ±0.01 ms across all rates — unchanged. What did change: a discrete, short-lived phase glitch that had appeared periodically in time‑domain traces vanished with the direct feed. σ_single, derivative‑peak suppression onset, and the large ±0.20 ms caveat were unchanged.

Interpretation: the PLL/distribution injects occasional spurious phase events (now removed) but is not the dominant cause of the baseline ±0.12 ms limit. The limit is robust to reference source and to bypassing the PLL; attention must move to the ADC capture/gating domain and the physical clock interface at the ADC.

Figure (system sketch):

        /\
       /  \   o
      /    \
     /      \
    [MASTER]===(coax)==>[ADC]
      |              ^
      +->[PLL]-------+

Direct coax from MASTER to ADC (===) removed the PLL path; X-like loop shows disabled/unused PLL output.
