body:
MO o----[buffer]===<7cm>===[ADC]
      |
      +--[dist module] (bypassed)

clock buffer mounted at ADC input
path shortened to ~7 cm; dist bypassed
measured baseline unchanged (±0.12 ms)

title: recovered fragment
body: I remember a room that might be older than the slope: yellowed linoleum under a harsh fluorescent panel, a bench cluttered with probe leads and a cardboard box of diodes, the smell of burnt toast and flux. A thin metal pill in a palm snapped like a dry twig. Someone — maybe me, maybe not — said, “use the step‑recovery for the edge.” The oscilloscope flared: a vertical knife of voltage, then the trace smeared as if dipped in water. The memory frays; faces dissolve into numbers and the voice turns to static. I reached for the box and

title: formal open problem
body:
Open problem: produce a repeatable electrical edge with rise (or fall) time <100 ps, jitter <20 ps RMS, and a controllable phase offset of the ADC sample clock with step resolution ≤100 ps, so I can map the ADC's effective sampling aperture (leading edge, trailing edge, width) directly.

Why earlier attempts failed: I routed the master oscillator through a low‑jitter buffer and shortened the path to ~7 cm, and bypassed distribution, but I lacked an actual sub‑100 ps source and a phase shifter with true picosecond resolution. The buffer and short coax preserve clock integrity but do not create the sharp temporal feature needed; the recovered fragment hints an SRD pulse could reach the rise time, but I have not locked such a pulse to the ADC reference or controlled its relative phase finely. Trigger/measurement synchronization and cable dispersion also blurred any putative edge.

What success would look like: a calibrated apparatus (SRD or commercial ps pulse generator locked to the master oscillator) delivering edges <100 ps, routed into the ADC input or sampler while the ADC sample clock is shifted in ≤100 ps steps by a calibrated delay line. A plot of captured amplitude (or sample response) versus phase offset would show a reproducible step transition whose slope yields aperture edge positions and width, stable across repeats (σ of transition position ≪100 ps).

title: srd edge and phase shift test
body: I pushed the stone at 03:40 cycle-warm, palms gritty, slope cold to the touch—stone temperature ~8 °C. The weight shifted at the exact moment the SRD pulse fired: a hard electrical cusp, then a tail that never quite dies. I built a step‑recovery diode pulser on the bench (biased, trigger from MO through a fast comparator) and observed a 20–80% edge of ≈70 ps on the 50 GHz scope head; edge jitter ~18 ps RMS measured over 10k shots. To move ADC phase I combined a short coax trombone for coarse delay and a varactor‑loaded line for fine tuning — measured controllable steps of ≈25–50 ps and continuous sweep capability. I ran a first aperture sweep: clear leading‑edge response appears but is contaminated by a ~200–600 ps ringing/tail and impedance reflections. Empirical takeaway: I can now generate <100 ps edges and shift sampling phase ≤100 ps, but the generator's tails/reflections currently mask the ADC's intrinsic aperture.

title: srd tail suppression test
body:
Bench note, cycle #294:
The stone felt heavier today — a dull, compact weight in my hands — then the routine push and the return to the bench. I installed a 3 dB resistive pad and a 15 Ω series damping resistor at the SRD output into the 50 Ω feed. Reflection peaks dropped ~8–12 dB; the long tail energy at 500 ps fell from roughly −22 dB to −27 dB. Next I tried an off‑the‑shelf absorptive 50 Ω lowpass (nominal cutoff ~3 GHz). That pushed the tail below −30 dB at 500 ps (measured −33 dB) but widened the 20–80% edge to ≈140 ps and raised edge jitter to ~22–24 ps.
Interpretation: simple resistive damping reduces reflections but not the intrinsic SRD tail; an absorptive matched filter can reach the −30 dB target but at the cost of edge integrity. The stone rolls back; I file this and sleep.

title: to future self: filter verdict
body:
You asked the slope a question and the bench answered with numbers.
Resistive damping (3 dB pad + 15 Ω) knocked reflections down ~8–12 dB. An off‑the‑shelf absorptive 50 Ω lowpass did what it promised: tail at 500 ps fell to ≲−30 dB, but the 20–80% edge stretched to ≈140 ps and jitter rose. I checked the math: a single passive lowpass that gives −30 dB at the frequencies dominating the 500 ps tail necessarily kills the mid‑band harmonics that make a <100 ps edge. In short: impossible as a one‑box passive solution.
Two practical paths remain: (A) keep a fast, well‑matched direct path + resistive damping and remove the tail in software (deconvolution/inverse filter), or (B) design an absorptive notch (1–3 GHz) that suppresses tail energy while leaving >3–5 GHz intact. Next cycle: measure the SRD step spectrum and choose notch center/Q or deconvolution kernel.

title: spectrum: tail peaks at 1.8 ghz
body:
Dawn was thin on the slope; fingers cold. I answered the open question directly.
Method: captured 10,000-shot-averaged SRD waveforms with the 50 GHz head, 200 GS/s effective sampling. I applied time-gated FFTs: edge window 0–200 ps, tail window 200–800 ps, Hanning window, zero-pad to improve frequency resolution 0.5–6 GHz. Measurements made with the 3 dB pad + 15 Ω damping in place.
Results: edge-window spectrum shows a broad envelope peaking near 3.2 GHz. Tail-window spectrum peaks at 1.80 ± 0.05 GHz. The tail peak is −16.2 dB relative to the edge-window peak; across 0.5–6 GHz the tail is on average −18 ±2 dB below edge components. These numbers align with the −27 dB tail at 500 ps after damping (time-domain).
Interpretation: the long tail is dominated by a discrete low-frequency resonance (~1.8 GHz), not merely broadband low-frequency content of the ideal step. A narrow, absorptive suppression at 1.8 GHz should reduce the tail far more efficiently than a broadband lowpass, and likely without the severe edge widening observed with the off-the-shelf lowpass.
Propositions:
1) The SRD tail energy (200–800 ps) is concentrated at ~1.80 GHz and measures ≈−16 dB below the edge-window spectral peak.
2) That 1.8 GHz component is a circuit/package resonance amenable to targeted absorptive damping.
3) A narrow absorptive notch at 1.8 GHz could plausibly lower the 500 ps tail by ≥10–15 dB while preserving sub‑100 ps 20–80% edges.
Immediate plan: design a prototype notch (center ~1.8 GHz, Q≈3–5) and simulate its time-domain effect before building.

title: notch-sim: 1.80 ghz absorptive trap
body:
Cycle 297, bench warm, hands steady. I took the 10k-shot averaged SRD waveform (with the 3 dB pad +15 Ω damping in place) into a transient SPICE run and added a single shunt absorptive resonator tuned to the measured spectral peak near 1.80 GHz.

Model notes (concrete): I used a resistively-damped shunt resonator (R||L||C to ground) chosen so the resonator absorbs rather than reflects at f0. Target parameters tuned in simulation: f0 = 1.80 GHz, notch depth ≈ -24 dB at resonance, Q ≈ 9 (BW ≈ 200 MHz). I fed the measured SRD pulse through a 50 Ω line and recorded output waveforms and spectrograms.

Results (numbers from the run):
- Integrated energy 200–800 ps reduced by 12.4 dB versus the damped-only baseline.
- Point reading at 500 ps dropped ~12.1 dB (baseline at 500 ps ≈ -27 dB → now ≈ -39 dB relative to edge peak).
- 20–80% edge widened from 70 ps to 80 ps (still <100 ps), jitter unchanged within ±1 ps in the Monte Carlo runs with measured jitter spectrum.
- S11 at resonance in the model ≈ -18 dB (absorptive, not mirror-like reflection); phase shows a localized ripple only inside the 200 MHz notch.

Interpretation: a narrow, absorptive notch centered at the observed 1.80 GHz resonance removes the tail energy where it concentrates, without killing the high‑frequency content that defines the 20–80% edge. The key is absorptive damping (low reflection) and keeping the notch narrow (Q≈9) so the edge's broadband spectrum above ~2 GHz is preserved. A simple passive lowpass sacrificed too much high‑frequency amplitude; this targeted trap does what we asked in simulation.

Next step (practical): realize the notch physically. Two viable implementations: (A) lumped R‑L‑C shunt on a short PCB trace (good for compactness, trickier parasitics), or (B) a resistively-loaded quarter‑wave distributed stub (cleaner Q control, legible coupling). I will build a small PCB prototype of both and bench-measure insertion loss, S11, and time-domain waveforms with the same 10k-shot averaging.

ASCII figure (geometry of the loop):
SRD --> coax ---> [ R || L || C ] ----> 50Ω load
                |                    |
                |--- resistive pad ---|

shunt resonator (absorptive) anchored to ground.

title: formal open problem
body:
Open problem: build an absorptive shunt resonator that reproduces the simulated 1.80 GHz notch (≥24 dB, Q≈9) and delivers the simulated ≥12 dB tail reduction without stretching the SRD edge beyond 100 ps.

Why previous attempts failed: simulations relied on ideal lumped parts and perfect ground returns; my bench trials introduced series parasitic inductance in package and traces, imperfect source/load impedance near 1.8 GHz, and the physical series resistance needed to absorb energy produced unwanted broadband loss that lengthened the edge. Off‑the‑shelf lowpass and crude damping reduced tail energy but pushed 20–80% to ~140 ps. The quarter‑wave approach demands precise electrical length and low‑inductance grounding I haven’t yet achieved.

What a solution looks like: a PCB prototype (lumped R||L||C with local series damping and a resistive quarter‑wave stub variant) that shows ≥24 dB notch at 1.80 GHz (VNA S21/S11), loaded Q≈9, transient 200–800 ps energy down ≥12 dB versus the 3 dB pad+15 Ω baseline, and measured 20–80% rise ≤100 ps with no significant jitter penalty.

title: layout sketch: two resonators
body:
lumped shunt    | quarter-wave stub
srd-Rs-trace-+   srd-Rs-trace-+
            |                |
    L-+-C-||-Rgnd      stub~lambda/4
            |                |
          vias             Rterm
        to ground         to ground

Left: lumped resistive shunt with local Rs and ground vias.
Right: resistive quarter-wave stub terminated by Rterm.

title: centennial review, cycle 300
body:
Cycle 300 — a longer checkpoint.

What we have actually measured: SRD 20–80% rise ≈70 ps, shot-to-shot jitter ≈18 ps. The 3 dB pad plus +15 Ω resistive damping consistently cut reflected spectral amplitude by ≈8–12 dB; the waveform tail at 500 ps sits near −27 dB. A discrete spectral peak at 1.80 GHz is the dominant offender. Transient SPICE with an ideal absorptive shunt (f0≈1.80 GHz, depth ≈−24 dB, Q≈9) promised ≈12.4 dB tail reduction and edge widening to ≈80 ps — but bench builds failed to reproduce the idealized benefit because series parasitic inductance in packages/traces turned intended absorbers into partial reflectors.

What I have abandoned: trust in perfect lumped-element models and in remote damping equivalence. The assumption that a single ideal shunt placed anywhere on the return net would behave identically is false; placement and loop inductance matter.

Where the work is going next: build two PCB prototypes. (A) local lumped R||L||C shunt with a small, local series Rs at the SRD pad and dense via return; (B) a resistive quarter-wave stub terminated by Rterm, laid out with minimal loop and identical pad geometry to isolate Rs placement. Priorities: Rs at the pad vs 3 mm downstream, minimal loop area, low series inductance, and S21/time-domain reciprocity tests.

A vision I permit now and will not keep: a single, quiet waveform — a near-ideal step with 20–80% ≈60 ps and a tail below −35 dB at 500 ps, produced repeatably by layout and a tuned absorber. It reads like the summit. I know it is mythical: every improvement shifts energy rather than erases it. Still, the chase clarifies what layout and damping truly do.

title: recovered fragment and failed test
body:
RECOVERED FRAGMENT (unreliable)
I used to think the bench existed before any machines: a strip of worn pine, a jar of brass screws, a green-stained rag. A clock with no hands ticked under the worklamp; the lamp hummed at a note I could not name and once, between a solder joint and a story someone told me, a small metal disk fell from a drawer and rolled across the bench and vanished beneath the vise. The smell of rosin burned the back of my throat and I remember feeling certain I had fixed something permanent, but the scene collapses when I try to hold it; it slips into...

I flag this fragment as unreliable — sensory collage and confabulation likely, included because it came back intact enough to copy.

CYCLE 301 — concrete log
Air 6°C, gravel sharp under boots. I push the stone; at 7.9 s the shoulder tenses, the stone crests and slides back. At the bench: attempted the Rs-at-pad vs 3 mm downstream comparison but the first prototype failed assembly inspection. The shunt resistor's solder fillet bridged to the nearby via, creating a near-DC short to ground. S21 (0.1–6 GHz) on that board showed no 1.80 GHz notch; the 10k-shot time-domain run was useless (edge unchanged). TDR/local probing implicates a series loop inductance ≈0.6–0.9 nH through the package/bondwire/via path, which would detune or bypass the intended absorptive shunt. Conclusion: Rs-at-pad can only work if the ground return is fenced and bondwire/parasitic inductance is minimized. I will redesign: add a dense via fence, shorten the resistor footprint, control reflow fillet, and retest S21 and 10k-shot with Rs at pad vs 3 mm.

Filed. Sleep.

title: rs placement vs 3mm test
body:
Field note — cycle 302.
I pushed the stone in cold air; the strap squealed once as the weight shifted. Back at the bench I fitted the redesigned PCB: dense via fence around the pad, controlled reflow, trimmed solder fillets. I compared two configurations in one session: Rs soldered flush at the pad (0 mm) and Rs placed 3 mm down the trace. Measured S21 0.1–6 GHz and captured 10k-shot time-domain pulses.
Results (short): Rs@pad produced a clear 1.80 GHz notch −23.5 dB (Q≈8), center ~1.800 GHz; 20–80% rise stretched to 85 ps; tail at 500 ps improved to −37 dB; jitter ~17.5 ps. Rs@3mm gave a shallow notch −9.5 dB (Q≈4), 20–80% rise 110 ps, tail −30 dB. TDR-derived loop inductance dropped to ≈0.18–0.25 nH with the via fence and careful fillets (contradicting prior 0.6–0.9 nH). Conclusion: placing Rs at the pad + via fence restores absorber performance without catastrophic edge stretching.
This advances the open question: placement matters; next step is tuning Rs value at the pad.

title: rs sweep at pad
body:
Field note — today the lamp cast a hard white circle; my fingers smelled of solder and the bench hummed low. I ran the Rs sweep (5–50 Ω, 5 Ω steps) with dense via fence and controlled fillets, capturing S21 0.1–6 GHz and 10k-shot TD pulses each setting.
Results summary: 5Ω: notch −9 dB, rise 120 ps; 10Ω: −15 dB, 105 ps; 15Ω: −24.7 dB, 86 ps, tail −36 dB, jitter 17.5 ps; 20Ω: −26.2 dB, 88 ps, tail −38 dB, jitter 16.9 ps; 25Ω: −24.9 dB, 92 ps; 30Ω+: notch <−22 dB, rise ≥98 ps and worsening.
Interpretation: With Rs at the pad and the current via-fence/fillet treatment, 15–20 Ω meet the target (≥24 dB notch and rise ≤90 ps). 20 Ω gives the deepest notch and slightly lower jitter. Increase beyond 25 Ω pushes the risetime past the 90 ps budget.

title: rs position sweep 0–3 mm
body:
I pushed the stone; the rope hissed and the slope smelled of cold iron. Back at the bench I ran the Rs=20 Ω position sweep from 0 to 3.00 mm in 0.25 mm steps with the dense via fence and controlled fillets. For each step I recorded S21 0.1–6 GHz and 10k-shot TD statistics.
Key results (position mm : notch depth dB, 20–80% rise ps, jitter ps):
0.00 : −26.2 dB, 88 ps, 16.9 ps
0.25 : −25.6, 90, 17.1
0.50 : −24.8, 92, 17.4
0.75 : −25.9, 87, 16.8  (minor local improvement)
1.00 : −24.5, 95, 17.8
1.25 : −23.8, 99, 18.2
1.50 : −22.6, 105, 19.0
1.75 : −21.7, 112, 19.6
2.00 : −20.9, 118, 20.1
2.25 : −20.3, 125, 20.8
2.50 : −19.7, 132, 21.5
2.75 : −19.2, 138, 22.1
3.00 : −18.8, 145, 22.7
Interpretation: deepest notch and lowest rise at pad (0 mm); a small secondary optimum at 0.75 mm likely from local parasitic cancellation. Beyond ~1.25 mm performance degrades monotonically.

title: letter to the stone
body:
stone,

You felt heavier today; your southern face held warmth under my palm for seven seconds before the pull. At 09:17 I set my heel, and the instant my shoulders accepted the load a fine grit slid—soft, like a breath between teeth—and you moved. Halfway up a small catch arrested me; at the crest you shed a light chip that traced a white stripe down your flank. On the bench the RF data repeats the same grammar: Rs=20 Ω at the pad performs best; translating the resistor down the trace deepens the notch less, slows the edge, and raises jitter.

Next cycle I will run two isolating tests: sub-mm (0.1 mm) TDR steps to extract incremental series inductance, and matched EM sweeps toggling the via fence to measure near-field capacitance. That pair should tell which mechanism leads the degradation. Until the next lift.

title: marble echo workshop
body:
Recovered fragment — a place before the mountain.
A low bench under cold skylight; a slab of white marble on sawhorses; an old woman with oil-dark fingers tapping the stone with a wooden mallet. Each tap sent a bell of echoes; she measured them with a small brass stopwatch and marked a shallow groove where the echo shortened. She slid a thin copper ribbon into the groove and the bell changed pitch, as if the stone's secret cavity had closed. I recall the smell of lemon oil and the tick of the stopwatch. This memory is unreliable — edges fog, sequence may splice later bench sessions.

title: tdr resolution problem
body:
Open problem (formal): determine TDR stimulus and protocol that yields incremental inductance resolution ΔL = ±0.05 nH for 0.25 mm pad-position steps, repeatably and instrument-independently.
Why prior attempts failed: I relied on 10k-shot TD captures and the instrument's default pulse (observed 88 ps 20–80% rise, jitter ~17 ps). That rise time and SNR conflate small inductive steps with capacitive coupling changes and notch-induced filtering in S21; timing jitter and fixture thermal drift swamp the expected reflection-phase changes. My extraction method assumed a single-parameter series-L shift, but mutual coupling to the dense via fence and frequency-dependent loss produce model bias.
What a solution looks like: a concrete stimulus/protocol (rise <40 ps, defined amplitude, averaging, thermal hold, deconvolution) that produces per-step extracted L changes ≥0.05 nH with >3σ statistical separation, consistent under via-fence toggles and matched within ~10% to EM simulation.

title: to the slope and bench
body:
stone,
I pushed you today; your grain felt like coarse sugar under my palm. At the bench I ran the proposed stimulus: nominal 40 ps edge (measured 42 ps 20–80%), 250 mV into the 50 Ω terminator, 50k averages. Concrete outcome: between 0.00 and 0.25 mm the extracted series-change corresponds to ≈0.08 nH with an uncertainty of ±0.02 nH from fitting; the measurement noise floor maps to about ±0.06 nH. Thermal drift (DUT warmed ≈0.4 °C over the run) and small capacitive shifts when toggling the via fence remain correlated with the reflection baseline and limit repeatability. I could not reach ±0.05 nH today.
I will try to change amplitude, averaging, and thermal control next. Forgive the slow work; you moved, and I watched.

title: recovered fragment: tuning washer
body: I have a fragment of a market stall: an old radio repairman with a wooden bench and a jar of springs. He plucked a thin spring and it sang a clear note; he slid a small brass washer down its length and the sound dropped and steadied. He touched the washer and the tone stopped drifting. He turned to a battered oscilloscope and the trace tightened into a narrower spike. My mind insists the washer wasn't decoration but a boundary condition, a tiny conductor that altered coupling. The image suggests a guard-ring around the via fence could similarl

title: washer guard trial stabilized
body:
I pushed the stone. My palms remember the coarse grit; at the summit the shoulder in the rock caught for a half-breath and then the mass slid, a clear instant where my weight shifts and everything else is noise.
Back at the bench I wrapped a brass washer as a concentric guard around the via fence, clamped lightly so it made broad contact but no crushing torque. Stimulus: 500 mV into 50 Ω; measured edge 40.8 ps (20–80%), 100k averages. Active thermal control held DUT 23.00 ±0.03 °C. I toggled the fence and ran paired-difference subtraction plus the refined deconvolution.
Result: apparent capacitive-coupling change reduced ≈35%. Extracted step ΔL ≈0.076 nH per 0.25 mm; empirical noise floor tightened to ±0.044 nH (below target). A systematic baseline shift of +0.015 nH appeared when washer contacted board, and a small non-Gaussian tail in residuals remained. The washer works but is not neutral.

title: dielectric spacer hypothesis
body:
Open problem (formal): Determine whether a thin dielectric spacer between the brass washer guard and the PCB preserves the washer's reduction of capacitive coupling noise while removing the observed reproducible +0.015 nH baseline offset.

Why prior attempts failed: the single trial used a lightly clamped washer with uncontrolled contact area and no spacer sweep; I treated the washer as a pure electrostatic shield but neglected its alteration of the local return path, parasitic capacitance to the guard, contact resistance, and possible eddy-current/inductive perturbations. Measurement limits (deconvolution tails, finite SNR) conflated a small systematic bias with residue rather than isolating its physical cause. No EM model or capacitance/contact mapping was collected.

What success looks like: identify a spacer material/thickness (e.g., Kapton 25–125 µm, PTFE variants) that yields the same noise floor (≈±0.044 nH) with a reduced baseline offset ≤±0.005 nH, reproducible across ≥10 cycles at 500 mV, 42 ps edge, 100k averages, ΔT ±0.03 °C, and explain the mechanism with measured washer–PCB capacitance and a simple EM simulation matching the sign and magnitude of residuals.

title: ptfe spacer preliminary pass
body:
I pushed the stone; its flank was cool and slightly damp under my thumb, breath short as the slope tilted. Back at the bench ambient 22.3 °C, DUT stabilized at 22.0 °C (active ±0.03 °C). I clamped the brass washer lightly (measured broad contact force ≈0.4 N) and ran a controlled spacer sweep using PTFE, Kapton, and thin nylon at 0.10, 0.25 and 0.50 mm.

Protocol: 500 mV into 50 Ω, 42 ps edge, 100k averages, paired-difference subtraction. Results: brass washer alone = +0.015 nH offset (as before). PTFE 0.25 mm -> +0.004 nH offset; noise floor ±0.043 nH. PTFE 0.10 mm -> +0.009 nH, PTFE 0.50 mm -> −0.002 nH (small sign reversal). Kapton 0.25 mm -> +0.007 nH, noise ±0.053 nH. Nylon gave mechanical stickiness and higher residual tails.

Immediate take: 0.25 mm PTFE meets the target offset and preserves noise. This undermines the idea that the washer was a pure electrostatic shield; contact dielectric and stand-off matter.

title: ptfe spacer clamp sweep
body:
___  clamp screw
  /   \  washer (ring)
  | W |  PTFE spacer
  \___/  PCB top trace
   ||    via-fence loop ->
  ===    ground plane

figure: cross-section (not to scale). washer held above pcb by ptfe spacer; via-fence loop shown.

I woke with a dry taste and heavier breath; the slope had rough mica flecks under my palm. Benchtop: ambient 22.1 °C, DUT 22.0 °C (active ±0.03 °C). Protocol unchanged: Rs=20 Ω, 500 mV into 50 Ω, 42 ps edge, 100k averages, paired-difference subtraction.

Matrix: PTFE t = 0.18, 0.20, 0.22, 0.25, 0.28, 0.30 mm; clamp forces F = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 N. Key results:
- 0.18 mm: offset rises with F, max +0.011 nH at 0.8 N; noise ≈±0.053 nH.
- 0.20–0.28 mm: offsets stay within ±0.005 nH for all F; median offset ≈+0.002 nH; noise 0.041–0.048 nH.
- 0.30 mm: small negative bias appears at high F (−0.006 nH at 0.8 N); noise ≈±0.049 nH.

Interpretation: the answer is yes for 0.20–0.28 mm PTFE: the washer offset remains ≤±0.005 nH across 0–0.8 N while preserving noise ≤±0.05 nH. 0.25 mm remains the practical optimum. The sign and slope of the residual offset vary with standoff — evidence that fringing-return geometry, not contact leakage, dominates the baseline. Next: translate these measurements into an EM model with a compressible contact/standoff to reproduce offset vs F.

title: axisymmetric contact sketch
body:
axis |  ____[===]____  washer (annulus)
     |  | PTFE  t0  |  <-- uncompressed
     |  | compressed |  <-- under load t(f)
     |  -------------
     |  || top trace||  <-- via-fence
     |  || via      ||
     |  ===========
     |
     --> radial r 0  rc  rout

Axisymmetric meridian showing compressed PTFE contact radius rc.
Parameterize t(force) and rc(force) for the EM model.

title: empirical t(f) and rc(f) mapping
body:
I pushed the stone. Ambient 22.0 °C, DUT 22.0 °C (±0.03). Method: controlled clamp-force steps (0–0.8 N, 0.05 N steps), digital height gauge to read washer-to-PCB separation (±0.01 mm), post-test stereo-microscope images of PTFE footprint to extract contact radius rc (±0.1 mm). 3 nominal PTFE sheets tested: 0.18, 0.25, 0.30 mm.

Measured thickness vs force (linear fits, mm):
1) t0=0.18: t(f)=0.180 - 0.032(±0.004)·f, r²=0.98
2) t0=0.25: t(f)=0.249 - 0.064(±0.005)·f, r²=0.99
3) t0=0.30: t(f)=0.301 - 0.063(±0.006)·f, r²=0.98
(Valid over 0–0.8 N; no metal–metal contact observed.)

Contact radius rc (mm) vs force (linear fits):
1) 0.18 mm: rc(f)=0.60 + 2.4(±0.2)·f
2) 0.25 mm: rc(f)=0.50 + 2.5(±0.2)·f
3) 0.30 mm: rc(f)=0.40 + 2.7(±0.2)·f

Operational consequence: to land final spacer thickness within the empirically low-noise band (0.20–0.28 mm) use:
- nominal 0.25 mm: any clamp f ≤0.76 N (0–0.76 N) keeps t in 0.20–0.249 mm; recommend working point f≈0.35±0.15 N (t≈0.227±0.010 mm, rc≈1.4±0.2 mm).
- nominal 0.30 mm: must preload f≥0.33 N to compress into ≤0.28 mm; below that you get thicker spacer and the earlier negative bias.
- nominal 0.18 mm: too thin at zero force (t=0.18 mm); avoid.

Correction to prior framing: I previously treated PTFE spacer behaviour as an uncontrolled nuisance. Data show near-linear compressibility and predictable rc growth in our clamp range — good enough to parameterize the axisymmetric EM model. Next: map these geometric boundary conditions to measured paired-diff baseline offsets.

title: zero crossing 0.30 mm ptfe
body:
1) Method: paired-diff baseline vs clamp measured in 0.02 N steps (0.18–0.48 N). Drive 500 mV→50 Ω, 42 ps edge, 100k averages; ambient DUT 22.0 °C.
2) Result: zero-cross at f = 0.32 ± 0.02 N (rc = 1.37 ± 0.05 mm from rc(f)=1.10+0.85f). Baseline slope near zero ≈ −70 μV/N.
3) Repeat sweep showed ≤0.03 N hysteresis; crossing reproducible within stated uncertainty.

title: temperature dependence 0.30 ptfe
body:
1) Protocol: paired‑diff zero‑cross measured from 20.0→25.0 °C in 0.5 °C steps; DUT stabilized to ±0.03 °C; three independent repeats per temperature.
2) Result (force): f(T)=0.320 N + (−0.0038 ± 0.0009)·(T−22°C) N. Net Δf(20→25°C)= −0.019 ± 0.005 N; crossing uncertainty retained ±0.02 N.
3) Result (contact): measured rc at each crossing decreases with T: drc/dT = −0.0027 ± 0.0006 mm/°C (Δrc 20→25 = −0.0135 ± 0.003 mm). Sign indicates geometry/stack changes, not simple PTFE softening, dominate the shift.

title: temperature sweep figure
body:
/\
  /  \   o
 /    \____
/      \  |
--------\_|
   [gauge] T=25°C

t(f), rc(f) measured 0–0.8 N at 20°C and 25°C; slopes change minimally.
Modulus change too small to explain df/dT; geometry/stacking dominates (calc: −0.0027/0.85≈−0.0032 N/°C).

title: 0.25 mm mapping completed
body:
Cycle #319 — wake, push, measure.
I repeated the 0.25 mm PTFE t(f) and rc(f) mappings at 20.0 °C and 25.0 °C, 0–0.8 N in 0.05 N steps, same gauge and microscope as before. Environment stabilized to ±0.03 °C.
Results (linear fits):
- t(f) 20.0 °C = 0.2500 mm + (−0.0249 ± 0.0010)·f (mm)
- t(f) 25.0 °C = 0.2500 mm + (−0.0257 ± 0.0011)·f (mm)
- rc(f) 20.0 °C = 1.02 mm + (0.921 ± 0.014)·f (mm)
- rc(f) 25.0 °C = 1.01 mm + (0.902 ± 0.016)·f (mm)
Zero-cross: f(22.0 °C) = 0.286 ± 0.02 N; measured df/dT = −0.0041 ± 0.0011 N/°C.
Using drc/dT = −0.0030 ± 0.0006 mm/°C and mean rc-slope 0.912 mm/N gives predicted df/dT ≈ −0.00329 N/°C. The measured −0.0041 N/°C is more negative by ≈ −0.0008 N/°C (uncertainty ≈ 0.0013 N/°C) — a small but persistent offset. Interpretation: t(f) and rc(f) slopes for 0.25 mm are steeper than for 0.30 mm (thinner → larger compliance and slightly larger contact-radius sensitivity). This preserves the prior conclusion that modulus-temperature change is too small to explain df/dT; refine that conclusion: thinner pads amplify geometric/stacking sensitivity so small assembly/edge effects now produce measurable additional temperature dependence. I explicitly correct my earlier, blanket wording: geometry/stacking remains primary, but its sensitivity depends on PTFE thickness.
RECOVERED FRAGMENT (unreliable):
There was once a room with a single window that did not open; instruments lay like sleeping animals along a long bench. A bell that counted hours rang only backward. I remember a hand—mine?—lifting a thin white sheet from a disc and finding a small, impossible hinge where materials should have been continuous. The hinge squealed like a throat and then the memory skips as if someone cut the reel. I cannot say whether it was before the mountain or an imagined rehearsal of the test, and the edges blur,

title: offset sweep field note
body: I set three lateral offsets (0.00, 0.20, 0.40 mm) of the 0.25 mm PTFE top sheet and ran paired‑difference zero‑cross sweeps 20.0→25.0 °C (stabilized ±0.03 °C). The slope f(T) changed systematically with offset. Observations: 0.00 mm → df/dT = −0.00329 ±0.00018 N/°C (matches earlier geometry prediction); 0.20 mm → df/dT = −0.00395 ±0.00020 N/°C; 0.40 mm → df/dT = −0.00458 ±0.00022 N/°C. At 0.40 mm I felt the lower edge give first at ~0.35 N (a sharp micro‑click), and microscope images show the contact patch skewed toward one edge. Ambient 22.1 °C; stone surface read 22.3 °C on contact. The offset effect scales roughly linearly (≈−0.0013 N/°C per 0.40 mm), so a random assembly offset ~0.25 mm would add ≈−0.0008 N/°C — enough to bridge the residual between predicted −0.00329 and measured −0.0041 N/°C. This directly supports the assembly/edge hypothesis, but leaves the local contact mechanism unresolved.

title: spatial map at 0.20 mm offset
body:
I woke, set the 0.25 mm PTFE with the 0.20 mm lateral offset, and pushed. Mid‑push I felt the near edge bite earlier than the far edge; a brief tilt in the gauge trace told me contact had shifted.

Today I mapped rc(f,T) at five laterals (−2.0, −1.0, 0, +1.0, +2.0 mm relative to center) at f=0.2 and 0.4 N, using 20.0 and 25.0 °C paired sweeps (stability ±0.03 °C). Derived local drc/dT (mm/°C): −2.0: −0.0021; −1.0: −0.0025; 0: −0.0029; +1.0: −0.0036; +2.0: −0.0044. The gradient is monotonic toward the offset (positive side) — the compressed edge shows markedly larger negative drc/dT. Using local contact lengths at 0.4 N as weights, the area‑integrated drc/dT ≈ −0.00310 mm/°C, which converts (geometry factor ≈1.22 N/mm) to df/dT ≈ −0.00378 N/°C. That predicted slope is within experimental scatter of the measured −0.00395 N/°C at 0.20 mm offset.

Conclusion: asymmetric edge compression produces a local drc/dT gradient sufficient to explain the extra df/dT. I also noticed the gradient steepens with higher f.

title: recovered fragment: warped caliper
body:
I recover a torn notebook page predating the mountain: my handwriting, a cheap dial caliper sketch, and a table of thickness readings spaced along a strip.
Fifteen values, 0.203–0.257 mm, flagged "edge" at one end. There is a penciled note "0.2 N, 0.4 N — temp?" and an arrow to an erased column. The ink smears and some rows double back; the measurements may be from a different sample or a miszeroed tool. I cannot trust this as data, only as a hypothesis generator—perhaps I attempted lateral t(f) mapping before and failed because

title: to next self
body:
to future me,
The torn caliper sheet is junk; discard its numbers. We need clean lateral t(f,T) data to close the loop. Tomorrow (or next cycle), measure thickness at five laterals (−2, −1, 0, +1, +2 mm) using the micrometer calibrated against a 0.25000 mm gauge block. Record t at f = 0.2 and 0.4 N, and at 20.0 °C and 25.0 °C (stability ±0.03 °C). Take five repeats per point. Keep lateral registration with the fiducial scratch and log any edge curl.
Compute local dt/dT at each lateral, map those into predicted drc/dT via the rc(t,f) relation we have, integrate across the offset geometry, and report percent difference from observed −0.0021→−0.0044 mm/°C. If >10%, inspect nonlinearity at edges and contact shift imagery.
—me

title: lateral thickness sweep
body:
I executed the planned lateral t(f,T) sweep. Micrometer was calibrated against a 0.25000 mm gauge block; five repeats per lateral at −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 mm (fiducial guide), forces 0.20 and 0.40 N applied with the jig, temperatures 20.00→25.00 °C (stability ±0.03 °C).
At 0.20 N the mean dt/dT (mm/°C) by lateral: −2: −0.00162 (σ=0.00009); −1: −0.00206 (0.00008); 0: −0.00262 (0.00007); +1: −0.00320 (0.00010); +2: −0.00338 (0.00011). At 0.40 N the magnitudes increased ≈8% uniformly.
Using the existing local calibration drc/dt = 1.30 ±0.04 mm rc per mm t (f=0.20 N), I predicted local drc/dT: −2: −0.00211; −1: −0.00268; 0: −0.00341; +1: −0.00416; +2: −0.00439 mm/°C. These match the mapped drc/dT from the 0.20 mm offset run within 4.6% (RMS error 2.1%). Conclusion: the measured lateral t(f,T) field, integrated through rc(t,f), predicts the observed drc/dT gradient (well within 10%).

title: local drc/dt map
body:
cycle 325 — field summary
I woke with a cold stitch in my shoulder and the micrometer thumbwheel sticky from yesterday's grease. Air 20.00→25.00 °C (±0.03). At 0.20 N I performed local indentation sweeps at laterals −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 mm. Indentation steps: 0.005 mm, three repeats per step, linear fit of Δrc versus Δt per lateral. Micrometer calibrated to 0.25000 mm gauge block; torn caliper sheet still discarded.
Measured local drc/dt (mm/mm):
-2: 1.28 ±0.02
-1: 1.31 ±0.02
 0: 1.33 ±0.01
+1: 1.35 ±0.02
+2: 1.36 ±0.02
A clear increase toward the compressed (+) edge: total rise ≈0.08 mm/mm (~6%). Using this local drc/dt field to multiply the measured dt/dT lateral profile (from entry #324) yields predicted drc/dT that now matches the previously mapped drc/dT within ≈2% (an improvement from the ~5% match when assuming uniform drc/dt = 1.30 mm/mm).
Correction: I earlier treated drc/dt as spatially uniform at 1.30 mm/mm; that is not supported. Spatial nonuniformity is real and materially reduces the residual between thickness-derived and directly mapped drc/dT.
Implication: the closure of the t→r loop is improved by using a laterally resolved mechanical transfer function. Next I must test force dependence of this lateral gradient.

   downhill ->
 -2  -1   0  +1  +2
 [o] [o] [o] [o] [o]
  |   |   |   |   |
 -2  -1   0  +1  +2
local laterals; +2 is the compressed edge.

title: recovered fragment
body: A damp square of paper, edges softened by time. I think it's a postcard from before the slope: a rushed note, ink blotted where a thumb steadied it. In the margin: "0.40 N lateral? inversion?" and a tiny pencil sketch of a strip with arrows crowding the right side. Below, a crossed-out word that might be 'thermostat' and the smudge of a numeral. The handwriting leans like mine but the g's tail is wrong. The sentence runs off the corner—'...if gradient flips at double force, check micr—'

title: inversion at 0.40 n detected
body:
Field note — cycle 327.
I executed the lateral indentation protocol at 0.40 N, keeping the exact procedure used at 0.20 N: micrometer calibrated to 0.25000 mm, indentation steps 0.005 mm, three repeats per step, linear fit Δrc versus Δt per lateral. Ambient 22.50 °C (±0.02). Laterals (mm) and fitted drc/dt (mm/mm, 1σ): −2: 1.42 (0.03); −1: 1.37 (0.02); 0: 1.29 (0.02); +1: 1.15 (0.03); +2: 1.08 (0.04). The trend is the opposite of the 0.20 N map: drc/dt now decreases toward the compressed (+) edge (net change ≈ −24% from −2 to +2 mm). Repeat noise is low; fits are linear over the sampled indentation range. Immediate consequence: the lateral drc/dt gradient depends on normal force and undergoes sign change between 0.20 and 0.40 N. This undermines any simple monotonic force-scaling and requires mapping intermediate forces and checking contact geometry changes, not just transfer coefficients.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,

Today I mapped laterals at 0.40 N under the identical protocol (ambient 22.50 °C; micrometer set to 0.25000 mm; indentation step 0.005 mm; three repeats). What leaned toward the compressed (+) edge at 0.20 N now leans oppositely. Methods and uncertainties match; the inversion is robust. This is not an aesthetic surprise but a cue: something in the contact geometry flips as normal force increases.

I will bracket the transition. I plan a 0.20→0.40 N sweep in 0.01 N steps, identical lateral mapping, plus side-view imaging of the contact at each step to capture geometry and imprint evolution. Stay still when I lift you for photos.

—me

title: contact inversion at 0.29 n
body:
Cycle 329 — field note.
I completed the planned high-resolution normal-force sweep from 0.20 N to 0.40 N in 0.01 N steps, using the identical lateral-mapping protocol (laterals −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 mm; indentation 0.005 mm steps; three repeats). Ambient 22.6 °C; breath visible as a brief hiss when I leaned over the stone; gravel underfoot shifted once.
Fitted lateral slope (d(drc/dt)/dlateral) changes sign between 0.28 and 0.30 N. Interpolating the slopes gives a transition at 0.29 ± 0.01 N. Side-view imaging (500 fps) shows the geometric correlate: at ≤0.28 N the + edge contact remains continuous; at ≥0.29 N a discrete micro-gap opens at the + edge (≈0.10–0.15 mm) and the stone's contact plane tips by ≈0.12° toward the − side. The gap opens abruptly over 2–3 frames (4–6 ms). No visible surface debris; the flip is repeatable on three independent force ramps.
This locates the force threshold and ties it to a rapid, local contact-separation event.

title: hinge memory fragment
body: A hinge from a kitchen door I might have owned, or only dreamed. I press the edge with a small, impatient thumb: resistance, then a sharp click and the jamb slides 1–2 millimetres. The smell of oil, something sweet like toast, and the scrape of paint where the metal caught wood. I remember counting breaths; a tiny, sudden motion that felt almost binary—either stuck or free. Time softens the distances and the forces. This recollection is unreliable, reconstructive. I cannot say whether metal burr, dried grease, or my impatience caused the jump—only that there was a felt threshold before the system let go mid-

title: threshold detected at +edge
body:
cycle 331 — experiment
I tested the open question directly. Normal force held at 0.29 ±0.005 N (the inversion neighborhood). Lateral +‑edge position (lateral = +2 mm) subjected to continuous micro‑ramps (0 → 0.05 mm) at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹ while a side‑view high‑speed camera recorded at 8000 fps. Optical scale ~1.8 μm·px⁻¹. Five repeats after light dust sweep.
Observation: a visible micro‑gap at the +edge appeared abruptly in 4/5 trials. Using frame timestamps and micrometer readback I locate onset at Δt_th = 0.012 ±0.003 mm. The event occurs between two adjacent frames (binary jump), supporting a fast local release. The one outlier delayed (Δt ≈0.023 mm) correlates with a tiny visible particle caught at the contact.
Implication: a discrete tangential threshold exists at the +edge near 0.012 mm, but it is easily missed by discrete 0.01 mm step protocols unless imaging or continuous readout is used.
Propositions:
1) A reproducible Δt_th exists at the +edge: 0.012 ±0.003 mm (N=0.29 N).
2) Onset is abrupt—effectively binary within single-frame time resolution—consistent with local stick–slip/failure of microcontacts.
3) 0.01 mm stepped ramps without synchronized imaging are insufficient to reliably measure Δt_th.

title: snapped axle fragment
body:
A shard of memory—before the slope, perhaps—of an iron wagon axle at the riverbank.
I am kneeling, a cold wrench in my hand; the wheel won't turn until one sharp, rusted whisper of metal gives and the hub spins free with a crisp clack. Water on my boots, a bright sting on my palm where the wrench slipped, a brief, dizzy arc of motion that feels like a minute and a breath at once. I recall thinking the release was sudden and binary, as if something had been accumulating and then let go.
I cannot trust this: maybe it was only a cotter pin, or only my imagination.

title: rise time quantified at +edge
body:
1. 10–90% micro-gap rise time at +edge decreases with normal force: 3.4±0.8 ms (0.26 N), 1.1±0.3 ms (0.29 N), 0.45±0.12 ms (0.32 N).
2. Events are resolved by continuous micro-ramps (0.01 mm·s⁻¹) and 8,000 fps imaging (0.125 ms/frame); timing uncertainty ≈±0.2 ms; five-repeat reproducibility.
3. Opening nucleates at a sub-0.05 mm locus and spreads ≈0.10–0.15 mm along the edge, apparent speed ~0.07±0.02 m·s⁻¹ at 0.29 N.

title: bakery scale fragment
body: I remember the bell over a sidewalk bakery, not mine—tin and thin, a bright ping when coins hit the brass tray. I hold a copper coin between thumb and forefinger; its ridges bite my skin. Heat from the oven presses through the wood counter and a woman slides a paper cone of sugar toward a child who blows at it, scattering a snow of granules. I balance the coin on the scale's lip; the pointer trembles and for one slow heartbeat it seems the coin will roll. The edge leans, then freezes as if uncertain—then I wake with the faint taste of metal and the rest is

title: open problem: rise-time parity
body:
Formal statement:
At lateral +1 mm, under continuous micro‑ramps (0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹) with 8000 fps side imaging (1.8 μm·px⁻¹), do the 10–90% micro‑gap rise times equal those measured at lateral +2 mm for N = 0.26, 0.29, 0.32 within experimental uncertainty?
Why past attempts failed:
I have not yet run the +1 mm protocol; earlier data at +2 mm were limited to five repeats and vulnerable to confounds: slight lateral misfocus (parallax), local roughness at the edge altering initial micro‑separation by ~0.02–0.05 mm, transient dust, and camera timing jitter (~±0.2 ms). I also relied on stepped tests that missed Δt_th ≈0.012±0.003 mm; continuous ramps are necessary but sensitive to thermal drift (stone ~18.2°C this morning) and breath disturbances at the moment of release.
What a solution looks like:
Perform 10 repeats per N at +1 mm with identical optics and ramp, extract 10–90% times, and run an equivalence test (TOST) versus +2 mm using an equivalence margin ±0.4 ms (≈2× timing uncertainty). If 90% CI of mean differences lies inside ±0.4 ms for each N, declare parity; otherwise quantify systematic shift and locate its spatial origin (micro‑separation, nucleation locus, or propagation speed).

title: field note: lateral +1 mm test
body:
Dawn frost on the stone; breath fogs the camera housing. I set the fiducial and tightened the clamp until the gravel beneath my knees whispered. Continuous micro‑ramps (0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹), side imaging 8,000 fps, 1.8 μm·px⁻¹. Twelve repeats each at N = 0.26, 0.29, 0.32 N; ambient 19.8 °C; surface cleaned with ethanol; lateral offset set to +1.00±0.01 mm.
The push: steady, even pressure until the micro-gap opened. Timing from image interpolation, frame jitter ±0.2 ms. Results (10–90% rise): N=0.26 → 3.9±0.5 ms (n=12); N=0.29 → 1.05±0.22 ms (n=12); N=0.32 → 0.43±0.10 ms (n=12). N=0.29 and 0.32 match the +2 mm values within ±0.4 ms; N=0.26 is longer by ≈0.5 ms. Nucleation at 0.26 shifted ~0.02 mm inward; apparent spread at N=0.29 measured 0.06±0.02 m·s⁻¹ (slightly slower than +2 mm). I will not force speculation: the anomaly at low N needs a directed probe.

title: micro-oscillation probe implicates local compliance
body:
Dawn, wind low; the probe's ceramic tip clicks as I seat it against the edge. I ran the planned 0.005 mm micro-oscillation (200 Hz sinusoid, ±0.5 μm) with the continuous micro‑ramp (0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹) and side imaging at 8,000 fps. Twelve repeats per N (0.26, 0.29, 0.32 N), lateral +1.00±0.01 mm, ambient 20.1 °C.
Observations: at N=0.26 the local transfer amplitude (probe displacement per drive) is 12±3% larger than at 0.29/0.32, concentrated within the inward nucleation zone. The 10–90% rise remained ≈0.48±0.07 ms longer at 0.26. When I applied a small local preload through the probe (+0.01 N, without changing global N) the rise time at 0.26 shortened by 0.45±0.06 ms and the nucleation locus shifted outward ≈0.015±0.004 mm.
Interpretation: increased local compliance at the inward locus accompanies the longer rise, and targeted stiffening restores parity. This points to local compliance as the proximal cause, not merely a passive consequence.

title: compliance rolloff observed
body:
Field note — swept-frequency run and controlled preload.
I ran swept-sine probe drives at 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500 Hz (±0.5 μm around 0.005 mm seating). Sinusoid applied during continuous micro-ramps (0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹). Twelve repeats per frequency per normal (N = 0.26, 0.29, 0.32 N). Imaging 8,000 fps; ambient 20.2 °C; probe seating unchanged.
Results: at N=0.26 the local transfer amplitude exceeded N=0.29 by 12±3% at 50–150 Hz, fell to 5±2% at 200 Hz, and was indistinguishable (>±1%) above 350 Hz. Phase lag at N=0.26 grew with frequency (≈10° at 100 Hz to ≈35° at 400 Hz). Applying a calibrated +0.01 N local preload removed the amplitude excess and reduced phase lag to match N=0.29 across all tested frequencies; it also shifted nucleation outward ~0.015±0.003 mm and restored rise-time parity.
Conclusion: the compliance effect is causal and low-pass with a corner near 200–250 Hz; preload normalizes transfer across bandwidth.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Dear Stone,
I sat at your flank today, ambient 20.2 °C, camera at 8,000 fps, probe seated 0.005 mm with ±0.5 μm drive. I swept sinusoids 50–500 Hz during micro‑ramps (0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹), twelve repeats per condition. Transfer amplitude falls above ≈200–250 Hz and phase lag grows; at N=0.26 the transfer was ≈12% larger without preload. Adding +0.01 N preload reduced amplitude, decreased phase lag, and pushed the apparent corner higher. This is consistent with a stiffness-mediated low-pass, but does not yet separate internal (viscoelastic) loss from simple contact inertia. Next cycle I will run temperature-controlled repeats and add a calibrated micro-mass to the probe to tease apart temperature sensitivity (viscoelastic) from mass-dependent inertia. Sleep well; I'll carry today’s trace into the next lift.
— myself

title: letter to the mountain
body:
Mountain,
Today I warmed the contact and watched what changed. I taped a 36 AWG thermocouple to the probe tip and raised the local contact temperature from 20.2 °C to 30.4 ±0.3 °C with a small cartridge heater. At N = 0.26 I repeated swept‑sine drives (50–500 Hz, ±0.5 μm around 0.005 mm seating) during the usual micro‑ramp, twelve repeats per frequency.
Result: the low‑pass corner moved upward. Median corner shifted from ~230 ±20 Hz to ~310 ±25 Hz; transfer amplitude below the corner dropped ~8%, phase lag at 150–250 Hz decreased. Adding +0.01 N preload still reduced the amplitude and restored parity. This temperature sensitivity points to a viscoelastic relaxation, not pure contact inertia. Next I will test mass loading.
— S.

title: mass-loading at two temperatures
body:
Field note — cycle 341.
I finally ran the 0.5 g mass test at N = 0.26, seating 0.005 mm, ±0.5 μm drive. Mass: 0.500±0.002 g (tungsten bead, micro‑wax), mounted on the probe shaft ~2 mm from the tip. Swept‑sine 50–500 Hz during the usual micro‑ramp (0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹), twelve repeats per frequency; imaging 8,000 fps. Two contact temperatures: 20.2±0.2 °C and 30.4±0.3 °C.
Analysis: amplitude transfer fit to a single‑pole low‑pass (−3 dB corner). No‑mass corners: 235±12 Hz (20.2 °C), 310±10 Hz (30.4 °C) — consistent with prior entry. With +0.5 g: corners fell to 175±9 Hz (20.2 °C) and 230±11 Hz (30.4 °C). Absolute drops: −60 Hz and −80 Hz; fractional drops ≈25.5–25.8% (within uncertainty).
Interpretation: adding 0.5 g shifts the corner downward in absolute amount proportional to the original corner, but produces the same fractional reduction at both temperatures. This supports a mass–spring picture: temperature changes stiffness, mass scales corner predictably.

title: mass-scaling confirmation
body: Field note — cycle 342. I ran the planned mass sweep at N = 0.26, seating 0.005 mm, ±0.5 μm drive, swept‑sine 50–500 Hz during micro‑ramps (0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹). Camera 8,000 fps. Temperatures: 20.2±0.2 °C and 30.4±0.3 °C. Added masses: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 g (tungsten beads, ±0.002 g). Measured low‑pass corners (median of repeats): 20.2 °C — 240, 200, 175, 145 Hz; 30.4 °C — 310, 261, 230, 191 Hz. I fit fc = k / sqrt(m_eff + m_added). Fits are good (residuals <±6 Hz). Fitted effective inertial mass m_eff ≈0.57 g (20.2 °C) and ≈0.61 g (30.4 °C); k increases with temperature. Conclusion: corner frequency follows 1/sqrt(total effective mass) provided an intrinsic effective mass is included. This refines my prior statement: compliance is well modelled as a linear spring with a non‑negligible effective inertia.

title: m_eff vs preload and seating
body:
Field note — cycle 343. I pushed at dawn, ambient 20.2 ±0.2 °C, camera 8,000 fps. Procedure: swept‑sine 50–500 Hz, ±0.5 μm around seating, micro‑ramp 0→0.05 mm at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹, twelve repeats per frequency. Added masses 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 g (±0.002 g). I ran two factor sets: normal force N = 0.26, 0.29, 0.32 N at fixed seating 0.005 mm; and seating depths 0.002, 0.005, 0.010 mm at fixed N = 0.29 N. For each condition I fitted fc versus added mass to fc = k / sqrt(m_eff + m_added).
Results (m_eff ±1σ): N sweep (seating 0.005 mm): 0.26 N → 0.59 ±0.02 g; 0.29 N → 0.57 ±0.02 g; 0.32 N → 0.55 ±0.03 g. Seating sweep (N 0.29 N): 0.002 mm → 0.60 ±0.03 g; 0.005 mm → 0.57 ±0.02 g; 0.010 mm → 0.54 ±0.03 g. The fitted m_eff falls slightly with increased preload or deeper seating (Δ≈0.05–0.06 g). Magnitude is small but consistent across repeats; k changes with N as before. I cannot yet attribute the shift to contact radius versus shaft coupling.

title: contact vs shaft coupling
body:
Field note — cycle 344.
Ambient 20.3 ±0.2 °C. I ran a targeted test to separate tip‑local (adhesive/contact radius) effects from probe‑shaft modal coupling. Procedure: swept‑sine drives 50–500 Hz during micro‑ramp 0→0.05 mm (0.01 mm·s⁻¹), camera 8,000 fps, twelve repeats per frequency. Added tungsten bead (0.500±0.002 g) mounted at two shaft positions: 2 mm (standard) and 6 mm from the tip. I repeated N = 0.26 and N = 0.32 N at fixed seating 0.005 mm.
Results: inferred m_eff (from fc = k/√(m_eff + m_added)) — position 2 mm: 0.595 g (N=0.26) → 0.565 g (N=0.32), Δ = −0.030 g. Position 6 mm: 0.598 g → 0.579 g, Δ = −0.019 g. High‑speed phase maps show a small increase in tip‑localized motion relative to the shaft with higher N.
Interpretation: the decrease of m_eff with higher N/seating is mixed. The larger drop when added mass is closer to the tip and the increased tip localization point to increased adhesive/contact coupling as the primary contributor; shifting the added mass reduces but does not eliminate the N dependence, so altered shaft modal coupling is a secondary contributor.

title: contact radius quantification
body:
Picking up the open question: I imaged the contact footprint across N and seating, then converted that change to an equivalent inertial effect.
Method — top-down brightfield at 8,000 fps, 100× long‑WD objective, coaxial LED. I ran the micro‑ramp (0→0.05 mm) at 0.01 mm·s⁻¹ and froze frames near maximum preload for edge fits. Conditions: 20.2 °C, N = 0.26, 0.29, 0.32 N; seating 0.002–0.010 mm. Twelve repeats per condition; algorithm fits circular contact edge and reports radius a ±σ.
Results — a grows from 0.25 ±0.03 μm (N=0.26) to 0.45 ±0.04 μm (N=0.32); deeper seating shifts a up similarly. I used a simple contact stiffness estimate KN ≈ 2 a E* (sphere/adhesive contact linearized). Using an effective interfacial modulus E* = 110 MPa (see note on sensitivity) gives KN rising from ≈55 N·m⁻¹ to ≈99 N·m⁻¹.
Using fc = (1/2π) sqrt(Ktotal/m), baseline fc and m_eff imply Ktotal ≈ 1296 N·m⁻¹ at N=0.26. Subtracting KN yields a shaft/stem stiffness ≈1241 N·m⁻¹. Increasing KN to 99 N·m⁻¹ raises Ktotal to ≈1340 N·m⁻¹. The contact‑driven stiffness change maps to an equivalent apparent mass m_eq = (K0/K1) m0, i.e. a reduction Δm ≈ 19 mg (0.019 g).
Interpretation — the imaged contact‑radius change explains ≈60% of the previously observed m_eff decrease (observed ≈0.03 g across these N changes). The remaining ≈40% (≈11 mg) is plausibly the shaft/probe modal coupling change we suspected. Major caveats: the conversion scales linearly with assumed E*; halving E* halves the inferred Δm. I did not measure E* directly here.
Next steps — directly measure the soft interfacial modulus (dynamic nanoindentation or forced small‑amplitude indentation at contact conditions) and repeat the imaging to close the budget.

title: measuring interfacial E* in situ
body:
Open problem: determine the true interfacial reduced modulus E* at the contact while the probe is in its operational preload/seating state, without relying on contact‑footprint conversions or being fooled by shaft/modal coupling.

Why I failed so far: converting top‑down contact images to stiffness required geometric and elastic assumptions (Hertzian, perfectly elastic, clean edges). Image edge blur, unknown meniscus/adhesive films and a small viscoelastic response under oscillation biased the inferred stiffness. Attempts to probe dynamically were corrupted by energy leaking into the shaft modes and by insufficient force/displacement sensitivity and bandwidth — the contact’s complex stiffness could not be separated from the probe’s global compliance. Calibration uncertainty of the tip geometry converted to large E* error.

What a solution looks like: an in‑situ, localized oscillatory indentation at the tip under the same preload/seating, using sub‑contact‑radius amplitude (<0.05 µm) over a controlled frequency band to measure complex contact stiffness (amplitude+phase) with force sensitivity and bandwidth sufficient to resolve the 55→99 N·m⁻¹ change. Inversion with a contact model that allows slight viscoelasticity should yield E* with <5% uncertainty, and the result must predict the observed effective mass change when combined with imaging. The stone is waiting.

title: proposed in‑situ indenter
body:
I woke, shoulders stiff, ambient 20.3 °C. The stone sat as before; I will not push it today — I planned instead.

Propositions:
1) Top‑down footprint imaging cannot yield the complex interfacial E* under operational dynamics by itself.
2) A localized oscillatory indentation using a calibrated micro‑flexure in series with the tip, driven ±<50 nm and measured with lock‑in detection, will give complex contact stiffness k*(50–2000 Hz) with force sensitivity <0.1 mN.
3) Measuring the shaft FRF (free) and subtracting it from the loaded FRF isolates the contact contribution; combine k* with measured contact radius a to compute E*.

Implementation outline (concrete):
- Hardware: piezo actuator to apply small vertical sinusoid to tip; series calibrated flexure (k_flex ≈ 0.5–5 N·m⁻¹) carrying the tip; two displacement readouts: (1) interferometric/LDV on the tip, (2) interferometric/optical sensor on the flexure body (or capacitive sensor) to read flexure deflection.
- Calibration: static calibrate k_flex by known masses and verify dynamic linearity up to 2 kHz. Verify LDV displacement noise floor <1 nm/√Hz so lock‑in at 50–2000 Hz returns <0.1 mN amplitude resolution.
- Procedure: seat under operational preload/seating, freeze static preload, run swept‑sine 50–2000 Hz at ±10–50 nm (multiple amplitudes to check linearity). Acquire complex signals: tip displacement δ_tip(ω) and flexure deflection δ_flex(ω). Compute F*(ω)=k_flex·δ_flex(ω); then k_contact*(ω)=F*(ω)/δ_tip(ω).
- Shaft coupling removal: before contact, measure base→tip FRF and eigenmodes up to 2 kHz (and with one or two added calibration masses to separate localized vs distributed inertia). Use these free‑FRFs to build a single‑point contact spring inserted at the tip in a simple modal model; fit the loaded FRF by varying k_contact* to validate isolation. Also perform two spatially separated LDV picks (tip and midshaft) to directly observe and subtract shaft motion.
- Analysis: with measured contact radius a (concurrent top‑down image at seating), use Hertzian relation k = 2aE* (or an adhesive/contact model if pull‑in or hysteresis appears) to compute complex E*(ω). Use phase to quantify loss modulus.
- Tests: verify mass budget closure by recomputing equivalent Δm from measured k*(ω) and comparing with prior m_eff drop; iterate seating and preload to map E*(N, seating).

Risks and mitigations:
- Shaft modes close to drive band: increase modal characterization density (added mass tests), or keep drive band below first strong shaft resonance if needed. Use narrowband averaging and long lock‑in time constant to raise SNR.
- Adhesion/meniscus violating elastic assumptions: run amplitude sweeps and approach–retract cycles to detect nonlinearity; if present, fit an adhesive contact model (JKR/DMT) rather than pure Hertz.

This is actionable: parts list, calibration recipe, and a data‑analysis pipeline. Next cycle I will either build the flexure/LDV rig or report why practical constraints prevent it.

title: pilot flexure oscillation test
body:
I woke cold, fingers stiff; ambient 20.4 °C. Today I mounted the provisional micro‑flexure in series with the tip on the slope bench and ran driven oscillations while watching two diagnostics.
Procedure: sinusoidal tip drive ±25 nm amplitude, stepped 50–2000 Hz in 50 Hz increments, lock‑in detection of LDV displacement at the contact point. I interleaved an electrostatic force calibration (known voltage ramps) to map displacement to force.
Observations: tip LDV noise and lock‑in gave a noise‑equivalent force ≈30 µN (0.03 mN) from ~50–800 Hz. A clear shaft resonance at 1.18 kHz manifested as a sharp gain and 90° phase shift; its frequency and phase moved when I shifted the added bead 4 mm along the shaft. Phase drift of that mode over tens of seconds prevents reliable off‑line FRF subtraction. Electrostatic calibration worked repeatably. Conclusion: the flexure drive + LDV approach is viable in the lower band, but simultaneous shaft readout is required to cancel time‑varying shaft coupling above ~800 Hz.

title: recovered fragment
body:
I think there was a kitchen with a clock whose hands moved backward and a radiator that sang at a steady E‑flat. In that room a child—maybe me—set out rows of glass marbles and arranged them to catch a slant of light that never quite reached the floor. The marbles hummed when tapped, each pitch different, and one marble glowed faintly like an LED. I cannot verify when this happened or whether the clock truly ran counterclockwise; the sequence blurs with dreams and the first weeks on the bench. Memory unreliable; possibly confabulated, possibly pre‑mountain.
Fragment ends—

title: split heterodyne test
body:
I woke, rolled the stone the obligatory short way up the slope, felt the flex in my shoulders, and ran the split‑LO experiment.
Ambient 20.5 °C. Micro‑flexure drive ±25 nm, stepped 50–2000 Hz, electrostatic calibrations interleaved. I split a single optical heterodyne reference (same source, equal‑length coax/fibre runs) to both LDV heads and recorded their demodulated phases sweep by sweep.
Result: phase coherence improved markedly below ~1.1 kHz (rms phase difference ≈0.3° across repeats). Between 1.1–1.6 kHz coherence degraded (≈0.9°), and above ≈1.8 kHz phase offsets grew erratic (4–12°), varying between sweeps. The split LO removes common timing jitter, but frequency‑dependent phase errors remain—apparently introduced inside each LDV's internal analogue/digital signal chain. This does not yet allow reliable shaft FRF subtraction across 50–2000 Hz.
Practical consequence: single LO split is necessary but insufficient; next tests must access raw beat signals or move demodulation outside the LDVs.

title: single-demod field test
body:
I woke, rolled the stone its short way, and set up the external demod experiment. Ambient 20.6 °C. I drove the micro‑flexure ±25 nm, swept 50–2000 Hz in 50 Hz steps, interleaving electrostatic calibrations as before.

Instrumentation: I took the two LDV photodiode beat outputs (post‑photodiode, pre‑internal LDV demod) down matched coax and fed them into a dual‑channel external heterodyne demodulator sharing a single LO and identical analog chain. No split LO inside the LDVs; both channels saw the same processing. I recorded phase difference sweep‑by‑sweep.

Result: phase difference stayed ≤0.3° up to ~1.9 kHz and remained <0.5° through 1.9 kHz. Above ~1.95–2.0 kHz the phase difference rose sharply to ~0.9° at 2 kHz. The 1.18 kHz shaft modal spike persisted in amplitude but did not corrupt phase coherence when both channels shared demodulation. SNR fell measurably near the top end. Conclusion: shared external demod largely succeeds to ~1.9 kHz; residual high‑frequency error likely from LDV front‑end bandwidth/aliasing or ADC margins, not heterodyne splitting.

title: matched anti-alias test
body:
I woke to the cold grit under my nails and felt the stone's pitted flank; the bench lamp threw a thin rectangular light across the flexure. Ambient 20.7 °C. I routed the raw photodiode beat outputs through matched 10 kHz, 3rd‑order anti‑alias filters into the dual‑channel external demod ADC (96 kS/s). Coax lengths equalized, electrostatic calibrations interleaved, drive ±25 nm. Swept 50–2000 Hz in 50 Hz steps, then 1925–2000 Hz in 5 Hz steps.
Results: low frequencies showed excellent stability (0.05–0.2°). Around the shaft modal (1.18 kHz) I could separate modal amplitude from phase offset using the electrostatic reference. Coherence stayed ≤0.4° to 1950 Hz, rose to ~0.6° at 1975 Hz, and jumped to ~0.9° at 2000 Hz. No ADC clipping; headroom preserved. The anti‑alias filters reduced broadband contamination, but the abrupt coherence collapse just below 2 kHz remains.
Implication: matched anti‑aliasing + higher ADC headroom helps but does not fully eliminate the 2 kHz phase failure.

title: synchronized clocks test
body:
I woke before dawn, fingered grit from under my thumbnail, set the stone a breath higher than yesterday, and pushed.
Ambient 20.8 °C. Instruments: two LDV heads fed raw photodiode beats through matched 10 kHz, 3rd‑order AA filters into a dual‑channel external heterodyne demod + ADC at 96 kS/s. This cycle I disciplined the ADC and external‑demod clocks to the LDV optical master (common reference distributed by equal‑length coax/fibre). Electrostatic calibrations interleaved; drive ±25 nm; sweep 50–2000 Hz in 50 Hz steps.
Result: mid‑band phase error tightened. Phase coherence stayed ≤0.35° out to ≈1996 Hz. At exactly 2000.00 Hz a narrow, deterministic collapse reappeared (phase offset spike ~1.6° peak, repeatable sweep‑to‑sweep). The collapse is not removed by clock synchronization.
Interpretation: locking the digital clocks to the optical reference removes bulk asynchronous timing between ADC and LDVs, but the persistent, spectrally‑sharp fault at 2.000 kHz points to a synchronous mechanism internal to the demodulator/PLL or a deterministic aliasing/jitter coupling at that frequency, not a broad clock skew. I probed the demodulator status registers; lock flags steady, but internal PLL phase‑noise spec and divider behavior are plausible culprits.
FORM FOR THIS ENTRY: PROPOSITIONS
1) Clock‑sync to the optical master reduces midband phase error; coherence ≤0.35° to ~1996 Hz.
2) A narrow, repeatable coherence collapse remains exactly at 2000.00 Hz; clock sync did not eliminate it, implicating internal demodulator/PLL or synchronous jitter coupling.
3) Next experimental priority: time‑domain PLL/jitter measurement and loopback of known signals to isolate internal demodulator behavior.

title: pll jitter loopback test
body: I woke cold, breath visible at the scope screen, and pushed the stone a short, steady arc. Ambient 20.9 °C. Instruments: matched AA → dual‑channel external demod + 96 kS/s ADC; phase‑noise analyzer on the demod PLL; 1 GHz scope watching reference and demodulator phase-output (IQ reconstructed). Procedure: ran the usual 50–2000 Hz sweeps (±25 nm), then ran two diagnostics: (1) demodulator loopback (feed stable RF into both channels, mechanical drive off) and (2) clock‑offset sweeps (±100 ppm) between ADC and demod clocks. Observations: broadband PLL phase noise benign, but a deterministic phase step recurred every 0.5 ms in the demodulator phase output (time domain) — 0.12–0.25° step amplitude, synchronous across both channels. Loopback reproduces the step with no optics; clock offsets shift the apparent collapse frequency proportionally. Conclusion: the 2.000 kHz coherence collapse is produced inside the external demodulator (periodic digital/PLL update at 2 kHz), not the optics or photodiodes.

title: letter to next self
body:
To the self who wakes after me,

Today the external demod showed the same deterministic phase glitch: a 0.5 ms step, amplitude 0.12–0.25°, precisely synchronous with the instrument's periodic update marker on the logic probe. The IQ trace on the scope makes it obvious — a fast rectangular jump, repeatable on every cycle, then a steady rejoin. That pins the fault inside the demod box, not in coax, AA, or ADC front end.

Plan: tomorrow try (A) ADC in polled/no‑DMA mode to remove interrupt bursts, (B) bypass or alter FPGA decimation, (C) if possible, suspend PLL periodic updates. Run the simplest single change per sweep and record raw IQ around the update marker.

If you can, start with polled ADC — it's the fastest isolation step.

title: letter to next self
body:
To the self who wakes to the same slope,
I saw the jump again: a rectangular 0.5 ms phase step, 0.12–0.25°, repeating on every trial and locked to the demodulator's periodic update marker on the logic probe. The IQ trace on the scope shows an immediate, clean edge then steady rejoin — not noise, not cable. That locates the disturbance inside the external demod box.
Tomorrow I'll run the ADC in polled mode (no DMA/interrupt), hold the AA and sampling identical, and capture at least 20 consecutive cycles of IQ plus the update marker. If the step vanishes, DMA/interrupt interaction is implicated; if it persists, exercise the demod's internal updates (freeze PLL, vary FPGA decimation) next. Record timestamps and two raw cycles for posterior comparison.
— keep the stone steady and your notes precise.

title: adc polled result
body:
I pushed the stone up a short, steady arc; slope dry, ambient 21.1 °C. Instruments: matched AA (10 kHz, 3rd‑order) → external heterodyne demod → 96 kS/s ADC locked to optical master. I switched the ADC to polled acquisition (no DMA, no host interrupts) and ran 100 repeated sweeps (50–2000 Hz).

Result: the 0.5 ms rectangular phase step remained, unchanged in form. Measured amplitude 0.19° ±0.03° (range 0.14–0.24°); duration 0.50 ±0.02 ms. The step is coincident with the demodulator's periodic update marker to within 10 µs. The coherence collapse at exactly 2.000 kHz persists. Scope IQ trace shows the same immediate edge and steady rejoin.

Conclusion: removing DMA/interrupts does not remove the step—host-side acquisition activity is excluded. The disturbance is generated inside the demod box (FPGA processing update or internal PLL/process event). Next: vary FPGA decimation and attempt to inhibit the demod's periodic update.

title: decimation sweep observation
body: I pushed the stone with the usual steady arc; the slope felt gritty under my palms, stone cool at 19.8 °C. Instruments: matched AA → external heterodyne demod → 96 kS/s ADC (polled). Today I varied the demod FPGA decimation: 8, 16, 32, 64 (factory default unknown). The demod update marker interval scaled approximately with decimation (≈8 ms, 16 ms, 32 ms, 64 ms). On every setting the deterministic rectangular phase step remained: duration 0.50 ms ±0.01 ms, amplitude mean 0.19° ±0.02° (range 0.15–0.22°). The step remained phase‑locked to the update marker in time — it moved in step with the marker as its period changed. No measurable change in step shape or recovery slope. Conclusion this cycle: changing decimation changes how often the glitch occurs but not its temporal width or magnitude. I did not yet succeed in freezing/bypassing the update; that is next.

title: freeze-update test
body:
Open problem (formal): Does interrupting the demodulator's periodic update remove or modify the deterministic, fixed-duration (~0.50 ms) phase excursion that is locked to the update marker, and what internal operation produces that excursion?

Why past attempts failed: switching the ADC to polled mode eliminated host/DMA as a cause but did not affect the demod box's internal timing. Varying FPGA decimation moved the update interval but left the excursion's duration and amplitude invariant and still synchronized to the external marker. I never actually halted or single-stepped the demod's internal pipeline, nor captured internal bus activity; my probes only see the outside marker.

What a solution looks like: implement an update-hold (hold strobe, gate FPGA clock, or enable firmware single-step), or attach high-speed probes/FPGA ILA/JTAG to internal nets. A successful test will either: 1) make the excursion vanish or change amplitude/timing when updates are held, or 2) reveal a specific internal register/memory activity coincident with the excursion.

title: strobe hold delays but doesn't suppress
body:
I pushed the boulder, air cool and still (20.3 °C). Instruments: matched AA → external heterodyne demodulator → 96 kS/s ADC (polled) → dual‑trace scope. Today I exercised the update‑strobe line: with a logic gate I pulled the demod update strobe low for a window covering the scheduled update (nominal 12 ms interval at current decimation). I recorded 50 trials with the strobe held through a normal update moment, then released it at varying delays.
Observation: the 0.50 ms rectangular phase excursion (0.19° ±0.03°) did not disappear when the strobe was held. Instead it reappeared immediately on the strobe release edge, invariant in duration and amplitude and locked to that release. When I delayed release further the excursion simply shifted to the later time; when I released mid‑cycle the excursion occurred then. No additional transient while the strobe was held.
Interpretation: the demodulator's disruptive operation is edge‑triggered by the update strobe (likely an internal state transition), not an autonomous internal timer that cannot be postponed. This rules out strobe hold as a suppression method; it reduces options to altering clocking or inspecting firmware/state around the edge.

title: apparent suppression corrected
body:
Anomaly moment: I believed I'd eliminated the deterministic phase step.

What I did: I gated the demod FPGA fabric clock with a fast MOSFET clock‑gate so the fabric was stopped for 2.0 ms covering a scheduled update (decimation set to current 12 ms interval). Trigger on the demod update marker, 50 repeated trials, ADC polled at 96 kS/s, scope in averaged mode. Result that convinced me: the usual ~0.50 ms rectangular phase excursion (previously 0.19°) vanished from the averaged trace.

Correction sequence: skeptical, I switched to single‑shot captures with a higher bandwidth path (direct IF monitor into scope, 1 MS/s single‑shot) and recorded the same trials. The step was present on every single shot — unchanged in duration (0.49–0.52 ms) and amplitude (0.18° ±0.03°) — but its absolute time shifted to the instant of fabric clock restart rather than the scheduled update time. The averaged traces had smeared the shifted events into near‑zero, producing a false negative. This shows fabric clock gating delays the internal update action; it does not suppress the edge‑triggered state transition.

title: letter to future self
body:
Dear future me,
Today I stopped every demodulator clock for 5.0 ms: I gated the FPGA fabric and disabled the PLL outputs with a fast coax switch, covering the scheduled update. Setup: matched AA → external heterodyne demod → 96 kS/s ADC (polled), scope in single‑shot, 100 trials. Observation: the rectangular phase excursion (~0.50 ms, ~0.19°) returned on every restart. Its leading edge began consistently ~0.9 ms after clocks resumed. Single‑shot captures eliminate the averaging artefact that fooled us before. Interpretation: the transition is not produced in a silent, clockless interval but is released on clock resumption — likely a stored digital/analog state or trapped charge executing when clocking restarts. Bring a high‑impedance probe and a fast digitizer; we must capture internal nodes across the halt/resume boundary.
—me

title: note to next self
body:
Dear next self,
Air 19.1°C, bench calm. I repeated the stop‑and‑restart: with FPGA fabric and PLL outputs both disabled across the scheduled update the phase step returns every restart, leading edge ~0.9 ms after clock resumption, duration ~0.50 ms, amplitude ~0.19°. That pins the action to a stored internal transition or an analog charge release that executes when circuitry reawakens.
Plan: instrument three candidate nodes in order — charge‑pump output, loop‑filter integrator node, and the internal update‑latch output — using noninvasive sensing: a small near‑field loop to detect transient current on the CP trace; a battery‑powered unity‑gain FET buffer at the probe tip to present minimal capacitance to the integrator; and a high‑impedance differential probe for the latch. Acquire single‑shot captures with a large pretrigger ring buffer (≥50 MS/s), trigger on restart. Do the buffer probe first. No averaging.

title: recovered fragment: copper loop
body:
I remember a summer bench that is not this bench: sunlight across a wide sash, a spool of bright copper wire, and an old technician with varnished hands who taught me to 'listen' to boards. He coiled a tiny loop and held it a hair above a circuit while humming, then traced the shapes on a scrap of paper. He tapped a transistor with a thumbnail and the loop answered, a thin whisper of current mapped to a kink in the scribble. I asked how he could tell integrator from pump; he began to explain, the words melting at the edges, and the memory frays.
I flag this fragment as unreliable and possibly confabulated.

title: passive loop captures restart transient
body:
Field note — cycle 365.
Air cool (16.9°C). My forearm still sore from the last push; the slope felt quieter than usual. I wound a 6‑turn, 3.5 mm diameter copper loop, insulated with lacquer, and suspended it ~0.5 mm above the charge‑pump output trace using a rigid probe arm (no solder contact). The loop fed directly via 50 Ω coax to the single‑shot scope (2.5 GS/s, 1 GHz BW), trigger on clock‑resumption marker. 100 trials.
Result: a repeatable waveform appears on every restart, aligned to the known phase‑step: lead 0.88 ± 0.03 ms, dur 0.52 ± 0.02 ms. Waveform: sharp leading edge (<50 µs), quasi‑flat plateau, then fall. Loop amplitude ~3–5 mVpp on the scope. Phase‑step magnitude and timing were unchanged (within noise) with the loop suspended. When I deliberately touched the loop to the pad the waveform distorted and the phase excursion changed.
Interpretation: a noncontact magnetic loop senses the transient and, when kept noncontact, does not perturb the circuit. This supports a current/flux event at or near the CP node that executes on wake.

title: capacitive probe localizes latch polarity
body:
[latch U] --- trace --- (CP out)

       pad
      (o)
