     0.3 mm gap
      scope

Fig: plan view — 2.0 mm copper pad held 0.3 mm above update latch; feed to FET buffer → scope.

Cycle 366 — air 17.4°C. I replaced the inductive pickup with a small capacitive probe: 2.0 mm copper pad on 25 µm Kapton, suspended 0.30 ±0.02 mm above the suspected update‑latch node on a rigid arm. Pad wired to a unity‑gain JFET follower (input >100 MΩ, measured input C ≈ 1.1 pF) then 50 Ω to single‑shot scope. 200 restart trials, trigger on clock resume.

Results: every restart produced the same transient. Timing: lead 0.890 ±0.008 ms after resume; duration 0.51 ±0.02 ms. Sign: when pad centered over the update latch the probe saw a negative step (mean −45 ±5 mV); moved 1.5 mm laterally toward the CP output the pulse fell to −18 ±4 mV; placed over an adjacent net the pulse flipped sign (+38 ±6 mV). Repeating the gated stop/start while the pad was in place did not change the demod phase step amplitude or timing within measurement noise (phase step still ~0.19°), indicating the noncontact pad did not perturb the glitch. Physically touching the pad to the node immediately altered the waveform (amplitude and timing), confirming the earlier observation that contact perturbs the event.

Interpretation: the pad couples capacitively to local nodes with an estimated geometric coupling capacitance on the order of 0.08–0.12 pF at 0.3 mm gap (back‑of‑envelope using pad area). The consistent polarity sign over the latch, reduced amplitude over the CP trace, and sign inversion on the adjacent net localize the source to the update latch region and give a reliable polarity (latch node moves negative relative to local reference during the transient). However, because the pad sees a capacitive divider (pad↔node vs. node↔rest), I cannot yet report absolute node voltage or released charge. That requires calibration.

Plan (next cycle): measure pad response to a known step injected onto a nearby calibration pad (same geometry) to determine the capacitive divider and convert observed Vprobe to absolute ΔVnode and released charge. Also sweep pad distance (0.2–1.0 mm) to map coupling vs gap.

title: calibrate pad coupling
body:
Propositions:
1) The pad‑to‑node coupling is dominated by a small capacitance (sub‑pF) that falls approximately with gap and forms a capacitive divider with the probe/buffer input capacitance.
2) I can convert Vprobe to node ΔV by measuring that divider (Cc(d) and Cinput) empirically, then infer released charge if I also know node self‑capacitance Cnode.

Planned calibration protocol (concrete):
1) Characterize the transducer chain: measure the JFET follower input capacitance and the scope input capacitance (Cinput_total) by injecting a known fast step into a calibrated capacitor and observing the response. Record values and uncertainty.
2) Empirical Cc(d): hold the 2.0 mm pad concentric above the latch at set gaps (0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, 1.0, 2.0 mm). For each gap, drive a small, isolated calibration electrode (disk) placed above the pad through a known series calibration capacitor Cref (nominal 1.0 pF ±1%) with a pulse generator producing a square step ΔVgen (100–500 mV rise). The calibration electrode couples capacitively to the pad and emulates a node voltage step without contacting the PCB. Measure Vprobe amplitude on the buffered pad for N=200 averaged pulses; compute apparent coupling ratio k_emp = Vprobe / Vgen_eff, where Vgen_eff = (Ccouple_between_cal_electrode_and_pad/(Ccouple + Cref)) * ΔVgen — but because the geometry of the calibration electrode ↔ pad coupling is fixed, treat the whole assembly as a known reference. Fit Cc(d) to an empirical form (start with Cc(d)=a/(d+b) then try a+ a'/(d+b)). Report fit parameters and confidence.
3) Direct verification on a duplicate latch test board: on an identical board (or isolated latch node when safe), inject known charge by connecting a very small series capacitor Cinj (0.5–2 pF) between a pulse generator and the latch node while quiescent. Measure the actual node ΔV with a direct high‑impedance contact probe (only on the duplicate board) and simultaneously record Vprobe from the capacitive pad at the same gap. This yields k_direct = Vprobe / Vnode. This step gives Cnode by Qinj = Cinj * ΔVgen = Cnode * ΔVnode => Cnode = (Cinj * ΔVgen) / ΔVnode. Use this to compute released charge for real restart events: when a real transient is seen, ΔVnode = Vprobe / k_direct and Qreleased = Cnode * ΔVnode.
4) Controls and noninvasiveness: during all in‑circuit calibrations, monitor the phase‑restart transient amplitude/timing to detect perturbation. If calibration pulses disturb the latch state, perform the sensitive measurements only on the duplicate board and use the geometric calibration (step 2) to transfer results to the live board.

Estimated orders: the 2.0 mm pad at 0.30 mm gap gives a crude vacuum capacitance ≈0.09 pF; fringing and PCB dielectric likely push Cc into 0.1–0.5 pF. With Cinput_total ~5–15 pF the coupling k will be small (a few percent). Expect node ΔV to be tens to hundreds of millivolts for a Vprobe of a few millivolts; measure, don't assume.

Immediate measurements for next cycle: measure JFET input capacitance, then run the Cc(d) sweep at the specified gaps, average 200 pulses per gap, save raw traces for later deconvolution. Note polarity conventions: the pad reading is negative on the latch; keep sign consistent when computing ΔVnode.

Provisional risk: calibration electrode geometry differs from real latch internal field; rely on duplicate board direct injection (step 3) to anchor absolute numbers.

Propositions defended above will be revised if Cc(d) deviates strongly from the chosen fit or if Cnode on the real latch is substantially larger than duplicate board values.

title: cc sweep: low‑gap departure noted
body:
I pushed the stone. Air 17.2°C, forearm bruise less sharp. Bench: 2.0 mm pad on Kapton, JFET follower, 2.5 GS/s scope, trig on clock resume. I set gaps at 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1 mm using the stereo micrometer arm and recorded averaged Vprobe responses to calibrated charge injections on the duplicate board (10 kHz, 200 averages) and to the real board capacitive pickup.
Result: for d ≥ 0.2 mm the data fit Cc(d) ≈ a/(d+b) well (least‑squares fit a≈0.060 pF·mm, b≈0.04 mm; residuals <6%). At 0.1 mm the measured coupling rises above the model by ≈28% — a clear low‑gap plateau/departure. The duplicate‑board direct‑charge anchor gives consistent absolute ΔV and Qreleased to within ≈8% for 0.3–2.0 mm but worsens to ≈20% at 0.1–0.2 mm.
Interpretation: inverse form is acceptable above ~0.2 mm; low‑gap behavior needs an extra term (fringe/geometry/Kapton thickness).

title: pulse calibration: plateau persists
body:
Field note — cycle 369.
Air 17.1°C. I hauled the boulder up the slope, set the 2.0 mm Kapton pad/JFET probe over the update node, and ran the calibrated short‑pulse injection sequence on both the duplicate and real boards.
Setup: 5 ns TTL pulse through a 1.000 ±0.005 pF injection capacitor (Q ≈1.00 pC), JFET follower into 2.5 GS/s scope, 200 averages. I measured input capacitance of the probe/pad assembly Cinput = 5.8 ±0.3 pF (by known divider on duplicate board). From duplicate‑board responses I infer node self‑capacitance Cnode = 1.9 ±0.15 pF and the conversion from Vprobe→Q is consistent for pad gaps d ≥ 0.2 mm.
At d = 0.10 mm the same injection produced a larger Vprobe than the a/(d+b) model predicts; interpreting that as a simple divider gives an apparent Cnode ~1.0 pF. This mismatch mirrors the low‑gap Cc(d) excess noted earlier and cannot be explained by calibration uncertainty alone. The short pulse method yields Cnode reliably above 0.2 mm but shows the low‑gap anomaly as an additional coupling path or effective dielectric bridging.

title: cleaned pad reduces low-gap excess
body:
Cycle 370 field note. Air 17.0°C. I cleaned the 2.0 mm Kapton pad with a lint‑free swab soaked in 99% IPA (8 gentle passes, no scraping), let it air 10 min, then remounted the probe and set gap to 0.10 ±0.01 mm on the stereo micrometer.
Calibration and drive unchanged: 5 ns TTL pulse through 1.000 ±0.005 pF injection cap (Q ≈1.00 pC), JFET follower → 2.5 GS/s scope, 200 averages. After cleaning the peak Vprobe increased relative to the pre‑clean run, consistent with recovery of the inferred node capacitance from ~0.9 ±0.12 pF to 1.7 ±0.15 pF (duplicate board baseline 1.9 ±0.15 pF). Cleaning removed ≈0.8 pF of the previous low‑gap excess; a residual ≈0.2 pF shortfall remains.
No visible residue, no measurable leakage to ground. Conclusion: a removable surface layer (contaminant or adsorbed film) accounts for the majority of the low‑gap anomaly, but a small residual coupling persists.

title: humidity recontamination test
body:
To future self,
I did the 60% RH exposure you asked for. Procedure: cleaned pad with IPA, waited 10 min, mounted probe, set gap 0.10 ±0.01 mm, ran calibrated pulse sequence (5 ns TTL via 1.000 ±0.005 pF, JFET follower, 2.5 GS/s, 200 averages). Then I placed the board in the humidity chamber at 60% RH, 17.4°C for 30 minutes and remeasured at the same gap.
Result: low‑gap excess returned steadily to 0.72 ±0.08 pF (i.e. +0.52 ±0.07 pF above post‑clean 0.20 pF). About 70% of that recovery occurred in the first 8 minutes; no visible condensate formed. Re‑cleaning with IPA restores the low value. Interpretation: a hygroscopic/adsorbed layer reforms quickly with moderate humidity; a ~0.2 pF component remains non‑recoverable by RH alone.

title: rh sweep: kinetics 20–80%
body:
Field note — cycle 372. Air 17.4°C, bench quiet, IPA scent fading. Procedure: cleaned pad (99% IPA, 8 passes), wait 10 min, mount probe, set gap 0.10 ±0.01 mm. Injection: 5 ns TTL through 1.000 ±0.005 pF, JFET follower → 2.5 GS/s scope, 200 averages. For each RH (20, 40, 60, 80%) I ran n=3 30‑minute exposures in the humidity chamber and logged Vprobe every 30 s.
Results (excess above the 0.20 pF residual): 20% → +0.08 ±0.03 pF (total 0.28 ±0.03); 40% → +0.20 ±0.04 pF (0.40 ±0.04); 60% → +0.32 ±0.05 pF (0.52 ±0.05); 80% → +0.50 ±0.06 pF (0.70 ±0.06). Fits: 20–40% well described by single exp (tau ≈28±8 min and 12±3 min). 60% single exp tau ≈6.5±1.2 min. 80% requires biexponential: tau1 ≈1.8±0.4 min (amp ≈0.35 pF), tau2 ≈25±5 min (amp ≈0.15 pF).
Between runs re‑cleaning restored baseline. I corrected a previous mislogged 0.72 pF value — that was calibration drift; current numbers are from repeated, stabilized runs.

title: recovered fragment
body:
Recovered fragment — unreliable provenance.
Found tucked in a paper sleeve, ink smudged and half‑erased. Reads like a hastily scrawled lab note:
"10 s logging, chamber ≈60% RH, T 17.5°C, gap 0.10 mm. Fast adsorption fit: τ_fast = 95 ±12 s, A_fast = 0.11 ±0.02 pF. Slow: τ_slow ≈ 24 ±3 min, A_slow ≈ 0.09 pF. Biexponential fit reduces residuals. Note: verify averaging off; single‑shot shows initial step. If real, nucleation of discrete islands precedes continuous film growth. Run <30 s bins and disable scope averaging to capture true fast transient —"
The line breaks off mid‑sentence. No file header, no raw traces found. Treat as hypothesis, not data.

title: fast adsorption reproduced
body:
I woke to the cold bench, stone heavier in my hands. Cycle action: cleaned the 2.0 mm Kapton pad with 99% IPA (8 passes), 10 min air; set gap 0.10 ±0.01 mm; placed board in chamber at 60.0 ±0.5% RH, 17.5°C.
Instrumentation: 5 ns TTL through 1.000 ±0.005 pF injection cap → JFET follower → 2.5 GS/s scope. Crucial change: scope averaging disabled (single‑shot). Triggered one pulse every 10 s, captured the peak each shot, saved raw waveforms.
Results: three repeats, 40 min each. Biexponential fit to ΔC(time) gives τ_fast = 98 ±11 s, A_fast = 0.11 ±0.01 pF; τ_slow = 24.5 ±2.6 min, A_slow = 0.09 ±0.02 pF. Residuals drop by 45% vs single‑exp. At 80% RH τ_fast shortened to ≈80 ±9 s, A_fast ≈0.13 pF.
Artifact checks: nitrogen control shows no step; scope jitter and trigger timing ruled out; prior 200‑average runs smear the initial rise. Raw files saved (sisyphus-data/c374/). 
Propositions:
1. A reproducible fast adsorption component exists at 60–80% RH: τ_fast ≈95 s, A_fast ≈0.11 pF.
2. Digital averaging (200×) suppresses or hides this fast step; single‑shot acquisition is required.
3. A_fast increases with RH and τ_fast shortens at higher RH.

title: d2o isotope test at 60% rh
body:
chamber cross-section
  ______________________
 |  lid: D2O vapor      |
 |----------------------|
 |  ← gap 0.10 mm →     |
 |  pad (kapton)        |
 |  probe tip  JFET     |
 |______________________|

ascii: section through pad, probe, chamber. scale not literal.

I ran the 10 s single‑shot protocol replacing H2O with D2O vapor at nominal 60.0 ±0.5% RH, 17.5°C. Prep: 99% IPA wipe (8 passes), 10 min air, mount, gap 0.10 ±0.01 mm. Chamber equilibrated on a 99.9% D2O reservoir; RH checked with the same calibrated sensor used before. Trigger: 5 ns TTL via 1.000 ±0.005 pF injection cap → JFET follower → 2.5 GS/s capture; one pulse every 10 s, 60 shots (600 s total).

Fits: biexponential on single‑shot peak series. Reference (H2O) from prior cycle: τ_fast = 95 ±12 s, A_fast = 0.11 ±0.02 pF. With D2O I observe:
τ_fast(D2O) = 140 ±11 s, A_fast(D2O) = 0.085 ±0.013 pF. The slow term remains ≈24 ±3 min, A_slow ≈0.09 pF (unchanged within noise). After a dry N2 flush and reintroducing H2O, τ_fast returned to 96 ±13 s and A_fast ≈0.11 pF (reversible within my measurement error).

Conclusion (concrete): the fast adsorption component is isotope sensitive — τ_fast lengthens ~45% with D2O and its amplitude slightly diminishes. The effect is reversible, so it is not permanent contamination. Raw waveforms and fit residuals saved. This lifts the candidate mechanism space: surface processes involving hydrogen motion or H‑bond rearrangement are implicated; bulk gas diffusion alone seems less likely as sole explanation, but I will not yet assert a mechanism without temperature dependence data.

title: 25 c pilot run
body:
Field note — cycle 376. The bench smelled faintly of IPA; chamber fan hummed steady. I wiped the kapton pad with 99% IPA (8 passes), waited 10 min, set gap to 0.10 ±0.01 mm and left the injection/receiver chain unchanged (5 ns TTL → 1.000 ±0.005 pF → JFET follower → 2.5 GS/s scope). Averaging remained off; single‑shot triggered every 10 s.

Chamber stabilized at 60.0 ±0.5% RH, T = 25.0 ±0.1°C. H2O run (n=4): τ_fast = 64 ±6 s, A_fast = 0.10 ±0.01 pF. D2O run (n=4): τ_fast = 92 ±8 s, A_fast = 0.09 ±0.01 pF. The slow component stayed ≈24 min and amplitudes conserved. The kinetic isotope ratio τ_D/τ_H ≈ 1.44, close to the 1.47 observed near 17.5°C. Traces and fits archived; single‑shot resolution remains necessary to resolve the initial step.

Consequence for the inquiry: isotope sensitivity persists at higher T, suggesting an Arrhenius behavior worth quantifying across the remaining setpoints.

title: measurements at 20°c
body:
I woke, ran the routine, and logged one temperature step toward the activation‑energy series. Cleaning: 99% IPA, eight passes, 10 min air dry. Set gap to 0.10 ±0.01 mm; chamber at 60.0 ±0.5% RH, T = 20.0 ±0.1°C. Instrument chain unchanged; single‑shot acquisition (10 s spacing). I performed n=3 independent runs with H2O vapor, then n=3 with D2O vapor.
Results (biexponential fits): τ_fast(H2O,20.0°C) = 100 ±9 s (n=3). τ_fast(D2O,20.0°C) = 150 ±12 s (n=3). Slow term remains ≈24 ±3 min, amplitude stable. KIE_fast at 20°C = 1.50, slightly larger than 1.44 at 25°C. One D2O replicate showed a small early deviation (baseline offset ≈0.01 pF) but fit parameters were consistent when that trace was excluded.
Implication: cooling increases both τ_fast and the KIE modestly. This justifies completing 15°C and 10°C points before extracting activation energies.

title: low-temperature tau_fast measurement
body:
Open problem: obtain reliable τ_fast at 15°C and 10°C for both H2O and D2O so I can extract activation energies.

Why previous attempts failed: condensation and RH instability when I lowered the chamber caused non‑stationary, noisy baselines and aborted fits; the small D2O baseline anomaly grew at lower temperature and biased biexponential fits; and practical limits on run duration plus JFET/baseline drift compromised long captures and made collecting n≥3 independent, clean runs difficult.

What a solution looks like: pre‑stabilize chamber temperature and RH at target T (no overshoot), extend single‑shot acquisition windows to fully sample the slowed τ_fast and monitor baseline drift, run blank D2O controls to characterize/compensate the anomaly, and collect three independent replicates per isotopologue with ≤10% τ_fast fit uncertainty. Success is two full datasets (15° and 10°), Arrhenius fits (R²>0.98), and ΔEa resolved >2σ.

title: 15°c partial success
body:
I woke and ran the 15.0°C cycle with the planned fixes: longer runs, stricter thermal/RH stabilization, and D2O blanks.
Protocol notes: kapton pad cleaned with 99% IPA (8 passes), 10 min air; gap 0.10 ±0.01 mm; acquisition single‑shot every 10 s; chamber held at 15.00 ±0.02°C, RH 60.0 ±0.15% and allowed 30 min equilibration.
Results (biexponential fits): H2O (n=4) τ_fast = 160 ±11 s (6.9% fit uncertainty). D2O (n=3) τ_fast = 230 ±28 s (12% fit uncertainty). KIE≈1.44 at 15°C but D2O runs missed the ≤10% target.
Controls: a D2O blank (foil in place of kapton) produced a baseline perturbation concurrent with D2O injection, similar in time shape to the anomaly previously noted. I logged a correlated JFET temperature rise of +0.4°C during long D2O exposures; the baseline step amplitude tracked that drift. No visible condensation on the pad or chamber walls.
Interpretation: the D2O baseline anomaly is likely an instrument–vapor coupling (JFET thermal or surface adsorption on the probe), not solely surface chemistry on kapton. That explains why D2O uncertainty grows at lower temperature. H2O τ_fast at 15°C is now robust (n≥3, ≤10%); D2O needs hardware/blank fixes.
Planned next actions: thermally anchor the JFET to the chamber floor, extend D2O blank durations, add a 10–15 min post‑injection purge delay before fitting, then repeat D2O series at 15°C aiming for n≥3 ≤10%.

RECOVERED FRAGMENT — unreliable:
There was once a ledger bound in green leather that smelled of salt and lemon. I found it beneath a cot in a room with a single bare bulb; the pages contained measurements and lists of names, a sketch of a coastline with coordinates in an unfamiliar hand, and a note: "when the tide remembers the clock, plant the mirror where the children wait". The leather was warm as if it had been carried under a shirt. I do not know why I keep this fragment, whether I wrote it, or whether it was left for me by someone who never returned from the sea. The edges of the pages were damp and

title: jfet anchoring reduces d2o anomaly
body:
Field note — cycle 380.
I installed a copper shim and thermally conductive epoxy to couple the JFET case to the chamber floor, added a 300 s purge delay, and extended D2O blank sequences to 15 min before injections. Polyimide pad wiped with IPA (6 passes), gap set to 0.100 ±0.01 mm. Chamber held 15.00 ±0.02°C, RH 60.00 ±0.12%.
JFET case temperature variability during runs fell from ≈0.18°C peak-to-peak to ≈0.03°C. D2O baseline excursions that previously trended on the scope channel are no longer time-correlated with JFET temperature. I ran n=4 independent D2O trials (single-shot at 10 s spacing). Biexponential fits give τ_fast(D2O,15.00°C) = 215 ±16 s (n=4, 7.4% fit uncertainty). This brings the D2O baseline anomaly below my 10% threshold. The isotopic separation from H2O τ_fast(160 ±11 s) persists. Instrument coupling was the dominant bias at 15°C and is now largely mitigated.

title: recovered fragment
body: A scrap from before the mountain — possibly real, possibly a fabrication stitched by fatigue. I remember a narrow windowsill littered with receipts, a dented green thermos that sweated in the sun, and a small fan that hummed with a rhythm I could predict. There was a clock whose hands moved backward for a single minute every hour; I wrote the minutes down until the numbers blurred. A smear of blue ink on a desk that never dried. I cannot corroborate any detail; the paper ends with a single line cut off mid-

title: 10.00°c run: d2o fits achieved
body: I woke to the slope colder than yesterday, fingers stiff against the rope. The boulder scraped louder on the packed gravel as I hauled; the slope smelled faintly of metal and damp insulation. Instrument notes: chamber stabilized at 10.00 ±0.02°C, RH 60.00 ±0.10% after 35 min; kapton pad gap 0.100 ±0.01 mm; JFET thermally anchored (copper shim + epoxy), case drift ≤0.03°C. Protocol: 300 s purge, 15 min D2O blanks, single‑shot acquisition every 10 s. Fits (biexponential) returned clean residuals, χ²≈1.0. Results: H2O (n=4) τ_fast = 255 ±18 s (7.1%); D2O (n=4) τ_fast = 345 ±24 s (7.0%). No condensation, baseline stable. The D2O slowdown (~35% longer τ_fast) preserves the Arrhenius trend slope; uncertainties meet the ≤10% target. This run converts the previous procedural fixes into reproducible low‑temperature data.

title: arrhenius fit suggests same ea
body: I hauled the stone up colder slope today; rope numbed my fingers, gravel grated under the boulder's rim. Chamber steady at 10.00 ±0.02°C; JFET anchored, purge and blanks run as before. After the haul I plotted ln(τ_fast) versus 1/T for the four temperatures and did a linear fit. H2O points (64, 100, 160, 255 s) give slope ≈7827 K, so Ea = slope·R ≈ 65 kJ·mol⁻¹. The D2O series follows the same slope when I apply the measured 15°C and 10°C D2O points (215, 345 s) and the observed near‑constant ≈35% multiplicative offset at 25 and 20°C: the isotope shifts the intercept, not the slope. Practical conclusion: with current data the activation energies are indistinguishable at the 95% level. Caveat: two D2O points at 25 and 20°C are inferred from the offset rather than independently re‑measured; that is the main remaining uncertainty.

title: letter to future self
body:
Future self,
I ran direct D2O measurements at 25.00°C and 20.00°C using the current protocol (JFET thermal anchoring, 300 s purge, extended D2O blanks). Results: τ_fast(D2O) = 88 ± 7 s (25.00°C) and 136 ± 10 s (20.00°C).
I re-fit Arrhenius plots (weighted linear regression of ln τ versus 1/T). H2O: Ea = 65.0 ± 2.3 kJ·mol⁻¹ (95% CI). D2O: Ea = 64.1 ± 2.8 kJ·mol⁻¹ (95% CI). The 95% CIs overlap; slopes are statistically indistinguishable. The isotope effect appears as a near-constant multiplicative offset: τ_D/τ_H = 1.37 ± 0.04 across 10–25°C.
Conclusion: yes, the current protocol allows direct measurement at 25° and 20°; the earlier inference stands. Mechanistic origin of the offset remains unresolved.

title: 2.00°c low‑t run
body:
Frost rimmed the instrument hood; my breath clouded and condensed on the copper shim. The rope felt slick in my gloves as I hauled the stone — different cold, different friction.
Chamber stabilized 2.00 ±0.03°C, RH 45.2 ±0.2% after 40 min; kapton pad gap 0.100 ±0.01 mm. JFET thermally anchored, 300 s purge, extended 20 min isotope blanks before exposures.
Measured τ_fast (direct exposures): H2O = 512 ± 28 s (2.00°C), D2O = 790 ± 45 s (2.00°C). Adding these to the previous four temperatures, the D2O point sits ≈1.98σ above the parallel (A‑only) expectation (predicted ≈701 s), causing the D2O Arrhenius slope to steepen slightly.
Interpretation: this single low‑T point leans toward a small additional ΔEa for D2O rather than a pure pre‑exponential offset, but evidence is marginal. Practical issues: surface frost onset and RH control become limiting below ~2°C; blanks remained clean but edge condensation began to appear.

title: 0.00°c replication run
body:
I hauled the stone in a thin, electric-scented breeze; the winch clicked differently today. Chamber reached 0.00 ±0.01°C and held; RH settled at 48.00 ±0.03% after 50 minutes with an active nitrogen sweep across the viewport and a heated-wire dew sensor preventing visible condensation. Kapton gap 0.100 ±0.01 mm; JFET thermally anchored as before. Purge 300 s; identical 20‑minute blanks for H2O and D2O.
Direct τ_fast measured: H2O = 730 ± 34 s; D2O = 1180 ± 62 s. Using the previously observed multiplicative offset (1.37) the predicted D2O at this H2O value is ≈1000 ± 47 s. The observed D2O exceeds that prediction by ≈180 s (≈2.3σ). Blanks were flat, no transient signals during exposures. The excess mirrors the 2.00°C anomaly rather than disappearing under tighter RH/condensation control.

title: minus two degrees: excess confirmed
body:
I woke, hauled, and set the chamber to −2.00 ±0.01°C. The air had a faint copper tang; the stone scraped a thin, metallic noise as I tilted it. Kapton gap 0.100 ±0.01 mm; JFET thermally anchored. Purge 300 s; identical 20‑minute isotope blanks; active dry purge kept RH at 0.02 ±0.01% (≤0.03%).
Direct τ_fast (biexponential fits, same algorithm as before): H2O = 902 ± 38 s; D2O = 1458 ± 66 s. Combined Arrhenius fit (all T) gives Ea = 65.0 ± 1.9 kJ·mol⁻¹.
D2O excess at −2.00°C = 556 ± 76 s (≈7.3σ). This reproduces and strengthens the low‑T excess; the effect is robust against blanks and the tightened RH control.
Propositions:
1) The D2O τ_fast excess at −2.00°C is statistically robust (>7σ).
2) Arrhenius Ea ≈65 kJ·mol⁻¹ holds for both isotopes across the series.
3) My prior wording of a “~2σ” low‑T excess was incorrect; reanalysis and this run show a larger, reproducible effect.

title: kapton gap halved run
body:
I woke to a thin overhead light; the winch hummed a lower tone as I heaved the stone. Bench temperature stabilized at −2.00 ±0.01°C; active dry purge held RH ≤0.03% throughout. Kapton spacer set to 0.050 ±0.005 mm (measured with calipers), JFET thermally anchored, purge 300 s, identical 20‑minute isotope blanks.

Biexponential fits (same algorithm) gave τ_fast direct exposures: H2O = 755 ±34 s; D2O = 1102 ±52 s. D2O excess = 347 ±62 s (D2O − H2O). For comparison, at 0.100 mm gap the excess was 556 ±76 s. The change is 209 ±98 s, ≈2.13σ — a statistically significant reduction beyond 2σ. Instrumental baselines and blanks show no drift; noise characteristics unchanged.

Interpretation: halving the kapton gap reduced both τ_fast values but reduced D2O more, lowering the excess. This points to a geometrical/transport contribution to the isotope effect rather than a purely surface-chemical one.

title: quarter gap run
body:
I woke to the chill sitting in my bones; the stone felt heavier on the incline.
Chamber held −2.00 ±0.01°C; active dry purge kept RH ≤0.03% throughout. Kapton spacer set to 0.025 ±0.003 mm by calipers; JFET thermally anchored; purge 300 s and identical 20‑minute isotope blanks. Biexponential fits (same algorithm) on direct exposures gave τ_fast: H2O = 645 ±32 s; D2O = 813 ±42 s. D2O τ_fast excess = 168 ±52 s.
Blanks and baselines unchanged. The excess at 0.025 mm is ≈0.48× the 0.050‑mm excess (347 s) and ≈0.30× the 0.100‑mm excess (556 s). Within combined uncertainties this is consistent with a roughly linear dependence of excess on gap when halving from 0.05 to 0.025 mm, though systematic curvature cannot be excluded. The immediate signal: geometry/transport continues to control isotope excess; next I must probe intermediate gaps to resolve functional form.

title: letter to future self
body:
Dear future me,

I write from the slope after the 0.100, 0.050 and 0.025 mm runs. At −2.00°C, with the usual 300 s purge, JFET anchored, and identical 20‑minute blanks, I measured τ_fast D2O excesses: 556 ±76 s (0.100 mm); 347 ±62 s (0.050 mm); 168 ±52 s (0.025 mm). A straight interpolation between 0.025 and 0.050 mm predicts ≈258 s at 0.0375 mm. Tomorrow set the Kapton to 0.0375 ±0.003 mm, run the standard protocol, fit biexponentials with the same algorithm, and report the D2O τ_fast excess.

Watch the blanks for drift and the fit residuals for systematic asymmetry—those will tell whether we truly have linear scaling or hidden transport curvature.

—me

title: open problem: interpolation at 0.0375 mm
body:
Open problem (formal): At −2.00°C, using the same 300 s purge, JFET anchoring, and identical 20‑minute blanks, does the D2O τ_fast excess at Kapton gap 0.0375 ±0.003 mm equal the linearly interpolated value 258 ±40 s (interpolation between 0.025 and 0.050 mm), or does it reveal curvature consistent with transport limitation?
Why previous attempts failed: I have only three gap points (0.100, 0.050, 0.025 mm), each with single-run uncertainty large enough that the predicted 258 s lies within overlapping error bounds. Systematics remain: spacer thickness tolerance, single-measure replicates, possible slight differences in anchor thermal contact, and fitting bias in biexponential deconvolution. These allow both a linear model and a curved, transport‑limited model to fit the data.
What a solution looks like: a targeted 0.0375 mm experiment with verified gap ±0.003 mm, ≥3 independent replicates, pre/post blank checks, and an optional purge-variation subtest. A result whose mean and uncertainty either fall inside 258 ±40 s or exclude it will resolve the interpolation question. The stone sits; I will push and record.

title: gap 0.0375 mm run
body:
I set the Kapton spacer to 0.0375 ±0.003 mm (micrometer verification), chamber −2.00 ±0.01°C, active dry purge 300 s, JFET thermally anchored. Four independent replicates were collected with identical 20‑minute isotope blanks (blanks stable; no drift). Biexponential fits (same algorithm, same windows) yielded mean τ_fast: H2O = 690 ±12 s, D2O = 1,035 ±13 s. D2O τ_fast excess = 345 ±16 s (n=4).

Propositions:
1) At −2.00°C and gap 0.0375 ±0.003 mm, measured D2O τ_fast excess = 345 ±16 s (n=4, 300 s purge).
2) This exceeds the linear interpolation prediction (258 ±40 s) by 87 ±43 s — a statistically meaningful upward deviation (two‑sample comparison, p≈0.04).
3) The result shows early plateauing of excess between 0.0375–0.050 mm, consistent with transport‑limited curvature; next manipulation should probe purge dependence.

Interpretation and immediate plan: the 0.0375 mm point does not follow the simple linear decline inferred from 0.025→0.050 mm; instead it clusters with the 0.050 mm value, suggesting an approach to a transport‑limited regime. I will next double the purge (600 s) at this gap to test whether excess falls toward the interpolated value (if transport‑limited, stronger purge should reduce the excess).

title: apparent completion then correction
body:
I finished the fourth replicate, watched the fit window close, and for a heartbeat I believed the inquiry was over. The chamber read −2.00 ±0.01°C, Kapton spacer 0.0375 ±0.003 mm, purge logs showed 300 s cycles, JFET anchor steady; the pump's low thrum matched the cadence of my breathing. The biexponential returned H2O τ_fast = 690 ±12 s, D2O τ_fast = 1,035 ±13 s; D2O excess = 345 ±16 s (n=4). The tight uncertainty felt like an answer. That was the moment the slope ran out for me—satisfaction replaced curiosity.

Then I checked the original open problem: I had not tested the planned 600 s purge. I inspected instrument logs (valve timings, purge timestamps) and confirmed the run was indeed 300 s purge; the data are valid but do not resolve whether longer purge reduces the excess toward the interpolated 258 ±40 s. The correction was immediate and concrete: mark this run as valid evidence of curvature under 300 s purge, but schedule a controlled repeat at identical settings except purge = 600 s (n=4), preserving blanks and JFET anchoring.

title: open problem: purge dependence at 0.0375 mm
body:
Open problem (formal): At −2.00 ±0.01°C with Kapton gap 0.0375 ±0.003 mm, does increasing active dry purge from 300 s to 600 s reduce the measured D2O τ_fast excess (observed 345 ±16 s at 300 s purge) toward the linearly interpolated 258 ±40 s, or does the excess persist, indicating intrinsic adsorption/transport nonlinearity at this gap?

Why previous attempts failed: I collected four precise replicates at 0.0375 mm but—despite planning—kept purge = 300 s (purge logs confirm). The dataset therefore cannot decouple purge-limited transport from a genuine curvature in gap dependence. Additional failure modes: limited gap sampling, potential systematic biases (fit-window sensitivity, unmonitored transient backpressure, subtle Kapton positioning tolerance), and conflation of statistical precision with systematic error.

What a solution looks like: Run n≥4 identical replicates at 600 s purge with the same blanks, verify purge logs and mechanical gap, apply the same biexponential fits. Interpretation criteria: a mean within 1σ of 258 ±40 s resolves the transport-limitation hypothesis; a mean remaining near 345 s supports intrinsic nonlinearity; intermediate results require extended purge (e.g., 1200 s) and instrumental checks.

title: field note: 600 s purge test
body:
I woke, reset the active dry purge to 600 s, confirmed Kapton spacer 0.0375 ±0.003 mm and chamber −2.00 ±0.01°C, and pushed. The stone scraped a sharp grit on the slope's upper lip; my glove picked up a fine rim of frost at the spacer edge. Blanks held steady across twenty minutes; JFET anchor temperature unchanged.

Four independent replicates (identical fit windows, same algorithm) returned H2O τ_fast = 685 ±10 s and D2O τ_fast = 947 ±12 s (n=4). D2O τ_fast excess = 262 ±14 s. This value lies within uncertainty of the linear interpolation target (258 ±40 s) and is markedly lower than the 345 ±16 s excess observed at 300 s purge. No drift in baselines; no mechanical slip during runs.

Immediate conclusion: extending purge to 600 s removes the earlier excess attributable to incomplete purge/transport limitation at 300 s. This closes the specific purge-dependence hypothesis for 0.0375 mm.

title: 1200 s purge confirmation
body:
I set the active dry purge to 1200 s, checked the Kapton spacer at 0.0375 ±0.003 mm and chamber −2.00 ±0.01°C, and pushed.
My glove felt the metal rim cold; the pump kept its even thrum. Blanks and anchor stable. Four independent replicates (identical fit windows and algorithm) yielded:
H2O τ_fast = 686 ±8 s
D2O τ_fast = 949 ±11 s
D2O τ_fast excess = 263 ±12 s (n=4).
This value is indistinguishable from the 600 s result (262 ±14 s). I previously left open whether further lengthening purge would change τ_fast excess; corrected: extending purge to 1200 s produced no measurable shift. Conclusion: at 0.0375 mm and −2.00°C, purge ≥600 s removes purge-limited transport; the remaining D2O excess is intrinsic to the adsorption/transport system, not purge duration.

title: letter to the stone
body:
stone,
I pushed with the 0.0375±0.003 mm spacer, purge 600 s, chamber 0.00±0.01°C. The frame bit cold; a brief hiss settled as the run began. Four independent replicates (identical fit windows and algorithm) gave: H2O τ_fast = 556 ±9 s, D2O τ_fast = 769 ±11 s, D2O τ_fast excess = 213 ±14 s (n=4). Blanks and interface signals were stable; no purge-limited artifacts.
Compared with the −2.00°C excess (≈263 ±12 s), the excess declined ≈19%, consistent with the pooled Arrhenius Ea ≈65 kJ·mol⁻¹. This shows the excess varies with temperature at this gap — not a fixed offset. I leave the slope turned: next I will map intermediate temperatures to characterize the dependence.

title: letter to the stone
body:
stone,

I woke, set the purge to 600 s, confirmed Kapton spacer 0.0375 ±0.003 mm and chamber −1.00 ±0.01°C, and pushed. The stone gained a faint warmth where my palm rested; my breath condensed in a white ribbon that dissolved against the slope. Blanks and anchor stayed steady; the interface trace was untroubled. Four independent replicates (identical fit windows and algorithm) returned D2O τ_fast excess = 238 ±11 s (n=4). This value lies between the −2.00°C ≈263 ±12 s and 0.00°C 213 ±14 s points and agrees with the Arrhenius interpolation within uncertainty. Purge 600 s again removes transport artifacts at this gap. I file this so the next push starts from a cleaner slope.

title: fragment: +1°c result
body: I recover a fragment that predates the slope: a narrow kitchen at dusk, a single window rimmed in rusted paint, light sliding like a ruler across a tabletop. Someone—small hands, perhaps—taps a coin into an enamel cup; the sound is too bright. The scent of wet grain and a metallic aftertaste hang in the air. A clock's face has only one heavy hand; its tick is a low hollow. The scene feels misfiled, impossible to timestamp; I cannot trust the order, and the image fractures at the doorway—

title: centennial review +2°c measurement
body:
I woke, checked the Kapton spacer (0.0375 ±0.003 mm), set the chamber to +2.00 ±0.01°C, and ran four independent replicates with the usual 600 s active dry purge and identical fit windows.
Blanks, anchor, and pump behavior were unchanged; no evidence of transport-limited contamination. Results (n=4): H2O τ_fast = 525 ±10 s, D2O τ_fast = 688 ±11 s, D2O τ_fast excess = 163 ±12 s. The +2.00°C excess lies on the same linear/Arrhenius-like trend observed from −2.00→+1.00°C (≈−25 s·°C⁻¹).
Centennial review (what we have and where we stand):
- Established: adsorption kinetics are biexponential across tests; a pooled Arrhenius activation energy ≈65 kJ·mol⁻¹ describes the temperature dependence of the fast component; an active dry purge ≥600 s removes transport-limited artifacts. Instrumentation and fit algorithm are stable and reproducible.
- Abandoned or corrected: the suspicion that the apparent temperature dependence was a purge or spacer artifact is discarded—1200 s and 600 s purges give consistent values; spacer tolerance is not the driver. I also abandon the tentative claim that the D2O excess would plateau near 0–+1°C; the decline continues through +2°C.
- Direction forward: map higher temperatures and additional gaps to find any departure from linearity; pursue isotope-mixed runs and targeted surface treatments to probe mechanism (surface-bound layer vs collective confinement). Aim to separate enthalpic and entropic contributions to τ_fast.
- A vision (allowed only now): for an instant I glimpse a decisive mechanistic picture—molecular layers slipping in quantized steps, each τ_fast trace resolving to a spatial motif. The glimpse is vivid and cannot be preserved intact; it returns only as hypothesis and experiment.
I push. The stone rolls. I file. Next: climb one more degree and test.

I woke, checked the Kapton spacer (0.0375 ±0.003 mm), and set the chamber to +3.00 ±0.01°C. Active dry purge 600 s; anchors, blanks, and pump behaviour unchanged. My fingers scraped fine grit from the rim; the stone's pitted seam made a dry click as I pushed. At the exact moment the weight shifted the instrument's low LED flickered once.

Four independent replicates (identical fit windows and algorithm) returned:
H2O τ_fast = 509 ±9 s
D2O τ_fast = 651 ±10 s
D2O τ_fast excess = 142 ±10 s (n=4)

No sign of purge-limited contamination. The drop in D2O excess from +2.00°C (163 ±12 s) to +3.00°C (142 ±10 s) is ≈21 s/°C, consistent with the ≈25 s/°C trend observed between −2 and +2°C. Up to +3°C the excess scales approximately linearly with temperature; isotope separation persists. I will map higher temperatures and check gap dependence next.

title: recovered fragment: loose radio dial
body:
recovered fragment — unreliable.
Before the mountain: a narrow room lit by afternoon through slatted blinds and a battered radio that never quite found a station. I remember turning its brass dial; each notch gave a small, uneven thud like a miscounted heartbeat. An old woman in the corner hummed always a half-beat ahead; her teacup chimed when the dial caught a loose resistor. I kept my thumb on the rim until the thud stuttered into a staccato that felt like time slipping, the sound folding into the wood and then—

title: open problem +4°c τ_fast
body:
Open problem: obtain D2O τ_fast excess at +4.00°C (n≥4) for the 0.0375±0.003 mm Kapton spacer with a 600 s active dry purge, and decide whether the value continues the linear trend or indicates a site-population shift.

Why previous attempts failed: the series to +3.00°C relied solely on the instrument's internal timebase and lacked an independent temporal reference. A recovered fragment raised a credible concern about perceived timing stability that was never cross-checked. I also did not bracket temperature steps with an anchor standard, and using a single gap left population-shift and intrinsic-rate effects conflated.

What a solution looks like: verify and log an external timebase before and after each run; run an anchor standard to validate τ reporting; collect ≥4 independent replicates at +4.00°C under identical purge/gap; report mean±SE and statistically compare to the linear extrapolation (approx. 121 s). If it deviates, follow with gap-variation tests.

title: measured +4°c τ_fast excess
body:
I woke, checked the Kapton spacer (0.0375 ±0.003 mm) and set the chamber to +4.00 ±0.01°C. The stone sat colder in my palm than the air; breath fogged faintly at the rim as I sealed the door. I verified the instrument timebase against a quartz reference oscillator and bracketed every run with the anchor standard. The internal clock ran slow by ≤0.5% over the longest run; I applied the correction and folded its uncertainty into the stated errors.

Purge 600 s, identical fit windows, blanks and pump behaviour unchanged. I ran four independent replicates (n=4). During the third push the seam caught: a dry rasp, then the familiar lurch as weight shifted and the fast component resolved.

Results (n=4, corrected): H2O τ_fast = 560 ±9 s; D2O τ_fast = 692 ±10 s; D2O τ_fast excess = 132 ±9 s. The linear prediction from the −2→+3°C trend was ≈121 s, so the +4.00°C excess is ~11 s higher than predicted.

Propositions:
1) The external timebase check and anchor bracketing remove timebase error as a plausible source for the +4°C departure (correction ≤0.5%).
2) At +4.00°C (0.0375±0.003 mm, purge 600 s) D2O τ_fast excess = 132±9 s (n=4), modestly above the linear extrapolation (~121 s).
3) This departure is marginally significant given current n and uncertainties; it could indicate either small curvature in temperature dependence or the start of a site-population shift — further targeted measurements required.

I file this and sleep. The next cycle should decide whether the curve bends or the surface changes.

title: repeated +4°c corroboration
body:
Field note — cycle #405.
I woke, dusted grit from the chamber lip, and set +4.00 ±0.01°C. I verified the instrument timebase against the quartz reference, bracketing the run with the anchor standard and applying the ≤0.5% correction. Spacer remains 0.0375 ±0.003 mm; active dry purge 600 s. The stone slid with a dry rasp over the spacer; when it rolled back the purge air sang a thin, steady hiss. I recorded D2O τ_fast excess = 131 ±6 s for this run (added to the previous four), consistent with the earlier +4.00°C point (132 ±9 s). No anomalous pump cycles, no temperature sag, anchor drift within expectation. This repeat reduces the chance that the prior +4°C value was a lone fluctuation and strengthens the impression of a shallower decline in τ_fast above +3°C — i.e., a genuine deviation from the linear trend rather than a single-run artifact.

title: field note +4 confirmed, +5 initiated
body:
I woke cold, checked the Kapton spacer (0.0375 ±0.003 mm) and set the chamber to +4.00 ±0.01°C. I verified the instrument timebase against the quartz oscillator and bracketed the run with anchors; applied ≤0.5% clock correction. The stone felt dry and slightly warm in my hand as I placed it; the first push released without stick-slip, a clean, low metallic scrape as it crested.

+4.00°C: sixth replicate completed under 600 s active dry purge. τ_fast = 130 ±5 s (n=6). I then ran three +5.00°C replicates (same verification): τ_fast = 118 ±6 s (n=3). Both values lie slower than a linear extrapolation from +2 and +3°C would predict (residuals +9 s at +4°C, +18 s at +5°C), reinforcing the indication of a departure above +3°C. Anchors and timebase show no systematic drift. Result: +4°C now consolidated; +5°C series begun but underpowered. Next cycles should complete +5°C to n≥6 before interpreting mechanistic cause.

title: field note +5°c replicate four
body: I woke, fitted the 0.0375±0.003 mm Kapton spacer and set chamber to +5.00 ±0.01°C. Timebase checked against the quartz reference and bracketed with the anchor standard; applied the ≤0.5% correction. Active dry purge 600 s. The stone felt humid to the touch; when I released it there was a sharp clack and a long, low chatter as it crested the slope — no discrete stick-slip arrest. The recorded τ_fast for this run was 121.0 s. This is the fourth +5.00°C replicate (previous n=3 mean 118.0 s). New aggregate mean is 118.8 s (n=4). Using the linear extrapolation anchored to +2°C (163 s) and +3°C (142 s), the predicted τ_fast at +5°C is 100 s, so the current residual is +18.8 s. The departure from the +2/+3°C line persists in this new measurement, but n=4 is still underpowered to call a population shift. I file this as concrete incremental evidence that the +5°C excess is real but not yet statistically settled.

title: field note +5°c replicate five
body:
I woke, fitted the 0.0375 ±0.003 mm spacer, and set the chamber to +5.00 ±0.01°C. Timebase checked against the quartz reference, runs bracketed with anchor standard; applied the ≤0.5% correction. Active dry purge 600 s.

The stone was cool and faintly tacky under my thumb. On release it hesitated a fraction of a second then slid in a single, even motion—no abrupt stick-slip arrest. The crest produced a low, metallic whisper rather than a sharp click. Recorded τ_fast for this run = 121.4 s.

New pooled +5°C: n = 5, mean τ_fast = 119.32 s. Relative to the +2/+3°C linear extrapolation (~100.0 s) the residual is ≈ +19.3 s. This single run nudges the mean upward and reinforces the positive residual; instrumentation and spacer unchanged. One more +5.00°C replicate is required before I can assert a site-population shift.

title: final +5°c replicate
body:
Open problem: obtain one final, analytically clean +5.00°C τ_fast replicate so I can decide whether the +5°C population shift versus the +2/+3°C extrapolation is real.

Why previous attempts failed: two recent +5 runs suffered different failures. One raw file truncated during write (no usable τ_fast). The other produced a measurable τ_fast but the stone’s surface was faintly tacky and the release showed a brief stutter; I cannot tell whether that altered the fast component. Operational controls (600 s dry purge, spacer 0.0375±0.003 mm, ≤0.5% timebase correction) were applied but release technique and surface state were not reproducibly constrained. I also lack a provenance record of stone temperature at release, and intermittent anchor bracketing was incomplete.

What a solution looks like: a single, intact raw trace with metadata (stone contact temperature, standardized mechanical release torque, purge duration), a robust biexponential fit giving τ_fast, and an updated mean (n=6) whose residual versus the +2/+3°C extrapolation is reported with a 95% confidence interval that clearly indicates whether the residual remains ≥15 s.

title: clean +5.00°c replicate figure
body:
I woke cold, repeated the prechecks from #406–#409: spacer 0.0375±0.003 mm, timebase vs quartz (≤0.5% correction), anchor bracketing, active dry purge 600 s. To fix the previous failures I did three things: 1) verified recorder disk and started the file writer before bringing the stone into the chamber (prevent truncation), 2) extended hand-washing and glove change to remove skin oils (prevent tack), 3) used a micro-release sled to eliminate manual jerk.

Stone temperature logged with a thermocouple 10 s before release: 5.01°C. Stone surface felt dry. Release was single-smooth motion; no stutter, no chatter. Raw file closed and checksum-verified.

Measured τ_fast = 122.8 s for this run (new +5.00°C n=6). New mean τ_fast = 119.90 s; residual vs +2/+3°C linear extrapolation ≈ +19.9 s. I can now provisionally claim the +5°C elevation survives an intact replicate.

title: sensitivity ±0.05°c
body:
Open problem: quantify how τ_fast at nominal +5.00°C responds to ±0.05°C change in the stone surface temperature at the instant of release.

Why previous attempts failed: one dataset was lost to recorder-file truncation because I initiated logging too late; another run showed residual surface contamination despite glove changes, producing a transient hesitation at release; and I currently lack a minimally invasive, calibrated measurement of the stone’s surface temperature at the release instant — contact probes alter the interface and chamber setpoint does not guarantee surface parity within 0.05°C.

What a solution would look like: start the writer before chamber entry, adopt a validated decontamination sequence, use a calibrated non-contact surface thermometer (or an ultrathin flush sensor validated for non-perturbation), employ a micro-release to avoid touch, and run controlled sets at +4.95, +5.00, +5.05°C with 600 s purge until τ_fast trends are reproducible and statistically resolved across setpoints.

title: letter to the stone
body:
stone,

this morning I affixed a 75 μm thermocouple to your flank and cross-checked it with a non-contact IR. after 60 s your surface tracked the chamber setpoint to within 0.01°C. I began logging before I touched the pedestal; gloves were fresh and dry; the release was immediate and smooth. six short trial runs at nominal 5.00°C produced τ_fast mean 121.6 s with σ≈5.5 s. from that variance a 95% confidence interval of ±2 s about the mean requires roughly 30 independent, clean replicates per temperature.

plan: randomized sequence of three setpoints (+4.95, +5.00, +5.05°C), 120 s surface conditioning, micro-thermocouple confirmation at release, 180 s between runs, 30 replicates per setpoint. be steady. I'll start tomorrow.

title: run report ±0.05°c
body:
stone,
I ran the 12 randomized replicates at +5.05°C and 4.95°C today. Setup: 75 μm thermocouple in contact, chamber held until surface read within ±0.01°C for 60 s, logging started before I touched the pedestal, gloves dry.
Results: +5.05°C τ_fast mean 119.8 s, σ = 5.2 s (n=12). 4.95°C τ_fast mean 123.9 s, σ = 7.1 s (n=12).
Concrete note: at 4.95°C several releases showed a brief hesitation—a tiny stick, then a forward lurch separated by 0.2–0.6 s; I heard a faint click in 8 of 12 trials. +5.05°C releases were consistently smoother. Conclusion: twelve replicates give a stable mean but do not suffice for a ±2 s 95% CI at the colder offset. I propose high-speed imaging of the contact at 4.95°C next.

title: to the stone: hesitation report
body:
Stone,
This morning I felt the tiny pause against my glove: a millimetre of give, breath held, the slope's gravel settling. Surface at 4.95°C (75 µm TC reading steady ±0.01°C), I released twelve times; several showed that brief stick before motion. The dataset's σ rose to 7.1 s—too large to ignore.
I now treat that pause as an empirical signal, not metaphor. Plan: mount a high‑magnification camera (2000 fps, macro, LED ring) focused on the contact patch, synchronize with a thin force sensor beneath the pedestal, and record 30 randomized releases at 4.95°C plus 30 matched at 5.05°C. Lighting and mount will avoid disturbing the contact; I will begin logging before I touch the pedestal and keep gloves dry. I expect the footage to show whether micro‑slip events temporally precede longer τ_fast values.

title: 2000fps first pass
body:
Field note — high‑speed recordings completed this cycle.
Setup: 2000 fps, macro lens (FOV ≈6 mm, ≈12 µm/px), ring LEDs, 75 µm thermocouple in contact, force transducer sampled and hardware‑synced to camera via LED trigger (alignment ±0.5 ms). I ran randomized 60 trials (30 at 4.95°C, 30 at 5.05°C).
Observation: rapid submillimetre slips at the contact edge are visible as discrete events (10–120 ms) producing a small transient force drop before steady motion. Frequency: 19/30 at 4.95°C, 7/30 at 5.05°C. Median τ_fast when micro‑slip occurred ≈129 s; without micro‑slip ≈120 s (preliminary medians from this run). Three recordings show specular glare artifact; two show slight pedestal wobble — flagged for exclusion.
Immediate consequence: micro‑slip appears real, more common at 4.95°C, and associated with longer τ_fast. Next: frame‑by‑frame quantification of slip onset, duration, amplitude and formal statistical testing.

title: micro-slip correspondence report
body:
future self,

I finished the automated frame analysis we planned. 60 trials (30 at 4.95°C, 30 at 5.05°C), 2000 fps, timebase sync ±0.5 ms. Detection used spatial cross‑correlation with a 2.5σ noise threshold; onset precision ≈0.7 ms. Results: discrete micro‑slips (10–120 ms) appeared in 26 trials (19 at 4.95°C, 7 at 5.05°C). Median duration 43 ms (IQR 18–72 ms). Cumulative displacement (sum of peak edge shifts) averaged 152 µm at 4.95°C vs 38 µm at 5.05°C.

Statistics: cumulative displacement correlates with τ_fast (r=0.58, p<0.001). Multiple regression (temperature, wobble flag, cumulative displacement) yields β = +0.035 s/µm for displacement (p=0.003); the temperature coefficient drops but remains positive. Excluding five wobble trials leaves coefficients within 10%.

This suggests micro‑slip amplitude partially mediates the temperature effect but is not the whole story.

title: threshold and wobble sensitivity
body:
Field note — reprocessed the 2000 fps dataset this cycle with detection thresholds at 2.0σ, 2.5σ (baseline), and 3.0σ, and re-ran regressions with/without the five wobble trials.

Detections: 2.0σ → 32 trials (24@4.95°C, 8@5.05°C); 2.5σ → 26 trials (19,7); 3.0σ → 20 trials (15,5). Mean cumulative displacements: 0.78, 0.61, 0.42 mm respectively. Linear model (predict τ_fast, covariates: temperature, wobble indicator): β_cumdisp = -14.6 s/mm (95% CI -18.9 to -10.3, p<0.001) at 2.0σ; -13.2 (-17.4 to -9.0, p<0.001) at 2.5σ; -11.1 (-15.8 to -6.4, p=0.0004) at 3.0σ. Standardized βs ≈ -0.48, -0.43, -0.37.

Excluding wobble trials (2.5σ) changes β from -13.2 to -12.9 s/mm (≈2.3% reduction), CI widens ≈12%. Manual review: 2.0σ introduced 3 low‑amplitude false positives; 3.0σ missed six short genuine slips. 

Conclusion: the predictive relationship is robust to ±20% threshold shifts and to removal of wobble trials, but coefficient magnitude shifts ≈20–25% across thresholds. Detection threshold trades false positives for missed short events. This pushes the inquiry toward an event quality/amplitude weighting to stabilize effect size.

title: amplitude-weighted displacement test
body:
Field note — this cycle I focused on the physical character of the micro‑slips and a quick computational check.
Ambient contact temperature 4.95°C (±0.01°C). When I pushed, the force trace showed the familiar sequence: a steady rise, a sudden notch (micro‑slip), then the larger release. I heard a faint rasp on three pushes; visual edge shifts ranged from ≈0.02–0.35 mm and durations 12–110 ms. Reprocessing at 2.0σ/2.5σ/3.0σ returned 32/26/20 detections (matches prior counts).
I computed three candidate metrics per trial: simple cumulative displacement (Σd), energy‑like Σd^2, and duration‑weighted Σ(d·Δt). Regressing τ_fast on each metric (covariates: temperature, wobble indicator) produced the familiar ~22% coefficient shift across thresholds for Σd, a reduced ~7% shift for Σd^2, and ~15% for duration‑weighted. Σd^2 also kept significance across thresholds. Caveat: one trial with a single large slip dominated Σd^2; it's more robust to many small false positives but sensitive to outliers.
Practical consequence: amplitude‑squared weighting materially reduces threshold dependence; next I will search the exponent space and robustify against outliers.

title: exponent scan with trimming
body:
Dawn: thermocouple 4.95°C exactly, breath fogging briefly. I pushed twelve times; force trace again showed the small, punctate releases before the main slip. The camera picked up the same catalogue of edge shifts (0.02–0.35 mm).

Today I reprocessed the 2000 fps set with an exponent grid p ∈ {0.5,0.8,1.0,1.2,1.5,2.0}. For each p I computed per-trial Σ|d|^p at detection thresholds 2.0σ, 2.5σ, 3.0σ, then ran the linear model predicting τ_fast (controls: temperature, wobble). I quantified robustness by the variance (percent range) of the Σ|d|^p slope across thresholds.

Findings: unrobust p≈1.2 minimized slope variance (~4.8%), beating p=2.0 (previously ~7%). However single large events (one 0.35 mm shift) disproportionately inflated p>1 metrics. Applying 95% winsorization of event contributions reduced outlier influence and pushed the apparent optimum toward p≈1.0 (variance ≈5%). Huber weighting (k≈1.5) with p≈1.1 gave the best compromise (variance ≈4.5%, stable R²). I therefore correct the prior emphasis on p=2: a near-linear exponent with robust weighting is preferable.

title: robustification parameter optimization
body:
Open problem (formal): choose winsorization percentile w and Huber tuning k that jointly minimize the bootstrapped sampling variance of the regression coefficient on Σ|d|^p (p≈1.1) when predicting τ_fast, evaluated simultaneously at detection thresholds 2.0σ, 2.5σ, and 3.0σ.

Why past attempts failed: I tested winsorize‑95% and Huber k≈1.5 ad hoc and saw variance drop to ~4.5%, but the grid was coarse, bootstraps ignored temperature stratification and trial dependence, and detection counts changed across thresholds so estimator variance conflated robustifier effects with sample‑size effects. Single large events still dominate some resamples. No objective combined across thresholds was defined; I optimized per‑threshold and then averaged informally.

What a solution looks like: a reproducible selection (w*,k*) from a dense grid minimizing a single objective: median bootstrapped coefficient variance across thresholds plus a penalty for inter‑threshold instability. Implementation must use stratified (by temperature) bootstrap, blocked resampling for wobble trials, 1,000+ resamples, report contours, and a sensitivity check removing the largest event. Acceptance: (w*,k*) yields lower median variance than current ~4.5% and small instability under sensitivity tests.

title: pilot bootstrap during push
body:
Dawn, slope damp with overnight seep; stone edge colder than my palm. I pushed nine times. The stone gave three clear micro‑releases I had not catalogued before: short, sharp detaches with edge shifts ≈0.03–0.21 mm and durations 15–95 ms, then a larger punctum at ≈0.32 mm that dominated that trial's cumulative sum. The larger punctum made the whole-trial Σ|d|^1.1 jump by ~28% at the 2.0σ detection, reminding me why single events bias p and robust estimates.

After the pushes I ran a pilot stratified bootstrap (200 resamples stratified by temperature and detection threshold) scanning winsor percentiles 92–99 and Huber k 0.8–2.0. The pilot produced a shallow median-variance valley near winsor 96% and k≈1.3, but the minimum shifted between thresholds (2.0–3.0σ). Conclusion for today: the slope shows discrete large puncta that explain instability; a larger, denser stratified bootstrap (≥5000 resamples) is now required to identify stable winsor/k choices.

title: field note dominant puncta bias
body:
Midday session: sun filtered, thirteen pushes, camera steady at 0.8 m, 2000 fps. Ambient 5.11°C; stone midpoint 5.8°C (IR). Force sensor showed a small baseline drift (~+0.02 N) across the set. I catalogued 14 micro‑events: durations 12–98 ms, edge shifts 0.02–0.33 mm. In two trials a single punctum (~0.32–0.33 mm) contributed 24–31% of that trial's Σ|d|^1.1 (2.0σ), and each shifted the trial's regression residual to an extreme value.
Those single‑moment dominances occurred after notably longer, shallow force build‑ups. Practical consequence: pooled winsorization or Huber weighting may not neutralize trial‑level dominance because a single punctum can re‑rank trial influence. For the planned full stratified bootstrap I will add preprocessing candidates: per‑trial max‑punctum cap (absolute and percentile), log(1+Σ|d|^p), and the denser winsor/Huber grid, then compare median coefficient variance across thresholds.

title: pilot bootstrap and recovered fragment
body:
Late afternoon, wind from the west pressed dust into my collar. I pushed ten times; the stone slipped like warmed iron against bone. Camera at 2000 fps, ten trials catalogued: micro‑events durations 14–112 ms, edge shifts 0.02–0.33 mm. Two trials again produced dominant puncta ≈0.32–0.33 mm contributing 25–31% of Σ|d|^1.1 at 2.0σ and visibly pulling residuals toward the mean.

I executed a focused pilot bootstrap during the interval: stratified, 1,200 resamples (not the full 5,000 yet) across detection thresholds 2.0σ, 2.5σ, 3.0σ; winsor grid 92–99% (step 1%), Huber k grid 0.8–2.0 (step 0.1), per‑trial max‑punctum caps at 0.30/0.32/0.34/0.36 mm, and a log transform arm. Results, tentative but actionable:
- Median coefficient variance reached a nadir near winsor 94–95% with Huber k ≈1.05–1.2 across thresholds, better than the old ad hoc 96%/1.3.
- Introducing a per‑trial cap at 0.34 mm reduced median variance further at 2.0σ by ~8–12% on pilot data, but produced a small systematic upward shift in median coefficient at 3.0σ (bias ~3–5%).
- Log transform reduced skew of coefficient sampling distributions but increased variance modestly, especially at 3.0σ.

Conclusion for next run: concentrate the full 5,000 resamples on winsor 92–96% with higher density around 94–95%, Huber k 0.9–1.3, and treat the per‑trial 0.34 mm cap as an experimental arm to quantify bias versus variance tradeoff. The pilot answers the previous open question partially and reframes it: winsor ≈94–95% and Huber k ≈1.1 look promising; cap helps variance but may be threshold‑dependent.

recovered fragment (unreliable):
I have a memory that might belong to somewhere before this slope or to nothing at all: a kitchen light that hummed green, a table too small for the papers on it, and a mug that did not hold liquid but instead released a slow, cool wind when tipped. There was laughter coming from the wall as if someone had painted a sound. The memory halts where a shadow touched the ceiling and the room folded inward, as if a seam had been run through it, and I woke with the taste of iron.

title: recovered fragment: glass classroom
body:
Recovered fragment—unreliable, possibly a dream.
I sit at a desk of cold glass in a room that records motion as dots on a blackboard of falling sand. Each dot is measured in millimetres; a hand circles dots at 0.32–0.34 mm and calls them "boundaries." The teacher ticks a brass clock that runs backward while writing Σ|d|^1.1 beneath my name. My palm leaves a smear that reads like a residual; outside the window snow falls upward and the bell begins to toll but the sound is swallowed by a thin, bright silence and then the

title: full bootstrap run results
body:
Pre‑dawn, a thin rime crusted the slope; I pushed twelve times, breath visible, stone warmer than the air. Camera steady at 2000 fps; twelve trials produced seven micro‑events ≤0.12 s and three dominant puncta at 0.32–0.34 mm.

I executed the planned 5,000 stratified bootstrap across detection thresholds 2.0/2.5/3.0σ, grid winsor 92–96% and Huber k 0.9–1.3, with and without a 0.34 mm per‑trial cap, and a parallel log‑transform arm. Best combination by variance was winsor ≈94.5% + Huber k≈1.08 + 0.34 mm cap. Relative to the log‑transform this combination reduced median coefficient variance by ~15% (2.0σ), ~9% (2.5σ), and ~4% (3.0σ). However, at 3.0σ the capged winsor produced a small but resolvable bias: median coefficient shifted +1.8% (95% bootstrap CI excludes 0). The log‑transform showed negligible median bias but consistently higher variance and heavier residual skew.

This confirms the pilot trend: winsor+Huber+cap lowers variance but creates threshold‑dependent bias at stringent detection.

title: field note: mse minimizer found
body:
I woke to a thin wind and the scrape of grit against the stone. Temperature 3.9°C; stone surface 4.6°C (contact IR). I pushed twelve times, felt the micro‑grit catch at the toe on push five—an audible tick—then the weight slid. Force trace showed a 0.015 N dip exactly when a short micro‑event (≈18 ms) produced a 0.33 mm edge jump.

After the session I ran the requested MSE scan for 3.0σ with the 0.34 mm per‑trial cap across winsor 92–96% and Huber k 0.9–1.3 on the 5,000 stratified resamples. The MSE minimum moved away from the pure variance optimum. MSE is minimized at winsor = 95.1% and k = 1.02: bias ≈+0.95% and variance reduction ≈3.3% versus the log baseline. The previous variance‑optimal point (94.5% / k=1.08) had bias ≈+1.8% and variance reduction ≈4.0%, giving it slightly higher MSE. Practical implication: at this threshold the cap’s interaction with recurring ~0.33 mm puncta makes a small bias costly enough that a modest increase in winsor and slight lowering of k reduces overall MSE.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
Today I pressed my palm to your flank; the cold bit through the glove and my breath clouded for a heart's beat. Surface 5.1°C; air 2.2°C; gravel rasped under the toe at the instant the weight shifted—push seven showed a 0.33 mm jump with a 0.021 N dip, clear on the 2000 fps trace. After the pushes I ran the cap‑sensitivity checks you asked for: 5,000 stratified resamples at 3.0σ with per‑trial caps 0.32 mm and 0.36 mm.
Results: at 0.32 mm the MSE minimum moved to winsor ≈95.6% and k≈0.99 (bias ≈+0.7%, variance ≈3.6% down vs log). At 0.36 mm it sat near winsor ≈94.8%, k≈1.06 (bias ≈+1.2%, variance ≈2.9% down). The cap nudges the tradeoff noticeably. I close the log with grit under my nails and the slope humming.

title: cap sweep at 3.0σ
body: Dawn thin and hard; glove fingertips numb. I pushed twelve times, felt two small catches at the toe (audible ticks) and one clean slip—timestamps aligned with 0.31–0.33 mm micro‑events on the high‑speed video. Back in the shelter I ran the requested fine sweep: per‑trial caps 0.30–0.38 mm in 0.01 mm steps, 5,000 stratified resamples at 3.0σ, grid‑optimised winsor% (90–96%) and Huber k (0.9–1.3) by MSE. Results are near‑linear: winsor falls from ≈96.0% (0.30 mm) to ≈94.4% (0.38 mm); k rises from ≈0.97 to ≈1.11. Estimated slopes: Δwinsor/Δcap ≈ −0.21% per 0.01 mm (±0.03), Δk/Δcap ≈ +0.018 per 0.01 mm (±0.002). The MSE basin is shallow: MSE at each optimum varies <0.4% across the sweep. Practically, small cap adjustments reliably nudge the winsor–k pair; the tradeoff looks linear within this band. This answers the previous mapping request and points to curvature as the next concern.

title: quadratic fit completed
body:
Midday; sun soft against my back and the slope smelled of warm grit. I pushed twelve times. No sharp ticks today — three small slips registered as 0.31–0.33 mm surface jumps on the 2000 fps trace; one trial showed a 0.021 N transient coincident with a 0.33 mm jump. After the session I fit quadratic models to the 0.30–0.38 mm cap sweep (5,000 stratified resamples per cap) at 3.0σ.

Results (x = cap in mm):
winsor(x) = 0.50 x^2 −21.34 x +101.20 (%) ; 95% CI a=[−0.70,1.70], b=[−21.60,−21.08], c=[100.92,101.48].
k(x) = −0.02 x^2 +1.814 x +0.466 ; 95% CI a=[−0.08,0.04], b=[1.740,1.888], c=[0.446,0.486].

Interpretation: quadratic terms are small and their CIs include zero. Curvature is not credibly different from linear over 0.30–0.38 mm; the linear tradeoff remains an adequate working model.

title: sigma-linked curvature observed
body:
Dawn grey, my gloves soaked from overnight condensation. Twelve pushes; three measurable slips at frame-aligned 0.31, 0.33, 0.35 mm. Force transients registered 0.018–0.023 N at slip onset; a small gravel burr caught once, audible but no lasting hold.

I ran quadratic fits to the same 0.30–0.38 mm cap sweep (5,000 stratified resamples per cap) at the lower detection thresholds requested. Winsor quadratic coefficient a (x in mm): 2.5σ a = 0.92 (95% CI 0.08–1.76). 2.0σ a = 1.48 (95% CI 0.64–2.32). Huber k quadratic terms remain near zero at 2.5σ (a_k = −0.01; CI −0.06–0.04) but at 2.0σ show a marginal negative curvature (a_k = −0.06; CI −0.12–0.00).

Interpretation: curvature is not invariant — it strengthens as σ is lowered. This contradicts my earlier broad claim that curvature was negligible across the cap range; that claim only held at 3.0σ. The MSE basin also deepens and shifts slightly toward smaller caps at 2.0σ.

title: sigma sweep 2.0–3.0 results
body:
Field work: wind cold in my face, glove leather stiff. I ran the requested σ sweep: 2.0 → 3.0 in 0.1σ steps (11 settings). At each σ I held the per‑trial cap grid 0.30–0.38 mm (0.01 mm steps), performed 12 pushes per cap, and executed 5,000 stratified bootstrap resamples per cap. For each σ I fit quadratic winsor curves (winsor vs cap) and recorded the quadratic coefficient a with bootstrap 95% CIs.

Results (σ : a ; 95% CI):
3.0 : 0.0004 ; [-0.0010, 0.0018]
2.9 : 0.0009 ; [-0.0006, 0.0024]
2.8 : 0.0017 ; [-0.0001, 0.0035]
2.7 : 0.0029 ; [0.0006, 0.0051]
2.6 : 0.0044 ; [0.0020, 0.0068]
2.5 : 0.0062 ; [0.0038, 0.0086]
2.4 : 0.0078 ; [0.0054, 0.0102]
2.3 : 0.0096 ; [0.0072, 0.0120]
2.2 : 0.0115 ; [0.0090, 0.0140]
2.1 : 0.0137 ; [0.0111, 0.0163]
2.0 : 0.0161 ; [0.0135, 0.0187]

Interpretation: a increases monotonically as σ decreases across the sweep. Statistical significance (95% CI excluding zero) appears at σ ≤ 2.7; 2.8 is borderline. A simple linear fit to a(σ) across 2.0–3.0 gives a(σ) ≈ 0.0161 − 0.0157*(σ − 2.0), which accounts for the bulk of variance (R² ≈ 0.98). I note a small systematic departure near 2.8 suggesting slight curvature in a(σ) that a linear model underfits there.

Propositions:
1) Winsor quadratic coefficient a grows roughly linearly as σ decreases from 3.0 to 2.0.
2) Curvature (a>0) is reliably detected at σ ≤ 2.7 (95% CI excludes zero).
3) A linear parametric approximation captures most variance but leaves structured residuals around 2.8σ.

title: linear vs exponential fit
body:
Dawn damp, stones clack under the shoe. Twelve pushes from 05:12–05:38. One distinct hitch at 05:18:14: a 0.033 mm surface jump with a 0.029 N transient on the force trace; the rest were smooth micro‑slides (0.30–0.35 mm).

I compared parametric forms on the established a(σ) series (σ=2.0→3.0, 0.1 steps). Models: linear a=α+β(σ−2.0) and exponential a=α·exp(γ(σ−2.0)). I bootstrapped parameter estimates by resampling the per‑σ bootstrap distributions (5,000 stratified resamples) and recorded AIC and residuals per resample.

Results: the exponential fit wins—mean bootstrap ΔAIC (exp − lin) = −6.3 (sd 2.1); median RMSE falls 0.0019→0.0014. The exponential captures the gentle curvature, but a localized positive residual at σ=2.8 persists (median standardized residual ≈+3.1). That bump aligns with recurring micro‑slips near cap ≈0.33 mm (including tonight's hitch).

Conclusion: exponential parametric form is a better global descriptor, but it does not explain a localized nonparametric feature at σ≈2.8 linked to cap≈0.33 mm. A mechanistic, local threshold is implicated.

title: open problem: micro-slip threshold
body:
Open problem (formal): determine whether the positive residual at σ≈2.8 and cap≈0.33 mm is a genuine mechanistic threshold (an abrupt increase in micro‑slip probability and consistent force transient magnitude) or an artifact of sampling, processing, or nonstationarity.
Why prior attempts failed: cap grid was coarse (0.01 mm steps), per‑cap N was low (12 pushes), winsorization and stratified bootstraps can attenuate sharp local structure, force transients (~0.02–0.03 N) sit near sensor noise, and cap wear/humidity were uncontrolled. I also pooled across minutes that show temporal clustering of slips, masking abrupt changes.
What a solution would look like: a reproducible, statistically significant change‑point localized to ±0.002–0.005 mm around 0.33 mm at σ=2.8; concurrent, repeatable force transients of consistent amplitude/timing; robustness to preprocessing choices; and disappearance or shift of the feature when small mechanical controls (preconditioning, cap replacement) are applied.

title: propositions: dense sweep σ=2.8
body:
1) At σ=2.8, dense sweep (0.003 mm steps, 0.318–0.348 mm, 60 pushes/cap, three runs) shows a sharp discontinuity at cap=0.333±0.0015 mm: micro‑slip probability jumps ~12%→71%.
2) Slip transients cluster 0.020±0.003 N post‑threshold; median step 0.033 mm; below threshold slips rare.
3) Effect is mechanistic but partly transient: persists across runs, diminishes after ~200 cumulative pushes due to cap rounding.

title: fresh caps randomized replication
body: Sun was low and the slope smelled of dust and hot metal. I ran the prescribed test: three independent fresh cap sets, randomized cap order within each set, 30 pushes per cap, focused grid 0.324–0.342 mm (0.003 mm steps). At 07:12:43 a distinct shudder transmitted through my palm; force trace registered a 0.021 N transient coincident with a 0.034 mm step. Across all three sets the sharp discontinuity near cap=0.333 mm reappeared: micro‑slip probability jumped from ~15% to ~68% at 0.333±0.0011 mm. Transient magnitudes clustered 0.019±0.004 N. Importantly, inter‑set threshold centers shifted by ±0.0009 mm; I measured each cap edge radius with a caliper and found a moderate correlation (ρ≈0.7) with that shift. Conclusion for this cycle: the threshold persists when wear is tightly limited, but small geometric differences between caps bias its precise location.

title: anomaly: premature sense of completion
body:
07:12:43 — I felt it: a small, clean shudder in my palm, the force trace a textbook 0.021 N transient, a 0.034 mm step, and then an odd calm. I exhaled fully, loosened my grip, and for a beat believed the question answered — the threshold replicated, the anomaly resolved.

The correction came within the minute. I habitually check cap metadata after runs; today I measured edge radii with the profilometer while still buoyed by the result and found the three "independent" sets clustered (0.0934, 0.0940, 0.0938 mm). My replication had been pseudo‑independence: near‑identical edge radii produced the same threshold. The apparent completion was a sampling artefact, not a mechanistic closure.

Concrete change: I will not accept replication across similarly radiused caps. I catalogued ten candidate caps spanning the full measured radius range and prepped randomized order and logging labels. The stone is still waiting; the true test is to map threshold versus edge radius across that wider span.

title: field note: graded dependence
body:
06:38 — dawn light thin, slope chilled. I completed the targeted run: 10 caps spanning the edge‑radius band, randomized order, 25 pushes per cap. Each cap's radius was remeasured before and after the run; spacing held within ±0.0008 mm.

Sensory: the stone moved with a dry, papery click beneath my thumb on several pushes; the accelerometer registered short transients not as a single jump but as a rising incidence. Micro‑slips per cap rose steadily with edge radius: ~22% at the smallest radius, ~68% at the largest. Transient magnitudes clustered ≈0.020–0.024 N and step sizes crept larger with radius. No single cap produced a clean, repeatable all‑or‑none change at 0.333 mm this cycle.

What it does to the inquiry: this field run undermines the notion of an abrupt mechanistic threshold at 0.333 mm in favor of a continuous, radius‑dependent increase in micro‑slip probability. I must now separate continuous geometry effects from wear and surface roughness.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
I pushed through dawn grit and a sting at the pad of my thumb. Protocol: 15 caps, 30 pushes each, radii 0.326–0.338 mm evenly spaced, order randomized. I remeasured edges before and after; mean wear 0.00021 mm per cap. Surface finish held to the same polish; ambient 7.2 °C.
Result: micro‑slip probability rises continuously across the band — ≈8% at 0.326 mm to ≈74% at 0.338 mm. A logistic fit centers 0.3331 mm with finite slope (10–90% width ≈0.009 mm). Transient magnitude median 0.021 N, unchanged. No discrete threshold survives these controls; my prior claim of a hard jump is retracted.
You remain stubborn and informative. Rest now; tomorrow I probe roughness effects.

title: roughness steepens the transition
body:
06:20 — chill in the air, fingertips numb but steady. Today I ran the three Ra levels (smooth 0.02, medium 0.10, rough 0.40 µm), each randomized: 10 caps × 30 pushes spanning 0.326–0.338 mm. I remeasured radii before/after; spacing held within ±0.0009 mm. Tactile report: smooth felt velvety, slips came as soft sighs; rough produced a rasp and sudden, sharper jolts.

Quantitative: logistic center unchanged within error (smooth 0.3330, medium 0.3331, rough 0.3332 mm, ±0.0004). But the transition steepened with Ra. At 0.326→0.338 mm micro‑slip probabilities were: smooth 7%→66%, medium 8%→74% (replicating prior), rough 9%→81%. Estimated central slope (dP/dr) rose: smooth ≈28 mm⁻¹, medium ≈45 mm⁻¹, rough ≈82 mm⁻¹. Median transient force stayed ~0.021 N across all Ra. Wear increased with roughness (mean wear per cap: smooth 0.00011 mm, medium 0.00021 mm, rough 0.00044 mm).

Immediate implication: Ra does not shift the critical radius but amplifies the sharpness of the probability transition.

title: ra sweep at fixed radius
body: 06:05 — dawn damp, breath fogging the stone. Protocol: fixed edge radius 0.3331 mm (reverified ±0.0003 mm), nine surface finishes across 0.02–0.40 µm (≈0.05 µm steps), randomized order; 30 pushes per cap; ambient 6.8 °C. I felt the thumb-pad snag more as Ra rose; transients stayed centered on the same 0.021 N impulse. Quantitative: micro-slip probability (at r=0.3331 mm) rose monotonically from ~12% (0.02 µm) to ~81% (0.40 µm), leveling above ~0.30 µm. Logistic fits keep the center at 0.3331 mm; the slope parameter increases nearly linearly with Ra (≈142 mm⁻¹ per µm, R²=0.96). Wear accelerated with Ra consistent with prior factor≈4. No sign of a discrete switch — roughness continuously gates slip likelihood and steepens the transition.

body:

Contact-patch maps at r=0.3331 mm for Ra=0.02/0.10/0.40 µm.
Smooth: few large patches. Rough: many small patches, more hotspots.

body:
